field_strength_why: Short landing pages have no hall of fame, no awards body and no long-running named controls, and I found no prize or hall of fame specific to this format. What exists is the conversion-copywriting and CRO community of 2009 to 2016, which published split tests with numbers. Two people in it wrote landing-page copy themselves, tested it in public with stated lifts, and are named by their peers: Joanna Wiebe and Michael Aagaard. Their evidence is real but has limits. Nearly all of it is self-reported or written up from their own data. Much of it covers single elements (a headline, a button, a form heading) or home pages, not whole one-screen pages. Most of the pages survive only as screenshots inside case studies. The third-best evidence comes from a research lab (MECLABS / MarketingExperiments under Flint McGlaughlin), not from a writer. The best-documented SaaS page wins on record (Conversion Rate Experts for Moz and Crazy Egg, and the Highrise long-form test) came from making pages longer, so "short wins" is not settled even for SaaS.

candidates.name: Joanna Wiebe
candidates.role: Founder of Copyhackers. Conversion copywriter who writes SaaS and ecommerce landing and home page copy and publishes the tests. Unbounce calls her 'the original conversion copywriter'.

evidence.claim: Wrote four challengers to Crazy Egg's home page, whose control had already been optimized by Conversion Rate Experts. One beat it by 13%, called 'statistically confident' (no level stated). The winning headline was 'pulled verbatim from a simple, catchy phrase a handful of survey respondents had used'. 'The 3 subheads were created based on the top 3 answers to our survey question.' The page was a long-form hybrid home page, not a one-screen page.
Same Crazy Egg project: Hiten Shah hired her in summer 2013 to rewrite the home page, and one challenger 'beat the uber-strong control by a solid 13%'.

Dressipi sign-up page: changing the button from 'Sign up now' to 'Show me outfits I'll love' produced a '123.9% lift in clicks on that very button, with 100% confidence' (Optimizely, checked with two other calculators). The headline change alone (a headline 'written the way Dressipi prospects talk') trended about 15% but never reached confidence. The metric was clicks, not purchases.

Social Media Examiner's interview summary reports the same Dressipi result: '123.9% lift in clicks with 100% confidence with the new headline and button', with the button changed from 'Sign up now' to 'Show me outfits I'll love'.

SweatBlock home page: she wrote 'the top 800 or so pixels of the page using PAS' for a pain-aware reader. The PAS variation with a woman hero 'produced a paid lift of 49%, with 99% confidence' against a control that had itself won a 'statistically significant paid lift of 108%' in an earlier Copyhackers test. Her proof line was '4 million towelettes sold'.

Mad Mimi pricing page: a curiosity-gap variation got 'a lift of 927% in clicks to sign up for Gold', but 'curiosity clicks didn't lead to an increase in sign-ups for Gold plans'. She reports the failure openly.
Unbounce's webinar page (copyright 2014) describes her as 'the original conversion copywriter' and founder and CEO of Copy Hackers.
Featured twice in Oli Gardner's Unbounce roundup '10 Super Smart People Talk Copywriting for Conversion' (January 31, 2013), alongside Michael Aagaard and Peep Laja.

Her method for SaaS landing pages, from a podcast: research first, writing in the customers' language. Her go-to framework is Desire, Obstacle, Solution, with PAS the other. She tests thank-you-page survey answers (to 'What was going on in your life that brought you to blank?') as a first-person headline 'in quotation marks'. Demo CTAs should say exactly what the prospect will see.
'You should put your headline in the first person and in quotation marks.' Button copy also goes in first person.

Unbounce's summary of her conference talk (May 3, 2016): 'tests show your customers will actually love you for it' (about taking their words), and 'why you should test your headline and button copy together'.

Her own company's page calls her 'the inventor of conversion copywriting' and says she has 'personally sold, run and delivered more than $3,000,000 in copywriting projects'. This is a course sales page and is discounted.

signature_pieces.title: Crazy Egg home page challenger (Variation D), beat the Conversion Rate Experts control by 13%
Dressipi sign-up headline and button ('Show me outfits I'll love')
SweatBlock home page PAS hero, about the top 800 pixels

candidates.way_in: The headline is the customer's own sentence, taken word for word from survey answers, reviews or sales-call recordings. It is often in first person and in quotation marks, so the visitor reads what he already says about his problem or his wish. The subheads are the next most common answers. The button finishes the sentence 'I want to...' in his voice and pays off the headline ('Show me outfits I'll love', never 'Sign up now'). For a visitor who arrives in pain, she opens on the pain customers named most (PAS). Otherwise she uses Desire, Obstacle, Solution.
candidates.proof_shape: The proof is the customer's wording plus one hard count. Customer quotes carry the headline and subheads, then comes a single number where one exists ('4 million towelettes sold'), then testimonials taken from the research and placed beside the claim. A trial or demo CTA says exactly what he will see after the click. Every claim traces back to something a customer said, and the copy never connects dots the reader has to connect himself.
candidates.voice: Conversational and specific. She uses the prospect's own words and slang instead of marketing language, short lines, first person on the buttons and a little cheek. She uses no category jargon and does not make the reader do the work.
candidates.concerns: Her best-documented wins are on home pages (Crazy Egg was a long-form hybrid; SweatBlock is an ecommerce home page) and on single elements (a button, a headline), not on one-screen pages for product-aware visitors. Every figure comes from Copyhackers. The SweatBlock win opened problem-first (PAS), which the app's spec forbids for product-aware traffic; in her manner PAS is used only when the research says the visitor is pain-aware. A quoted first-person headline is a customer quote, so in this app it must come from a verbatim on file (a ledger row) and is never generated. Whole pages can be read only as screenshots, so an exemplar would have to be transcribed. Her recent public output is mostly teaching and courses, so weigh the case studies, not the courses.

candidates.name: Michael Aagaard
candidates.role: Danish conversion copywriter and CRO consultant. Founder of ContentVerve.com, Senior Conversion Optimizer at Unbounce from 2015, and instructor for landing page copywriting in CXL Institute's landing page optimization course.

evidence.claim: Saxo Bank forex free-trial PPC landing page, a 'split test that was done by Michael Aagaard'. The control did not mention the free trial 'until the second sub-headline'. The treatment clarified the value proposition with a clear headline and body copy, added a relevant photo and award badges, and reduced friction in navigation and CTAs. It raised conversion 'by almost 100%' (99.4% in the title) and cut cost per conversion by 48.2%. No confidence level was reported. Written up by Paul Cheney, MarketingExperiments, October 5, 2011.

At MarketingSherpa Email Summit 2013 (written up by David Kirkpatrick, who calls him a copywriter with ContentVerve): 'Start your free trial' to 'Start my free trial' gave a 90% lift in sign-ups. He has 'consistently seen lifts of 30% to 90%' across sites, but similar tests in Danish did not work. Moving the CTA well below the fold converted 304% higher at 98% confidence, with 'several other things going on in the treatment'.

His own Unbounce post (February 19, 2014): 'Order Information and Prices' to 'Get Information and Prices' gave a 14.79% conversion lift (sample not disclosed). His method is to draft with 'get' and finish with what the prospect gains. 'Order' conveys 'the intent of the marketer – not the desire of the prospect', and 'Join Now' and 'Sign Up' are 'straight-up orders'.
Oli Gardner's 2013 Unbounce roundup says Aagaard has conducted more than 250 A/B tests focused on copywriting and how copy affects conversions.
Unbounce AMA (November 30, 2015): 'founder of ContentVerve.com, international speaker and, as of this year, the Senior Conversion Optimizer at Unbounce.'

His CXL Institute lesson 'The 5 most important landing page copy elements' names headline (message match), benefits/features, credibility, the 'expectation manager' and the CTA. Headline formula: '(Do something difficult) in (short amount of time) without (problem)'. Expectation questions include 'When will you contact me? ... What is the price? Will I get spammed?' CTA formula: 'When I click the button, I'd like to: (get a free quote)'. The CTA should 'Focus on what you get - not what you part with'.
Unbounce (May 3, 2016) describes him as 'widely known as one of the most passionate and enthusiastic people in the CRO industry', speaking on six years of testing.
His current site describes him as 'Senior CRO Consultant with 15 years experience' and keynote speaker. It shows no case studies ('NEW WEBSITE COMING SOON!'); ContentVerve's archive is not online.

signature_pieces.title: Saxo Bank forex free-trial PPC landing page (control vs treatment)
'Start my free trial' CTA and CTA-placement tests (12 case studies in 30 minutes)
'Get Information and Prices' form headline and the 'get' exercise
Landing page copywriting part 2: The 5 most important landing page copy elements (CXL Institute lesson)

candidates.way_in: Message match, then the gain. The headline repeats the ad's offer and says what the visitor gets. He drafts it by writing 'Get...' and finishing with the gain, often in the shape 'do the hard thing in a short time without the problem'. The offer itself (the free trial) goes in the headline, never held back to the second subhead.
candidates.proof_shape: Credibility sits beside the ask: relevant facts and figures, award badges, a peer's testimonial and a short FAQ drawn from real questions. Then come 'expectation managers' at the button, answering who, what, when and how much: who will call and when, whether he will get spam, what it costs, what arrives first. Friction comes out of the form, and the CTA goes where the visitor has what he needs to decide. This is the closest fit of any candidate to the B2B demo variant.
candidates.voice: Plain and literal, written from the prospect's side of the deal ('get', never 'order'). Buttons are first person and finish 'When I click the button, I'd like to...' ('Start my free trial', 'Get a free quote', 'See plans & pricing'). No orders ('Submit', 'Sign up', 'Join now'). Clarity over wit.
candidates.concerns: Most of his evidence covers single elements (buttons, form headlines, CTA placement) and comes from his own talks. He says the 'my' vs 'your' lift did not hold in Danish. His +304% win for a CTA below the fold (with other changes) cuts against the spec's first CTA above the fold, though his lesson is to place the CTA by how much information the visitor needs, and for a simple product-aware offer that means above the fold. Very little of his copy can be read as a whole piece, and ContentVerve is offline, so an exemplar would have to be rebuilt from screenshots in third-party write-ups. Today he is known mainly as a speaker and coach.

candidates.name: Flint McGlaughlin (MECLABS Institute / MarketingExperiments)
candidates.role: Head of MECLABS Institute (MarketingExperiments, MarketingSherpa), credited as Editor-in-Chief of MarketingExperiments. A researcher and teacher whose lab published landing-page experiments and the Conversion Sequence Heuristic. A strategist, not the writer of the treatments.

evidence.claim: 'Clarity trumps persuasion' is his phrase (July 13, 2008 web clinic write-up). Lab tests reported there: on MarketingSherpa's membership barrier page, a feature matrix and a member testimonial raised sign-up from 1.12% to 1.97% (+75.89%). Co-BrandNews went from 3.9% to 6.6% in 30 days. A web-hosting table's figures are internally inconsistent.

MarketingExperiments 'Clarity Trumps Persuasion' (December 16, 2009; McGlaughlin credited as Editor-in-Chief and contributor) organizes the first seconds of a page around three questions: 'Where Am I?', 'What Can I Do Here?', 'Why Should I Do It?'. The 201% gain appears only in the subtitle.

January 6, 2010 write-up by Daniel Burstein: 'How changing the first seven seconds of user experience drove a 201% gain'. No baseline, metric or sample is given in the text, and the treatments are credited to 'our scientists'.

His value proposition components as summarized from his B2B Summit talk (Dan McDade, August 29, 2012): 'Appeal – I want it'; 'Exclusivity – I can't get the exact product or service elsewhere (the "only" factor)'; 'Clarity – I understand it/you (clarity trumps persuasion)'; 'Credibility – I believe in it/you (specific, quantifiable, verifiable)'. The summary also gives the same three seven-second questions.
The MECLABS Conversion Sequence Heuristic, described as a 'patented, repeatable methodology', diagnoses pages by 'Motivation, Value Proposition, Friction, Incentive and Anxiety'.

Book: 'The Marketer as Philosopher', '40 Brief Reflections on the Power of Your Value Proposition'. MECLABS calls itself 'the world's largest independent research program focused on understanding why customers say "yes."' (self-description; no experiment count given).

signature_pieces.title: Clarity Trumps Persuasion (web clinic write-up with MarketingSherpa barrier-page test)
Clarity Trumps Persuasion: Where Am I? What Can I Do Here? Why Should I Do It?
The Marketer as Philosopher: 40 Brief Reflections on the Power of Your Value Proposition

candidates.way_in: Orientation before persuasion. In the first seven seconds the headline and subhead answer 'Where am I?' and 'What can I do here?' in plain words, then 'Why should I do it?' as the one thing he cannot get elsewhere (exclusivity), said so he understands it at once. There is no hype and no clever line that delays understanding.
candidates.proof_shape: Specific, quantifiable, verifiable credibility attached to the exclusive claim: a feature comparison he can check, a named member's testimonial, a number with its source. Friction is cut (fewer fields, fewer steps). Anxiety is answered right at the point of action (privacy, cancellation, what happens next). An incentive is added only where the value cannot carry the click alone.
candidates.voice: Sober, exact and anti-hype. Every line answers the question the visitor has at that point on the page, in terms of value to the customer, not to the marketer. No adjectives doing the work of facts.
candidates.concerns: He did not write the treatments; MECLABS analysts did, and he is known for teaching. He qualifies only as a strategist whose structure (the conversion heuristic and the seven-second questions) became a reference for this format, and the spec already holds much of it. All figures are reported by the lab itself, and some write-ups are inconsistent or give only a headline number. His manner overlaps with Ogilvy's (the one specific fact, no adjectives) and Hopkins's (reason why) in the current set. If the owner wants only people who wrote their own pages, stop the list at two.

candidates.name: Jason Fried
candidates.role: Co-founder and CEO of 37signals (Basecamp, Highrise, HEY). Founder who says he writes the company's marketing sites himself.

evidence.claim: 'I still write all of our marketing sites, all the key pages.' 'The top five pages on the site (landing page, pricing page, features), that's me.'

His post 'Writing decisions: Headline tests on the Highrise signup page' (January 13, 2009): a version making the 30-day free trial the headline, with a subhead saying signup takes less than 60 seconds, gave 30% more clicks on Sign Up than the original 'Start a Highrise Account'. A testimonial version gave +7%. Run over 4,000 page views. The post does not say who wrote the variants.
Later Highrise tests were run by Jamie and Ryan Singer, not Fried: 'The long form page had a 37.5% increase in net signups compared to the original' across 42,000 visitors.

The short 'Person Page' (a big photo of a smiling customer and minimal copy) had a 47% increase in paid signups over the long form. Adding content back 'performed over 22% worse than the original design'.

Basecamp's home page today is long (roughly 2,000 to 3,000 words). It opens with a founder letter from Fried ('Tell me if this sounds about right.', 'Nothing fit. So we invented Basecamp.') under the headline 'Manage projects, coordinate teams, and master your company with Basecamp.'

signature_pieces.title: Highrise signup page headline test
Basecamp home page with founder letter

candidates.way_in: Either the offer stated flat ('30-day free trial', signup in under a minute), or a founder's note that names the mess the category has made in the reader's own day ('Tell me if this sounds about right') and then offers the product as the plain alternative.
candidates.proof_shape: Plain pricing, years in business, customer quotes and screenshots, and what the product deliberately does not do.
candidates.voice: Plainspoken first person ('we', 'I'), short declarative sentences, opinionated and a little wry, no jargon.
candidates.concerns: His pages are long home pages and letters, not one-screen pages. No tested result can be traced to copy he wrote: the 2009 post is his, but the authors of the variants are not named, and the larger Highrise tests were run by others. His recognition as a copywriter is anecdotal. He fits the long sales page, letter or pricing-page formats better than this one.

candidates.name: Oli Gardner
candidates.role: Unbounce co-founder and landing page teacher and speaker. Says he coined 'attention ratio'.

evidence.claim: In a 2016 Unbounce interview he says he coined 'attention ratio' while answering comments in the Landing Page Conversion Course. His audit criteria include 'How well do the page match the ad', and he estimates '98 percent of them didn't do it right' (an estimate, not a test). Dan Levy says Oli 'had a hand in all of our content and all of our campaigns' early on.
He curated the 2013 Unbounce roundup that named Aagaard, Wiebe and Laja as the people to read on conversion copy.

candidates.way_in: Message match: the headline repeats the ad's words, and the page has one goal (an attention ratio of 1:1).
candidates.proof_shape: Design-led (directional cues, one focal action). No copy-specific proof shape documented.
candidates.voice: No distinct copy voice documented.
candidates.concerns: He is famous for teaching, and I found no documented results for copy he wrote. His two principles (headline matched to the ad, one destination) are already in the spec. Not a persona.

candidates.name: Peep Laja
candidates.role: Founder of CXL (ConversionXL) and Wynter. CRO researcher and teacher.

evidence.claim: The 2013 Unbounce roundup says he studied 500 headlines from successful online businesses (research, not a split test).
A Substack post claims Crazy Egg hired Laja and saw a 64% lift. This is unverified and probably a mix-up: the documented page work at Crazy Egg is credited to Conversion Rate Experts and Copyhackers.

candidates.way_in: No distinct writing move documented. His teaching is a clear value proposition led by research.
candidates.proof_shape: Not documented for his own copy.
candidates.voice: Not documented for his own copy.
candidates.concerns: A teacher and strategist with no verified result for copy he wrote. Wynter's message tests measure clarity and appeal, not conversion. Not a persona.

candidates.name: Talia Wolf
candidates.role: Founder of GetUplift, a CRO strategist known for 'emotional targeting'.

evidence.claim: CXL (Pablo García, November 2, 2023): after GetUplift's customer research and 'emotional story' across the site, 'After a 3-week test, POWERUP Toys' new homepage led to a 96% increase in sales (from 0.57% to 1.12%)'. Overall site conversion rose 57.75% in 2 months. Who wrote the copy is not stated.
A webinar recap says adding emotional copy to a 3,000-word landing page raised signups 41% and revenue 15% (not read at source).

signature_pieces.title: POWERUP Toys home page (emotional storytelling)

candidates.way_in: Opens on the feeling the buyer wants, as found in customer research, carried by user-generated images.
candidates.proof_shape: Customer stories and user-generated visuals.
candidates.voice: Warm and emotional.
candidates.concerns: Her evidence is ecommerce home pages and a 3,000-word page, not short product-aware SaaS pages. The figures come from her agency through second-hand write-ups, and she is a strategist with an agency. Her emotion-first move is close to Collier's in the current set.

candidates.name: Conversion Rate Experts (agency)
candidates.role: UK CRO agency whose pages are written by its team. The case-study pages name no individual writer.

evidence.claim: Moz PRO: 'Using a statistically significant sample of more than 5,000 visitors, we achieved a 52% increase in sales.' 'Our page was six times longer than the control.' Offer: 'a 30-day full-featured membership for just $1'. 'Within the first four months of work, we increased annual revenues by $1 million.'
Crazy Egg home page: 'The redesigned page is about 20 times as long as the control.' 'Our new page outperformed the control by 30%.' The 363% figure appears only in the title.

signature_pieces.title: Moz PRO landing page ($1 trial)
Crazy Egg home page (20x control length)

candidates.way_in: Answers the visitor's questions, found through surveys, in the order he asks them.
candidates.proof_shape: Objections answered one by one, with testimonials and demonstration, plus a low-risk trial offer.
candidates.voice: Not distinctive; the pages are team-written.
candidates.concerns: Their documented wins came from making pages much longer, so they belong with the long sales page or SaaS home page formats, not this one. They are useful as a warning that for considered SaaS purchases short does not always win. The pages are written by a team with no named writer.

top_picks.name: Joanna Wiebe
top_picks.why: She is the only practitioner with several attributed, self-written, publicly tested rewrites of landing and home page copy: Crazy Egg +13% over a control Conversion Rate Experts had already optimized, Dressipi's button +123.9% clicks, SweatBlock +49% paid conversions at 99% confidence. Peers recognize her (Unbounce: 'the original conversion copywriter'). She has a manner no current master has: the customer's own sentence as the headline, the subheads taken from the top survey answers, and a first-person button that completes the headline. Caveat: all figures come from Copyhackers, the wins are mostly on home pages and single elements, and in this app her quoted headline must come from a verbatim on file.

top_picks.name: Michael Aagaard
top_picks.why: He wrote and tested landing-page copy at volume (250+ copy tests by his count). His Saxo Bank free-trial PPC page roughly doubled conversions and cut cost per conversion 48.2% (written up by MarketingExperiments), and his CTA tests ('Start my free trial', 'Get Information and Prices') are among the most cited in the field. He taught landing page copy for CXL Institute and was Unbounce's Senior Conversion Optimizer. His manner is distinct and fits this format and its B2B demo variant closely: message match, a headline built from what the visitor gets, and 'expectation managers' at the button saying who, when, what it costs and what arrives first. Caveat: most evidence is element-level and self-reported, and very little whole copy can be read.

top_picks.name: Flint McGlaughlin (MECLABS / MarketingExperiments)
top_picks.why: He is a strategist, not a writer, and ranks only on his lab's published landing-page experiments and on a structure the field adopted: 'clarity trumps persuasion', the seven-second questions (Where am I? What can I do here? Why should I do it?), and value proposition as appeal, exclusivity, clarity and specific, verifiable credibility, with friction and anxiety handled at the point of action. That gives a describable orientation-first manner. If the owner wants only people who wrote their own pages, the list for this format stops at two.

notes:
Research only; no repository file was changed. Read for context: /home/user/legiit-copy/supabase/functions/_shared/engine/formats/specs/landing_page_short.ts, /home/user/legiit-copy/docs/03-copy-research.md Section 5.2, /home/user/legiit-copy/docs/04-copy-standard.md Section 12, /home/user/legiit-copy/supabase/functions/_shared/engine/prompts/manners.ts.

How the picks fit the spec. Wiebe's manner matches the headline-in-his-words and button rules. In this app her quoted first-person headline has to come from a voice-of-customer verbatim on file, because the engine never generates a testimonial. With no verbatim on file, her way in falls back to the customer's plain words from research, unquoted. Aagaard's 'expectation managers' map directly onto the spec's 'what arrives first' at the first CTA and onto the B2B demo section (who calls, when, what it costs). McGlaughlin's seven-second questions map onto the headline, subhead and first-CTA trio, but overlap with Ogilvy (the one specific, no adjectives) and Hopkins (reason why) in the current set.

Conflicts to resolve before building. (1) Aagaard's +304% win for a CTA below the fold (with other changes) cuts against the spec's 'first CTA above the fold'. His own rule is to place the CTA by how much information the visitor needs, and for a simple product-aware offer that means above the fold. (2) Wiebe's SweatBlock win opened problem-first (PAS), which the spec bans for product-aware traffic. Use PAS in her manner only when research marks the visitor as pain-aware. (3) The best-documented SaaS page tests favour longer pages: Conversion Rate Experts' Moz page was six times longer than the control (+52% sales, n>5,000), their Crazy Egg page about 20 times longer (+30%), and Highrise's long form gained +37.5%. Highrise's later short 'person page' then beat the long form by 47% in paid signups. Length is unsettled, and the 150-600 / 300-750 word band is a choice, not a finding.

Exemplar availability. None of the three has a whole short landing page readable as text. Their pages survive as screenshots inside case studies (Copyhackers, MarketingExperiments), so an exemplar would need transcription and a rights check. Aagaard's ContentVerve archive is offline, and web.archive.org could not be reached from here.

Not in the set and not adjacent: none of the candidates is Halbert, Carlton, Hopkins, Schwartz, Bencivenga, Sugarman, Ogilvy, Caples or Collier. Schwartz's most-aware rule (lead with the offer) and Caples's tested headline already cover parts of this format.

Discounted or unverified: a Substack claim that Peep Laja lifted Crazy Egg 64% (not supported by any primary source). Copyhackers' 'inventor of conversion copywriting' (a self-claim on a course page). Third-party roundups citing '307% headline' and similar lifts with no traceable test. Searches for published, attributable results by SaaS conversion copywriters Joel Klettke, Lianna Patch and Momoko Price found none. Harry Dry and Julian Shapiro are known for teaching and curating landing-page copy and were not assessed in depth. Neither Wiebe nor Aagaard has an industry award I could find, so peer recognition rests on Unbounce, CXL and MarketingSherpa naming them.

field_strength_why: The long-form promotion is the home format of direct response's best-documented writers. Peers who ran the biggest mailers name the same few people as the best at it: Kurtz at Boardroom on Rutz and Bencivenga, Bencivenga on Makepeace, Bly on Bonner, Makepeace and Masterson. The format also has named controls with stated run lengths: International Living (Bonner, 25 years), the WSJ letter (Conroy, 1975 to 2003) and Newsweek (McLean, unbeaten for 15 years). The weak spot is the numbers. Almost none are audited. Most come from the writer himself (Makepeace) or from the client company or a company-linked trainer (Kurtz for Boardroom, AWAI for Agora). Several of the most famous letters with hard longevity records are also short subscription letters under this format's 3,000-word floor.

candidates.name: Clayton Makepeace
candidates.role: Freelance and royalty copywriter (1970s to 2020) for Weiss Research, Phillips Publishing, Blanchard, Security Rare Coin, Rodale and Agora. He wrote long letters and magalogs of up to 24 pages, usually signed by the client's expert (Martin Weiss, Dr. Julian Whitaker).

evidence.claim: In his own words (AWAI, 2005): his launch promotions for Phillips Publishing's Health and Healing 'mailed 90 million pieces in three years and sold over 2 million subscriptions.'

Gary Bencivenga, in an interview Makepeace conducted (about 2005; reprinted by Scott Martin), on the Health and Healing package: 'a grand slam World Series winning blast in the bottom of the ninth inning' that 'built that newsletter to astronomical heights.' On writers whose controls he would not want to compete against: 'there are about five or six writers who I would feel that way about, and you're certainly at the top of that list.'

Makepeace to Daniel Levis: 'Between 1998 and 2003, I didn't have a single bomb for Weiss Research... Every single one of my new packages beat my old controls.' He also says a testimonial headline 'out pulled my benefit-oriented headline by more than 50%.'

AWAI tribute page. Sandy Franks: 'I was about to hand out AWAI's first-ever Copywriter of the Year Award to a legend in our industry, Clayton Makepeace.' Bob Bly: 'Among copywriters, he was the best of us.' Brian Kurtz calls his controls 'legendary' and 'Monster hits, game-changers.' AWAI sold his training, so it is an interested source.
Bob Bly (AWAI, 2010) calls Bill Bonner 'one of the three greatest copywriters around today'. The article names Bly's other two greats as Michael Masterson and Clayton Makepeace.
Makepeace says he was 'running very long copy, up to 24-page sales letters.' With magalogs it became 'value-added copy that rewarded the reader for plowing through my 24 pages.'

Game of Conversions reports that Makepeace wrote in a 2006 issue of his Screaming Eagle newsletter that his copy had brought in 'more than 3 million new customers and over $1 billion in sales.' The same site has line-by-line breakdowns of six of his promotions.

signature_pieces.title: Health and Healing launch magalog, 'Give me 90 days and I'll help you...' (Dr. Julian Whitaker, Phillips Publishing)
signature_pieces.year: Not stated in the sources read (the newsletter's launch)
signature_pieces.where_to_read: Free breakdown with long excerpts at https://gameofconversions.com/clayton-makepeace-health-and-healing/. The full annotated piece is in Game of Conversions' paid swipe library.

signature_pieces.title: 'Shameless Two-Faced SOBs!' (Weiss Safe Money magalog)
signature_pieces.year: Early 2000s (the copy promises gains in 2004 to 2005)

signature_pieces.title: 'Invest Without Fear' (Weiss magalog) and 'The 23-Cent Lifesaver' (supplement magalog)
signature_pieces.year: 2004 for Invest Without Fear; the other is undated
signature_pieces.where_to_read: Breakdowns indexed at https://gameofconversions.com/clayton-makepeace-sales-letters/. The full promotions are in paid swipe files.

candidates.way_in: He starts from the feeling the reader already has and turns it up. A headline complex names it with famous specifics ('Shameless two-faced SOBs! While urging you to buy their shares, top executives at Microsoft, Cisco... are quietly dumping billions'). Then a letter from the expert follows, either as a renegade proclamation ('I have never been more confident of any stock market forecast I've ever made') or as a plain trade ('Give me 90 days and I'll help you:' then five benefits running from everyday aches to the big fears). The lead type is proclamation or promise.
candidates.proof_shape: Proof follows every claim: promise, proof, promise, proof all the way down. A forecast is followed at once by the expert's dated calls with their dollar sizes. Numbers are made into pictures ('23 cents'). Testimonials and trades are retold as small stories. Real, usable content (tips, a quiz, 'five facts your doctor can't tell you') proves the product before the price. One everyday analogy carries the mechanism (diesel in a gas car). The last objections ('7 health lies') are answered right beside a stacked offer of free reports with stated values and a large guarantee.
candidates.voice: Hot and vivid on top of a tightly reasoned case. Levis calls it 'hair-on-fire emotion' plus 'meticulous, thoroughly reasoned argument.' Strong verbs ('whacked', 'ripped', 'naked and alone'). The expert speaks in first person and conversationally ('I'm concerned, no, make that worried'). Sentences stay short, with a long one where the fear or the hope needs room.
candidates.concerns: Almost every result is his own claim or comes from AWAI, which sold his courses. Bencivenga's praise is the strongest independent support. His best pieces are 16 to 24 page magalogs, past the 8,000-word band, so the persona must carry the move, not the length. The manner leans on fear, a named enemy and a hand-picked track record. In this app those proofs work only when the ledger holds the calls, counts and studies; with none on file, the move has to fall back to the product's own run. No free archive of whole pieces was found (Scott Martin says his blog went offline after his death in 2020), so an exemplar means buying a paid swipe and checking rights. He is already named in the writer's prompt.

notes:
New personas for this format, in order: Makepeace, then Rutz, then Bill Bonner. Bonner is the closest call. On the weighted criteria he sits just below Rutz, because his peer support (Bly, AWAI) is thinner and he rests on one letter. But his International Living letter (25-year control per AWAI; about 3,221 words; signed by one person; 'Dear Reader') is the best freely readable whole exemplar of exactly this spec's form and length. His way in (indirection: a sensory second-person scene with no product, then 'But this paradise is real. And affordable.' and prices as proof) duplicates no current manner. If the owner wants three new names, add Bonner. If he wants only the best-evidenced, add Makepeace and Rutz.

Already covered: Bencivenga and Halbert are in the set and are among the format's acknowledged masters. Schwartz, Carlton and Collier also wrote in it.

Format caveats:
- The letters with the hardest longevity records are short subscription letters below this format's 3,000-word floor: Conroy's WSJ letter (775 words, 1975 to 2003), McLean's Newsweek letter (unbeaten for 15 years), and Jayme's magazine packages. They are masters of the short direct mail letter, not the long-form argument, so they are not ranked here. They would fit a short-letter format if the app ever adds one.
- Makepeace's and Rutz's signature pieces are magalogs (16 to 52 pages, mostly editorial content). The persona should carry their move into the spec's one-person letter, not their length or magazine dress.
- Mel Martin (company-reported: Book of Secrets, 20 million names, 500,000 copies, about $20 million) is a master of fascinations, not of the argued letter. He suits a bullets layer better than a sales-letter persona.

Evidence quality: no figure here is audited. Makepeace's numbers are his own. Rutz's and Mel Martin's come from the client's executive (Kurtz), who also sells Rutz's archive. Bonner's and Palmer's come from AWAI, which is commercially tied to Agora and sold Makepeace's training.

Not ranked:
- Known mainly for teaching: Michael Masterson (Mark Ford; in Bly's top three), Dan Kennedy, Bob Bly.
- Self-reported only: Evaldo Albuquerque.
- Result is a video, better judged under the VSL formats: Mike Palmer ('End of America').
- Strong reputations but little public copy, so no describable manner: Makepeace's and Rutz's protégés (Parris Lampropoulos, David Deutsch, Kim Krause Schwalm, Carline Anglade-Cole).

Exemplars and rights: the persona needs a whole piece to study. Bonner's letter is free at swiped.co (later web revision; Agora's copyright). Makepeace's and Rutz's whole pieces are only in paid libraries: Game of Conversions' swipe library, Kurtz's 208-promotion 'Lost Files' USB ($295), and the Tax Hotline package in the Overdeliver swipe file. Rights need checking before any enter the teaching library, and per CLAUDE.md they are studied, never reproduced.

App fit: Makepeace's and Rutz's proof moves (the expert's dated track record, compounding arithmetic, counts) work only with ledger rows. The enemy-naming and fear in their health and financial pieces will draw compliance flags in factual review; that is the user's decision, never a softening by the engine.

Suggested lead types: Makepeace proclamation or promise; Rutz secret (indirect feature); Bonner story (indirect scene).

No repository files were changed. Scratch extracts are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-legiit-copy/bdc51b44-f382-51f2-84bb-7be84d74cd99/scratchpad (il/il.txt is the International Living letter text).

field_strength_why: This format has no recognized masters, not in the way Halbert or Bencivenga are masters of the sales letter. No award (AWAI, Caples, Effie, DMA) has a category for opt-in pages, no hall of fame names anyone for them, and every result I found was either self-reported or the practitioner's own data repeated by someone else. Three people have credible evidence. Aagaard is a tester who published controlled split tests with numbers on sign-up, newsletter and e-book opt-in pages. Jackson is credited by peers as the originator: his 'one decision webpage' (about 1997) is called the first opt-in page, and he reports a 68% page. Pagan's Double Your Dating opt-in, built with Jackson, is the format's best-known long-running control: a swipe archive dates it 2001 to about 2009, and Brunson's book says it was 'the foundation for Eben's entire company'. The most-cited pieces can only be seen as screenshots or as the practitioner's own description, not read as text.

candidates.name: Michael Aagaard
candidates.role: Conversion copywriter and CRO specialist who ran ContentVerve. He wrote and split-tested sign-up, newsletter and e-book opt-in copy for clients and for his own pages, and published the results (ContentVerve, Unbounce blog, MarketingSherpa Email Summit 2013).

evidence.claim: Unbounce post by Aagaard, 16 Oct 2013. On Bettingexpert.com's sign-up form (a client), adding '100% privacy – We will never spam you' cut sign-ups 18.70%. After three follow-up tests, 'We guarantee 100% privacy. Your information will not be shared.' raised sign-ups 19.47%. On his own free CRO e-book page, '100% privacy – I will never spam you!' against 'I guarantee 100% privacy.' gave 24% fewer downloads. No sample sizes or confidence are given.

CXL credits the privacy tests to Content Verve, 'the company he runs': '100% privacy—we will never spam you!' reduced conversions 18.70% 'at a statistical significance of 96%'. The positive wording 'increased their signups by 19.47%'.

Aagaard's ContentVerve post (republished 19 Jun 2013, 'originally appeared on ContentVerve.com'). Adding a few bullets that say what the free updates contain lifted newsletter sign-ups 83.75%. A benefit-focused headline and button on Bettingexpert's sign-up form lifted sign-ups 31.54%. An earlier valuable-sounding but less relevant headline cut them 12.45%. His rule: frame the headline around what the prospect gets, starting with 'Get'. No samples given.

MarketingExperiments write-up of his MarketingSherpa Email Summit 2013 talk: changing 'Start your free trial' to 'Start my free trial' 'resulted in a 90% lift in sign-ups'. He has 'consistently seen lifts of 30% to 90%' from this change across sites, but in Danish it 'doesn't seem to work'. This is a trial sign-up, a format next to opt-in.

Unbounce post by Aagaard, 19 Feb 2014: changing the button 'Order Information and Prices' to 'Get Information and Prices' gave a 14.79% lift. On a betting-forum landing page, a 'Get' headline 'significantly outperformed a vague question headline' (no figure given).

signature_pieces.title: How to Write High-Converting Sign-Up Form Copy (With Case Studies & Examples)
signature_pieces.where_to_read: Originally on ContentVerve.com; republished at https://www.duncanjonesnz.com/michael-aagaard-how-to-write-high-converting-sign-up-form-copy/ (variants shown as screenshots)

signature_pieces.title: Bettingexpert.com sign-up form and his own free CRO e-book page, privacy-line tests (in 'How Failed A/B Tests Can Increase Conversion Rates')
Get Prospects to Say 'Yes' With This Simple Landing Page Copy Hack

candidates.way_in: Open on the word 'Get' followed by the thing he walks away with, in his terms, never the act of joining: 'Get [the specific free thing] that [does the job he wants done]'. If what he receives is generic (updates, a newsletter), the next line says exactly what arrives. No question headline, and never 'Subscribe', 'Sign up' or 'Join now'.
candidates.proof_shape: Clarity stands in for proof. Two to four plain bullets say what the free thing or the emails contain; in his ContentVerve test, adding such bullets lifted sign-ups 83.75%. Beside the field, reassurance appears only if it is worded without the fear word ('spam' lost in both of his tests). The button repeats the gain in the first person ('Get my...', 'Start my...'). There are no testimonials and no tease; the page is settled by testing, not by argument.
candidates.voice: Literal, benefit-first and plain, with short words. The headline is in the second person and the button in the first. No wit and no curiosity gap: every line answers either 'what do I get' or 'what does it cost me'.
candidates.concerns: Every figure is his own, mostly without sample sizes; only CXL gives a significance level, for one test. He tested elements (headline, button, privacy line, bullets) rather than whole pages, so this persona is more a method than a voice. It sits close to what the app's opt-in spec already does (first-person button, bullets that say what is inside, no 'spam'), so it may add little variety. His winning positive privacy line contradicts the spec's ban on any privacy promise. The my/your lift did not replicate in Danish.

candidates.name: Dean Jackson
candidates.role: Real estate marketer turned direct response strategist and co-host of I Love Marketing. Around 1997 he built what he called a 'one decision webpage' for a real estate site, and peers credit it as the first opt-in (squeeze) page. He helped set up Eben Pagan's Double Your Dating opt-in.

evidence.claim: I Love Marketing episode 1. Joe Polish says Dean is known as 'the first person to ever use an opt-in page using online marketing'. Dean says he was 'the first person that I know of that was doing it' and dates it to 'like 1997 I think', for livinginwinterhaven.com. The page mirrored 'the table of contents page of Cosmo magazine', with teasers reading 'free inside, more inside, free inside' and an opt-in that said 'get free instant access', with name and email the only option.

Same episode, on the Double Your Dating opt-in: 'When we set up [Eben's] opt-in page for Double Your Dating... the copy that we setup then is almost identical to the copy that they still use today'. They tested by letting '200 people come to the site' and counting opt-ins. A version that fits on one screen 'gets a slightly better conversion rate' (no figures).

Listbuilding Lifestyle Show transcript: his Email Mastery book page gets '68% opt in from cold magazine traffic' from full-page Success Magazine ads. The page adds no new information and works 'like a placeholder', confirming the visitor is in the right place. He says his Cosmo-style version 'became the standard'. The 'first' claim is the host's, not Dean's.
The I Love Marketing episode 311 summary lists 'The Landing Page Origin Story: How (and why) Dean created the squeeze page'.

Live Email Mastery page (emailmastery.com redirects here): 'Email Mastery Book' / 'An Amazing 9-Word Email That Revives Dead Leads...' / 'PLUS: get winning subject lines, sample 9-word emails, and word-for-word campaigns you can copy to reconnect, revive, and convert more leads!' / Name, Email / 'Download Now!'
Miles Beckler says Dean Jackson's opt-in page 'converts over 60%'. He gives no source.

signature_pieces.title: livinginwinterhaven.com opt-in page (Cosmo table-of-contents layout, 'free inside' teasers, 'get free instant access')
signature_pieces.where_to_read: Not published; described in his own words in I Love Marketing episode 1, https://ilovemarketing.com/episode-001/

signature_pieces.title: Email Mastery book opt-in page (68% from cold magazine traffic, self-reported)
Double Your Dating opt-in page (with Eben Pagan)

candidates.way_in: The page is the cover of the free thing. The headline is its title, said as a name ('Email Mastery Book'). Under it comes one cover line that names the mechanism inside as what it does for him, ending in an ellipsis ('An Amazing 9-Word Email That Revives Dead Leads...'). It repeats the ad or link that sent him, word for word where possible, so he knows he is in the right place. The page itself does not argue.
candidates.proof_shape: The contents are the proof. In the short version, one 'PLUS:' line stacks the concrete extras (winning subject lines, sample emails, word-for-word campaigns you can copy). In the long version, five or six cover-line teasers are laid out like a magazine table of contents, each tagged 'free inside', followed by a single opt-in for 'free instant access'. There are no testimonials, no counts and no bio, and the page offers exactly one decision.
candidates.voice: A friendly showman writing in cover-line fragments ('An Amazing...', 'PLUS:', 'free inside'). Plain words and no pressure, with no sentences of persuasion. The reader is offered one choice, and the page reads like a magazine he already wants to open.
candidates.concerns: The claim that he was first comes from him and his own circle (his co-host Polish, his podcast host), with no independent date. The 68% is self-reported and depends on the ad pre-selling: it is cold magazine traffic that has just read a full-page ad. The original 1997 page cannot be read. His current page asks for name and email and says 'Download Now!', both against the spec. His doctrine that the page adds nothing leaves little copy to imitate unless the table-of-contents version is used. His teaching fame (I Love Marketing, the 9-word email) is larger than his published pages. He shares the Double Your Dating page with Pagan, so the two may be one persona.

candidates.name: Eben Pagan (David DeAngelo)
candidates.role: Founder of Double Your Dating, writing as David DeAngelo. A free newsletter and ebook opt-in page was the front of his business for most of the 2000s, and it was set up with Dean Jackson.

evidence.claim: Swiped.co swipe-file archive, 'Original Double Your Dating Lead Magnet from Eben Pagan (David DeAngelo)': the headline is 'You're About To Learn Secrets That Most Men Will Never Know About Women...'. The page was used 'starting in 2001 all the way to about 2009' and is tagged Control. The bullets and form appear only as screenshots.
Russell Brunson, DotCom Secrets (reader highlights of the book's text): 'This simple lead "squeeze" funnel was the foundation for Eben's entire company.'
Dean Jackson says he and Pagan set up the Double Your Dating opt-in together, and that its copy stayed 'almost identical' for years.

Miles Beckler describes the page as a 'red-colored headline with a hook,' 'six bullet points,' and 'an invitation and a call to action', and says it 'generated about $20,000,000'. He gives no source; other blogs give different figures.

signature_pieces.title: Double Your Dating free newsletter and ebook opt-in page ('You're About To Learn Secrets That Most Men Will Never Know About Women...')
signature_pieces.where_to_read: Screenshots at https://swiped.co/file/double-your-dating-lead-magnet-eben-pagan/ (the text is not transcribed anywhere I could reach)

candidates.way_in: Tell him what he is about to learn, and that most men like him never will: 'You're About To Learn Secrets That Most Men Will Never Know About Women...'. The headline names him by what he is missing, sets him apart from 'most men', and trails off into the bullets.
candidates.proof_shape: Six bullets, according to descriptions of the page (the text exists only in screenshots). Each is a situation he knows, with the counterintuitive answer withheld. Then comes a short invitation to the free newsletter and ebook and the call to action. The proof is how specific the bullets are and what the free content holds; the page carries no testimonials or counts.
candidates.voice: A confident insider talking to one man, in an older-brother tone. Contrarian and direct, in the second person, promising knowledge other men lack.
candidates.concerns: Authorship is shared with Dean Jackson (it is the same page lineage). The dates and the 'Control' tag come from a swipe archive, not from Pagan. Revenue figures are unsourced and conflict. The text exists only as screenshots, and web.archive.org could not be reached from here. Its central move (secrets most men will never know) runs against the spec's bans on 'the secret to' openers, curiosity lines with no result in them, and every bullet being a secret. The tone is tied to the dating niche.

candidates.name: Joanna Wiebe
candidates.role: Conversion copywriter and founder of Copyhackers. She writes and tests sign-up and opt-in copy, but her best-known work is SaaS landing pages.

evidence.claim: Social Media Examiner interview. On Dressipi's sign-up page, changing the button from 'Sign up now' to 'Show me outfits I'll love', together with a new headline, gave a 123.9% lift in clicks 'with 100% confidence'. Copyhackers' own opt-in, with choice-and-consequence messaging ('Yes, get the free guide' / 'No, I reject the persuasion guide'), took signups from about 50 a day to around 200 a day.
CXL cites her rule that 'your button copy should complete the sentence' 'I want to _______'. This is advice, not a test.

signature_pieces.title: Dressipi sign-up page headline and button test ('Show me outfits I'll love')
Copyhackers 'Free 2015 Persuasion Guide' opt-in and exit popup

candidates.way_in: A headline in the prospect's own words, lifted from reviews, surveys or interviews, that names the want the way he says it.
candidates.proof_shape: The button finishes 'I want to ___' with the result ('Show me outfits I'll love' instead of 'Sign up now'). The page proves itself by matching his words to the free thing; there are no testimonials.
candidates.voice: Conversational, specific and a little cheeky, in the second person with contractions.
candidates.concerns: Her opt-in results are self-reported, and the 123.9% figure is clicks, not sign-ups. Her reputation rests on SaaS pages, not opt-ins. The choice-and-consequence decline ('No, I reject the persuasion guide') is a guilt decline, which the spec forbids. Her 'I want to' button rule is already in the app's research (docs/03 Section 5.3).

candidates.name: Russell Brunson
candidates.role: ClickFunnels co-founder and funnel author (DotCom Secrets). A strategist whose squeeze-page teaching is widely copied; he writes his own pages.

evidence.claim: DotCom Secrets (reader highlights of the book's text): 'The more curiosity you can put into the headline, the more likely they will be to give you their email address'. 'My lead "squeeze" funnel pages are short and simple because I'm only asking for an email address'. With 'a reverse squeeze page, you'll get less leads, but they'll be more qualified because they watched your video'.

signature_pieces.title: DotCom Secrets, squeeze page and lead funnel chapter

candidates.way_in: A curiosity-loaded headline about the result, next to a picture of the free thing. In his 'reverse squeeze page', a short story video comes before the ask.
candidates.proof_shape: The perceived value of the lead magnet carries the page, with the story kept very short so it does not distract from the offer.
candidates.voice: Enthusiastic insider, leaning on hype and 'secrets'.
candidates.concerns: He is famous for teaching and software. I found no verified result for any opt-in page of his own (his 108 Split Test Winners book exists, but I did not read its squeeze-page tests). His curiosity-first headline runs against the spec's ban on 'a curiosity line with no result in it'. He qualifies as a strategist rather than as a master writer of this format.

candidates.name: Frank Kern
candidates.role: Internet marketing consultant and launch strategist who writes his own copy.

evidence.claim: Swipefile.com analysis of the Frank Kern email signup page (frankkern.com): it leads with outcomes rather than effort, uses an orange 'Yes, I want this' button, and previews the free content. No results are given.

In a Warrior Forum thread on a 'really simple' squeeze page Kern promoted, commenters said the page would probably not convert on its own and that the email copy was the stronger piece. I saw this only in a search summary and did not open the thread.

signature_pieces.title: frankkern.com email signup page
signature_pieces.year: c. 2017 screenshot (date of capture not stated)

candidates.way_in: Outcome over effort: a casual promise of the result without the work, next to his photo.
candidates.proof_shape: A preview of what is in the free lessons, plus his own persona; there are no counts.
candidates.voice: Laid-back, irreverent and first person, with a 'Yes, I want this' button.
candidates.concerns: I found no documented results for any of his opt-in pages. His reputation comes from launches, consulting letters and courses, not from this format.

candidates.name: Alex Cattoni
candidates.role: Founder of Copy Posse; copywriter and copy teacher.

evidence.claim: Her subject-line split-test report opt-in ('100 subject lines that drive more clicks and engagement') converted 79%: 3,528 sign-ups from 4,483 unique visitors. A newer variant 'shows an 85% conversion rate' but was not yet significant. The traffic source is not stated.

signature_pieces.where_to_read: https://copyposse.com/blog/two-high-converting-landing-pages-and-why-they-work/ (only the headline is in the text; the rest is images)

candidates.way_in: A number, the artifact and the outcome, all in the headline at once ('100 subject lines that drive more clicks and engagement').
candidates.proof_shape: An authority banner under the headline, then a breakdown of the contents and a short bio. The button for instant access sits above the fold and repeats at the end.
candidates.voice: Direct, upbeat and benefit-first.
candidates.concerns: A single page whose result is self-reported, almost certainly on her own warm audience. Her fame is mostly as a teacher. This page is already in the repo corpus (controls_other_formats-40).

candidates.name: Peep Laja (CXL)
candidates.role: Founder of the CRO agency CXL. A strategist who ran a published six-round optimization of an opt-in page; the copywriter is not named.

evidence.claim: CXL case study on TruckersReport: email opt-ins rose from 12.1% to 21.7% (+79.3%) over six rounds of tests. In the headline round, the control 'Get a truck driving job with better pay.' beat every challenger. The article describes the work as 'we' and names no copywriter. The winning page appears only as an image.

signature_pieces.title: TruckersReport opt-in page optimization

candidates.way_in: A plain imperative stating the outcome ('Get a truck driving job with better pay.').
candidates.proof_shape: Benefit bullets and form design, refined round by round through testing.
candidates.voice: Plain and functional.
candidates.concerns: The figures come from the agency's own report, and no writer is named. This is a strategist's process, not a writer's manner, so it cannot be a persona. The tests are already in the repo corpus (split_tests_pages-58 to -62).

candidates.name: John Caples
candidates.role: Copywriter (BBDO) and author of Tested Advertising Methods. The free-book coupon at the foot of his mail-order ads is the print ancestor that the app's opt-in spec names ('the masters' free-report coupons').

evidence.claim: A U.S. School of Music ad in Picture-Play (Sep 1928 to Feb 1929), the advertiser of Caples' 'They laughed when I sat down at the piano', carries the coupon 'Please send me your free book, "Music Lessons in Your Own Home"' (OCR text). This page's headline is not 'They laughed', so it shows the advertiser's coupon, not Caples' own copy.

signature_pieces.title: They Laughed When I Sat Down at the Piano (U.S. School of Music), coupon for a free book
signature_pieces.where_to_read: Magazine scans in the Media History Digital Library (lantern.mediahist.org); a clean transcription was not found

candidates.way_in: Not an opt-in page: the free book is offered in the coupon at the end of a full story ad that has already done the selling.
candidates.proof_shape: The ad's story and test results carry the proof; the coupon names the free book by its title.
candidates.voice: Caples' own voice, already defined in the app's manners.
candidates.concerns: He is already in the set and wrote no opt-in pages. The coupon is the last block of a long ad, not a standalone 60 to 250 word page. I did not verify his authorship of the piano ad at a source here.

top_picks.name: Michael Aagaard
top_picks.why: He has the most documented evidence in this exact format. He wrote and split-tested opt-in copy on sign-up forms, a newsletter and his own e-book page, and published the numbers: +83.75% from bullets that say what arrives, +31.54% from a benefit headline and button, and -18.70% and -24% from 'never spam' lines. CXL and MarketingExperiments repeated the results, one of them with significance. All the data is his own, and his manner is closer to a method than a voice, so as a persona he mostly reproduces what the app's current spec already does.

top_picks.name: Dean Jackson
top_picks.why: His peers credit him as the originator of the format: his 'one decision webpage' from about 1997 is called the first opt-in page, and he says his Cosmo table-of-contents layout 'became the standard'. He also set up the Double Your Dating opt-in, the format's best-known control, and reports 68% opt-in from cold magazine traffic on his current page. His manner (the page as the cover of the free thing, with 'free inside' teasers and 'free instant access') is the most distinct move the app does not have yet. Every result is self-reported, though, and little of his copy can be read.

top_picks.name: Eben Pagan (David DeAngelo)
top_picks.why: His Double Your Dating opt-in is the longest-running opt-in control I could document: a third-party swipe archive dates it 2001 to about 2009, and Brunson's book calls it the foundation of his company. Pagan co-wrote it with Dean Jackson, it can only be seen as screenshots, and its 'secrets most men will never know' move runs against several of the spec's bans. If the owner rules him out for those reasons, the next choice is Joanna Wiebe, whose in-format evidence is self-reported and secondary to her SaaS work.

notes:
Research only; no repository files were changed. I read supabase/functions/_shared/engine/formats/specs/optin.ts, docs/03-copy-research.md Section 5.3, docs/04-copy-standard.md (the opt-in paragraph and Section 12) and the repo corpus entries for opt-in pages.

1) The same page is behind two picks. Jackson and Pagan share the Double Your Dating opt-in. Jackson's own words describe the method; Pagan's page is the exemplar. If only one persona comes from that lineage, Jackson is the safer choice: he wrote his own pages, and his move does not depend on the 'secret' frame.

2) Evidence that bears on the spec. The spec bans any privacy promise near the form. Aagaard's tests show the word 'spam' hurting twice, but his positive line ('We guarantee 100% privacy. Your information will not be shared.') won by 19.47%. NextAfter experiment #4354 (Harvest Ministries devotional sign-up, June 2016, verified at https://www.nextafter.com/?p=12850) removed the line 'We take privacy seriously and hate spam, so we'll carefully protect your e-mail address.' Conversion fell from 27.1% to 18.1% (-33.3%, 99.1% confidence, n=682). So the evidence supports 'never use the word spam', not 'never reassure'. The owner may want to revisit that rule; I changed nothing.

3) Spec conflicts inside the candidates' manners:
- Jackson's live page asks for name and email and says 'Download Now!'.
- Pagan's frame is built on 'secrets'.
- Wiebe uses a guilt decline.
- Brunson uses curiosity-first headlines.
A persona built from any of them would need those moves translated into the spec's terms (email only, a first-person button naming the thing, a result in the headline).

4) Already in the set: Caples, through the free-book coupon the spec's lineage names. None of the nine current manners wrote opt-in pages.

5) Considered and set aside:
- Brian Dean's Backlinko 'content upgrade' (0.54% to 4.82%, self-reported): an in-post box, a different format, already in the corpus.
- Bryan Harris (Videofruit), Derek Halpern (Social Triggers), Noah Kagan (OkDork) and Neville Medhora (Kopywriting Kourse): their signup forms are analyzed on swipefile.com, but I found no in-format results, and their fame comes from teaching and blogging.
- Ben Settle: his opt-in is distinctive (full disclosure of daily emails and pitches) but undocumented.
- Leadpages templates: the company's, with no named writer.
- Perry Marshall: the page Mequoda reviewed (2006) is a sales letter, not an opt-in.
- Dan Kennedy: the GKIC 'free gift' offer is a long physical-package lead page, not a 60 to 250 word opt-in.
- Joe Polish: the consumer awareness guide is a print lead ad with no documented results.
- Harry's prelaunch page (100K+ emails in a week): a company and referral mechanic, not a writer's manner.

6) Sources I could not reach: web.archive.org (blocked here), so the Double Your Dating page text and Jackson's 1997 page could not be read. The Strategic Coach transcript where Polish dates the invention to 1997 returned 403, and so did one Social Media Examiner page. The 1997 date therefore rests on Jackson's own 'like 1997 I think' in I Love Marketing episode 1.

7) If the owner wants one new opt-in persona that changes the output, Jackson's cover and table-of-contents manner adds the most. Aagaard's would mostly confirm the spec as it stands.

field_strength_why: No copywriting masters are recognized for upsell (OTO) pages specifically. No award, hall of fame or Caples/AWAI category covers the format. I found no named control with a stated run time. Every result figure I found is self-reported or company-published by a founder or vendor (Brunson via Success magazine, Firestone via his own Zipify blog, Belcher and Georgi on their own sites). The person who codified the format is a funnel strategist (Brunson), not a copywriter known for controls. None of the nine current manners has documented upsell-page work. Sugarman only states the principle (sell more right after the first commitment) and describes doing it on the phone. Three practitioners have enough evidence and a describable manner to serve as personas. Their evidence is practitioner evidence, not master-level.

candidates.name: Russell Brunson
candidates.role: Funnel strategist, ClickFunnels co-founder, author of DotCom Secrets and The Funnel Hacker's Cookbook. He wrote the OTO script that became the format's standard structure.

evidence.claim: DotCom Secrets OTO script, in order: Confirm Initial Decision; Smart => Why; 3x 2x Question; Exclusive; Results, Fast, Speed; The One Thing; Future Pacing; CTA; Guarantee; Value Stacking; Scarcity; Second CTA; Testimonial Rush. The OTO video is 'usually... three to five minutes long' and closes 'price points from $97-$2,000'.

Book highlights: 'Wait! Your order is not yet complete'; 'Rule #1: Don't Sell More of the Same Thing.' 'Rule #2: Don't Sell a Random Product.'; three structures: 'The Next Thing', 'Do It Faster', 'Need Help?'; 'Getting the second yes is 80% offer structure and 20% script.'

'We use this script for the OTO on all of our offers (not just the Two-Step Funnel)... use this script for any upsell situation'; more of the same 'rarely works' because 'he has already scratched that itch'.
His first upsell: a $200 kit after a $37 potato-gun DVD. 'One out of three people who bought the DVD bought the $200 kit' (Brunson quoted by Success).

The Funnel Hacker's Cookbook (2017), OTO Recipe #1 wireframe: a progress bar 'Step 1: Create Account / Step 2: Customize Order / Step 3: Order Complete', headline, subheadline, video, 'YES! Add To My Order Now... Add to Order - Just $27', 'No Thanks, I Don't Need This Now'. It points to the Funnel Scripts 'OTO Need Help / Coaching / Done For You Service' and 'OTO Next Thing / Next Step' scripts.
ClickFunnels says 'a free digital copy is available for download' of the Cookbook.

A reviewer's notes on the OTO step: 'Confirm decision to limit buyer's remorse. Keep the loop open.' and 'Tell them about the ONE Thing that stands out in product. Can't explain everything. Future pace. Value stack. Testimonials.'

signature_pieces.title: The OTO Script (Funnel Scripts section of DotCom Secrets)
signature_pieces.where_to_read: DotCom Secrets (Hay House edition); reader highlights on Goodreads; summary at dansilvestre.com

signature_pieces.title: OTO Recipe #1: OTO Page, and Recipe #2: Downsell Page
signature_pieces.where_to_read: The Funnel Hacker's Cookbook, free digital copy via ClickFunnels

signature_pieces.title: Potato-gun DVD and $200 kit upsell (story)

candidates.way_in: He keeps the order open rather than closing it. A progress bar shows the buyer on step 2 of 3 ('Customize Order'), under 'Wait! Your order is not yet complete'. In the first beat he confirms the purchase and says why it was smart, so buyer's remorse never starts. Then he turns the result the buyer just bought into a speed or certainty question (the '3x 2x question': get it two or three times faster?). The add-on is always one of three things: the next thing the purchase now needs, a do-it-faster shortcut, or done-for-you help or coaching. Never more of the same, never something random. For this app, the question becomes a statement and 'Wait!' keeps its reason (the order is open).
candidates.proof_shape: 'The One Thing': he picks the single part of the add-on that produces the faster result and does not tour the rest ('Can't explain everything'). He future-paces the buyer reaching the goal with it. Then a value stack (often the most valuable part pulled out as a bonus), the guarantee, a reason to act now, a second CTA, and a closing run of testimonials. In this app the testimonials come only from the ledger, and the stack has no 'FREE' line on a part the price pays for.
candidates.voice: The founder talking to camera for three to five minutes: first person, upbeat coach, short plain sentences, with the CTA said twice. The page itself is a headline, a subheadline, the video and two buttons. The Yes button is in the buyer's voice ('YES! Add To My Order Now...'). The No is plain and says nothing about him ('No Thanks, I Don't Need This Now').
candidates.concerns: He is a strategist and teacher first. The script is a template he says his team uses 'on all of our offers', and who wrote each OTO page is not documented. The only results are self-reported (the 1-in-3 kit take rate and the '$97-$2,000' claim). The two-comma awards are his own company's, not independent. Several of his moves are banned by the app's spec and must be removed when adapting: the 'Exclusive' (not-for-everyone) beat as flattery, a scarcity reason that isn't real, a run of unledgered testimonials, and a question the page answers itself. His Rule #1 (never more of the same) is the opposite of Firestone's, Georgi's and Belcher's evidence for consumables, so use his manner for info and digital products.

candidates.name: Ezra Firestone
candidates.role: E-commerce founder (BOOM! by Cindy Joseph), Zipify CEO (maker of the OneClickUpsell Shopify app), Smart Marketer. He publishes split tests on his own post-purchase upsell offers.

evidence.claim: Byline Ezra Firestone, April 2, 2018: at BOOM!, '$1,000,000 of that has been generated by post-purchase upsells' (of $10,000,000 total revenue). The first upsell is 'more of what they just ordered'; 'always — always — make them a second upsell offer'. The Boom Clean launch had a '28% upsell conversion rate'. The post's unit counts do not reconcile.

Split test, Feb 12, 2020, byline Firestone. Control 'Add one more Trio to your order now and receive 21% off' converted 8.2% ($5.32 per visit). Challenger 'Add two more Trios...' converted 3.25% ($3.91 per visit). A fixed 4oz jar beat a 2/4/8oz size choice. Long-form vs short-form copy was 'a wash'. Sample sizes are not stated in the text.
Split test, Jan 6, 2021, byline Firestone: 'add another Boomstick Color to your order and get $6 off' converted 13.59%, vs 10.3% for '...get 15% off'.
Quoted by Foundr: 'you probably get a 20% take rate on that basket builder if it is relevant'.
Quoted by Zipify (2025): 'We offered 2 travel-size sprays + wipes post-purchase — 70% take rate. $10 offer, pure margin.'
Describes himself as 'the Founder of a $175 million Shopify store' (Zipify promotional page).

signature_pieces.title: Winners & Losers: Split Testing Upsells w/ Ezra Firestone, Episode 1 (Boomstick Trio)
Winning Upsell Split Test: Discounting Dollar Amount vs. Percentage
Lessons Learned From $1,000,000 In Upsells

candidates.way_in: The offer is the headline, given as one instruction in the buyer's next action: 'Add one more [the thing you just bought] to your order now and receive $X off.' There is no preamble and no bridge. For a consumable, the first offer is more of what he just ordered or its small companion (travel sizes, wipes, a refill). Only those who say yes see a second offer.
candidates.proof_shape: The product photo and the saving, stated as a dollar amount (dollar-off beat percent-off). One fixed quantity and one fixed size: a single unit beat a two-unit bundle, and a fixed jar beat a size choice. Short copy is enough, since adding a long-form section changed nothing. Small, cheap add-ons ($10) do the heavy lifting.
candidates.voice: Retail-plain: one or two sentences in the store's own voice, with the product named, the quantity, the dollar saving and 'to your order now'. No story and no persuasion beyond the offer. It reads like a store clerk's suggestion at the till.
candidates.concerns: Founder and vendor: he sells the upsell app, so his figures are both self-reported and promotional. Sample sizes are mostly not stated, and one post's unit counts do not add up. He says 'the design and copy we use on these pages', and who wrote the copy is unrecorded. His pages are tens of words, well under the app's 300-word floor. As a manner he fits the app's physical-product branch ('why more of the same at a discount is the next thing'), not info products. In this app a dollar saving needs a ledger row.

candidates.name: Perry Belcher
candidates.role: Internet marketer and offer strategist (perrybelcher.com). He documents his own post-purchase continuity upsells with a premium.

evidence.claim: On the American Gun Association membership sold 'on the back of our gun-related front ends': with 'no premium. We had a 7.7 % conversion' (also given as 7.5% of front-end buyers). After adding a Hoffman Richter knife as a premium: 'We went to a 23 % conversion'. With the knife customized 'with their name and the anniversary date they joined': 'we went to 32 %'.

On his video upsell: 'By the time I got down to close, I was only talking to 25.5% of the people... I ran them off, talking about what they were getting, not what they wanted. We got an immediate double in conversion rate when I pushed the close earlier.' And: 'The longer this becomes, the worse that I do.'
On timing: waiting until tomorrow to sell a tripwire buyer something else means 'our results would reduce by 90 percent.'
The post assumes, but does not show, that he is the same man as the marketer.

signature_pieces.title: American Gun Association membership upsell with the personalized knife premium (described in 'Tripwire Offer | 13+ Secrets to Creating an Irresistible Tripwire Offer')

candidates.way_in: He shows the offer the moment the first purchase lands, never the next day. He opens with the premium: a physical gift tied to who the buyer is, such as a limited-edition knife engraved with his name and the date he joined. The membership follows.
candidates.proof_shape: The premium carries the offer: it is shown, made personal, and made limited. Benefits are kept to a few lines, said as what the buyer wants rather than what he gets. The close comes right after the premium. His own viewer data showed most viewers gone by a late close, and moving the close up doubled conversion.
candidates.voice: A short spoken pitch on video by the seller himself. It is direct and conversational, gets to the close fast, and does no feature walk-through.
candidates.concerns: All figures are his own, from a page that reads like a transcribed talk, and the baseline appears twice as 7.7% and 7.5%. No page copy is reproduced verbatim, only his account of it. notes:
The format has no recognized copywriting masters, and I am saying so plainly. The best evidence comes from funnel strategists and e-commerce founders reporting their own numbers on their own sites. I found no independent controls, awards or halls of fame for this format. The three picks give three genuinely different manners, and each fits a different offer type.

1. Brunson suits info and digital products: the next thing, faster or done-for-you, never more of the same.
2. Firestone suits physical consumables: more of what was just bought at a dollar saving, in one line.
3. Belcher suits continuity offers: premium first, then an early close.

The app's spec already contains Brunson's skeleton and Firestone's physical-product branch, so the personas add voice and way in, not new structure.

Elements the app bans that must be dropped when adapting:
- Brunson's 'Exclusive' and testimonial-rush beats, his 3x/2x question (make it a statement), and 'FREE' bonus framing.
- Belcher's 'limited edition', unless the offer block holds it.
- Any stack value, dollar saving or buyer count without a ledger row.

Brunson's 'Wait! Your order is not yet complete' is close to the app's order-open line, provided the reason is stated.

Other people checked and not ranked:
- Justin Goff: Roy Furr says he has 'seen recently from Justin Goff' an upsell formula Furr traces to Halbert and Kennedy direct mail (breakthroughmarketingsecrets.com). The formula itself sits in a video I could not read, and none of Goff's upsell copy is public.

- Frank Kern, Ryan Deiss, Dan Kennedy, Clayton Makepeace, and Agora/Stansberry back-end writers: no documented upsell-page work found.

Two sources are weak. The Funnel Hacker's Cookbook text was read from a copy hosted on g2crowd.com; ClickFunnels separately confirms a free digital copy exists. The Brunson Goodreads pages are reader highlights of the book, not the book itself.

field_strength_why: This format has no recognized masters in the sense the existing manners have them. The checkbox bump as a named form comes from Russell Brunson's funnels: he says his company started it about 2010 to 2011 and shipped it as a ClickFunnels feature in April 2015. There is no award category for it, no hall of fame, no named control, and no published split test of bump copy by a named writer. Every figure in circulation is reported by a vendor (SamCart, JVZoo, Zipify) or by the seller himself (Brunson, consultants' clients). The people known for bumps are platform founders, strategists and teachers, not copywriters whose bumps get swiped and annotated. Across eight candidates, the only whole bump by a named practitioner that I could read in a published source is Brunson's "Conversion Krusher" bump, reproduced in DotCom Secrets (2015). Only he clears the bar, and he clears it as the strategist whose structure became the standard. He does not clear it as a copywriter whose bumps are known to be the best.

candidates.way_in: The box comes first, in the buyer's own yes: an arrow pointing at an unchecked box and "Yes, I'll Take It!" Under it, a caps label that frames the moment as a one-time deal ("ONE TIME OFFER:"), then a question that names the add-on by its product name and type ("Want our 'Conversion Krusher' Video Sales Letter template?"). The question is the pitch. Beyond its name and type, the thing is never explained.
candidates.proof_shape: No numbers, no testimonial, no story. One compressed sentence makes two claims, that it works and that it is easy ("It's proven to work and easy to install"), set off in bold underline. The rest of the case is the price made small against what he is already buying ("for just $37!"), an instruction to act ("Click YES to add this to your order now"), and a parenthetical saying the offer exists only here ("This offer not available at ANY other time or place"). Under this app's rules, the "proven" line needs a ledger row and the exclusivity line needs the offer block to state it.
candidates.voice: A seller at the front of the room, talking to one buyer: second person, exclamation marks, one word in caps for stress (ANY, YES), "just" before the price, underlines on the claim and on the scarcity line. Five short units in about 45 words: the yes line, the label with the question, the claim, the instruction with the price, the parenthetical. It is fast and makes no apology for selling.
candidates.concerns: Every figure is self-reported or company-reported, rounded, and inconsistent across his own sources: 34%, up to 40%, 33+% and 38%, and $37 and $47 in the same passage. He credits his team ("My team does a similar thing with our order-form bumps"), so he is best treated as the strategist whose structure became the format's standard, not a proven bump writer. The one readable exemplar breaks several of this app's rules: an unledgered proof claim ("proven to work"), scarcity that holds only if the offer block says so, a product label a cold reader would ask about ("Conversion Krusher"), and an opening question that order_bump.ts may flag as "a question the body answers itself". The app's spec already encodes his structure (Yes line with the thing and the price, two or three sentences, priced below the main item). A Brunson manner for this format would therefore change mostly the voice, not the shape. The DotCom Secrets copy I read is an archive.org upload of the 2015 Morgan James edition.
