notes:
Bottom line for the owner: this format has no recognized masters. I would not build a persona just for order bumps. If Brunson is added as a manner, it should be on the strength of other formats (the webinar research in docs/03 Section 5.10 already leans on Expert Secrets). Here his bump would serve as the commerce-family exemplar for this format. Rules that would apply to that exemplar: keep his shape (yes line with the thing and the price; a label; one sentence on what it does for the main purchase; the price made small; the only-here line only when the offer block says so), give the "proven" sentence a ledger row or cut it, and swap the product-name question for the plain name of the thing (rules 38 to 40). The current spec (order_bump.ts, docs/04 Section 9) already follows his structure in Ogilvy's plain voice. A Brunson manner would mostly add his voice: exclamations, a caps label, "just $X".

Verified at source today: the DotCom Secrets 2015 passages and Fig 11.12 (read from the archive.org PDF, text and rendered page), the ClickFunnels 2015 blog figures, SamCart's 30-40% and 20-40% lines quoted in docs/03 Section 5.5 (still on SamCart's guide, dated Mar 30, 2026), Julie Stoian's quotes on Teachable, John Ainsworth's quotes on Tropical MBA, the Jim Edwards episode description, Hormozi's classic-upsell definition, and Ezra Firestone's Zipify quotes.

Not verified: Brunson's naming claim (Goodreads did not render), Todd Brown's posts (they redirect to Facebook, and web.archive.org is blocked), and the 2014 Marketing in Your Car bump episode (the transcript pages did not load).

Two points the owner may want to decide:
- Pre-checked boxes. Todd Brown (unverified) and JVZoo (vendor help docs, seen in search results only) report higher take rates when the box is pre-checked. The app forbids pre-checking, and other sources flag consumer-protection and refund risk.
- Brunson's numbers are rounded and inconsistent across his own sources: $37 and $47 in one passage; 33+%, 34%, up to 40% and 38%. Treat them as his reports, not benchmarks.

Coverage gaps: the session's web-search cap (200 calls per turn, shared across agents) ran out before I could look for teardown screenshots of other book-funnel bumps (Hormozi, Myron Golden, Grant Cardone, Tony Robbins and Dean Graziosi), Agora or supplement order forms, and mail-order ancestors of the bump (Bob Stone's "deluxe alternative", gift-subscription lines on magazine order cards). field_strength_why: No hall of fame, award category or peer canon covers the order form as a format of its own. Whoever writes the letter writes the form, and the form is almost never credited, swiped or tested on its own. The numbers that are specific to this format come from CRO firms and UX researchers who test one element at a time: Aagaard's button, Conversion Rate Experts' guarantee, UIE's line at the account step. Those results describe rules, not one writer's manner. The mail-order writers who made memorable coupons and forms (Karbo, Kennedy, Halbert, Sugarman) have results only for the whole piece. Of those, only Karbo's figures were printed by a third party (Time, 1973). Calling anyone the master of this format would overstate the evidence. The picks below are the best evidence available, not recognized masters.

The guarantee is quoted at theessence.substack.com/p/the-secrets-behind-the-incredible, and the ad is widely reproduced in swipe files; this repo's corpus lists it as a control without its text.

candidates.way_in: The coupon talks in the reader's voice at his most skeptical. It concedes the doubt first, then names the thing and the terms in one breath, so the terms become the reason the doubt no longer matters. The coupon wording below is from memory and was NOT verified at a URL in this session: 'Joe, you may be full of beans, but what have I got to lose? Send me the Lazy Man's Way to Riches. But don't deposit my check or money order for 31 days...' To imitate it: the buyer speaks to the seller by first name, admits his doubt in his own slang, then lists the terms that make saying yes safe. This spec bars a question as the acceptance line, so the doubt has to be stated, not asked.
candidates.proof_shape: Risk reversal as a mechanism the buyer can check for himself. His own check is held uncashed (31 days in the ad, 'one month' in Time) and comes back uncashed in the return mail if he sends the material back. An accountant's sworn statement sits beside the money. The coupon carries no testimonial; the terms are the proof. Online, the equivalent is what is charged today and when, stated as a fact he can see on his card statement, plus the refund route in one sentence (never hidden continuity).
candidates.voice: Two voices kept apart. The coupon uses the buyer's plain, wry first person and calls the seller by first name. The guarantee uses the seller's flat, regular-guy first person ('I won't even cash your check'). Short words, no hype adjectives, money stated as a plain number.
candidates.concerns: Only one piece. The results are for the whole ad, not the coupon on its own, and Time's figures probably came from Karbo. The coupon's exact wording is not verified here. The original ad site was down. The question in the coupon conflicts with the spec's rule against a question in the acceptance line. Authorship rests on the standard attribution and on Time quoting the ad as his words. The uncashed-check device does not carry over literally to card checkout.

candidates.name: Dan Kennedy
candidates.role: Direct-response copywriter and info-marketer (Magnetic Marketing, GKIC). Author of The Ultimate Sales Letter and No B.S. Direct Marketing. Wrote order forms for his own products and seminar back-of-room sales.

evidence.claim: In No B.S. Direct Marketing (Entrepreneur excerpt), Kennedy writes that he took 'great pains to create order forms' for audiences and product tables. He says they 'mimic the best mail-order order forms in completeness and clarity' and credits them with 'consistently achieving exceptional results'. He reports 'selling more than $1 million of my resources from the stage per year, for more than 10 years running.'

In the same excerpt he reports that changing a 'Buy Now' button to 'Click This Button to Buy Now' produced 'a statistically meaningful increase' in conversions. He also writes that 'A lot of businesses don't even use order forms when they could and should.'
The Ultimate Sales Letter's 28-step 'Kennedy System' includes 'Step 13: Spark Immediate Action'. No step is titled for the order form.

signature_pieces.title: No B.S. Direct Marketing, discussion of the order form as a physical device
signature_pieces.year: 2006 (first edition; year not verified this session)
signature_pieces.where_to_read: Excerpt at entrepreneur.com/growing-a-business/why-giving-clear-instructions-can-increase-your-marketing/313316; the full text is in the book.

signature_pieces.title: The Ultimate Sales Letter, Step 13 'Spark Immediate Action'
signature_pieces.where_to_read: The book. Internet Archive copies are lending-restricted.

signature_pieces.title: Magnetic Marketing and GKIC seminar order forms
signature_pieces.where_to_read: Circulate in swipe files. No complete Kennedy order form was read at a URL in this session.

candidates.way_in: The form is written to sell on its own, because at the back of a room it is the only paper in the buyer's hand. It opens on the buyer's decision, then lays out every term he needs (what he gets, each payment choice, the price, the cutoff) with the 'completeness and clarity' of the best mail-order forms, in his words. The structure below is from memory of his forms and was NOT verified at a URL in this session: a 'YES! I want...' headline, then checkbox lines that each begin 'I understand that...' and restate one term as something the buyer affirms. To imitate it: turn each term of the deal into a sentence the buyer signs off on.
candidates.proof_shape: Completeness is the reassurance: he never has to ask about a term. The form states a reason to act now (his Step 13), and the guarantee is restated where he signs. Kennedy judges the form by orders taken, and reports a button-label test judged on conversions.
candidates.voice: A blunt, plainspoken businessman. Short declaratives, with checkboxes and numbered choices instead of paragraphs. No apology for the price.
candidates.concerns: All results are self-reported, and they cover stage selling rather than mail. Much of his fame comes from teaching. No complete Kennedy form was verified as readable online. The 'I understand' structure needs sourcing before it is built. His fast-action urgency habit could drift into the dateless urgency the spec forbids.

candidates.name: Michael Aagaard
candidates.role: Conversion copywriter and CRO practitioner (ContentVerve). Writes and split-tests the button and form copy at the point of action.

evidence.claim: MarketingExperiments (David Kirkpatrick, March 15, 2013) reported Aagaard's MarketingSherpa Email Summit 2013 talk. The control 'Start your free trial' lost to 'Start my free trial', which lifted sign-ups 90%. Aagaard: 'I've consistently seen lifts of 30% to 90% by simply changing the possessive determiner 'your' to 'my''. He also cautioned that similar tests in Danish did not seem to work.

Same article: copy at 'the last critical moment' should state the value and relevance of what the visitor gets rather than what he must give up, and the test should track the final conversion, not only the click.

signature_pieces.title: 'Start my free trial' vs 'Start your free trial' button test
signature_pieces.where_to_read: marketingexperiments.com/?p=12262 (secondhand report). His own site, contentverve.com, returned HTTP 503 when checked.

signature_pieces.title: How to Write Copy that Converts (Conversion Hotel keynote)

candidates.way_in: The button and the line nearest it are the buyer's own sentence naming what he gets: the literal action, then 'my', then the thing the click starts or sends ('Start my free trial', 'Send my kit').
candidates.proof_shape: Each element at the point of action is judged by the final conversion, never the click. Copy that states what the visitor gets beats copy about what he must give. Anything placed beside the button is there to remove the last doubt, and it is tested one variable at a time.
candidates.voice: Literal, short, first person, value first. No clever wording on the button.
candidates.concerns: Narrow: his work covers the button and nearby microcopy, not a whole order form. The 30-90% range is his own report, relayed by a reporter, and the sites are not named. The effect did not replicate in Danish. His own site was down. The spec already encodes his rule ('my' in the button, 'your' banned), so a persona adds little beyond that rule. I remember a test of his in which 'we will never spam you' lowered sign-ups (the spec bans that line), but I did not verify it this session.

top_picks.name: Joe Karbo
top_picks.why: His coupon and guarantee are the best-known order device in mail order, and he has the only third-party figures here (Time, 1973: 139,000 copies in six months, 10% returns), though they cover the whole ad. He is also the only candidate whose order device can be imitated end to end: the skeptic's concession as the acceptance line, the guarantee as something the buyer can check himself (his uncashed check comes back), and a sworn accountant's statement where the money changes hands. Caveats: one piece, the coupon wording is unverified, and its question form has to be recast for this spec.

top_picks.name: Dan Kennedy
top_picks.why: A working writer who wrote his own forms and argued for them in print, using the standard of the 'completeness and clarity' of the best mail-order forms. He reports more than $1 million a year for 10+ years of back-of-room sales on those forms, but that figure is self-reported, partly teaching fame, and no complete form of his was verified.

top_picks.name: Michael Aagaard
top_picks.why: He has the only published split tests in this format by a named person who wrote the copy himself: 'my' beat 'your' on the button, 90% in the reported case and 30-90% across his sites, judged on the final conversion. His manner is narrow (the button and the line beside it), and the spec already contains his rule.

notes:
1. Plain answer: this format has no recognized masters. Ranking candidates on the evidence, three deserve a slot, all with caveats. Halbert (in set) is the peer-named obsessive about order forms, by his own claim relayed by Kennedy, but none of his order-form copy could be read at source. Sugarman (in set) has a recognizable ordering paragraph, also unverified because the ad scans are images.

2. Design implication for the owner: the spec requires the form to restate the close in the close's words and add nothing. So most of a form's manner comes from the piece it closes. A persona can change only three things here: the acceptance line, the guarantee sentence, and the trust lines. A Karbo manner gives those three a distinct option: the skeptic's concession, risk the buyer can check, the seller's flat 'I'. A Kennedy manner would add term-by-term 'I understand that...' affirmations, but that structure is from memory and must be sourced before anything is built. Aagaard's and Conversion Rate Experts' findings are rules already in the spec, not separate voices.

3. No exemplar is ready to hand. None of the top three has a complete order form verified readable online this session. Karbo's ad is hosted at joekarbo.com, which returned 522 twice, and it circulates in swipe files. Building his exemplar means sourcing a scan of the ad and coupon.

4. Problems with existing repo citations, worth re-checking (I did not change any file):
- 'Christensen via Forde' ('I write the offer card before anything else') and 'Ingram via Bly' ('Add an offer summary box. Stress the deadline.') could not be found by search this session.
- The AWAI Carlton interview the corpus cites (awai.com/2003/05/john-carlton-reveals-his-secrets/) says nothing about order forms or price order. The 'highest-priced option first' quote in docs/03 Section 5.6 needs its own source URL.

5. Not finished: the session's shared web-search budget ran out partway through, so several leads could not be followed. These are unverified and unranked:
- Victor Schwab's coupon chapter in How to Write a Good Advertisement. Internet Archive copies are lending-restricted, and Schwab is described as a pioneer of keyed-coupon testing.
- Herschell Gordon Lewis's order-form rules (books restricted).
- Ted Nicholas on coupons.
- Walter Weintz's Reader's Digest tokens and Yes/No devices.
- Malcolm Decker's 'so simple an idiot can understand it', via Denny Hatch's 19-point checklist (expertclick redirected to a closed page).
- Mark Joyner's order-form redesign, credited in Maria Veloso's Web Copy That Sells with a 30%+ lift in orders (O'Reilly returned 403; seen only in a search snippet).
- Bill Jayme's subscription order cards.
Lois K. Geller's five order-form tips in Adweek were read: price and extra charges upfront, room for names and email, where to send it, a source code. They contain no results.

6. Possible next step: a follow-up turn with a fresh search budget could source the Karbo coupon scan, a complete Kennedy or GKIC order form, and Schwab's coupon chapter. Those are the three items that would firm up the picks.

field_strength_why: No individual copywriter is a recognized master of the thank-you page. The format has no awards category, no named control credited to a writer, and no tradition of swiped or annotated thank-you pages. The practitioner literature is vendor listicles (ClickFunnels, Unbounce, KickoffLabs) and one Copyhackers teardown (Wiebe, 2013), none of which names anyone as the best at it. The only commercial evidence specific to this format comes from two sources. The first is a company: Harry's 2013 prelaunch referral page, with figures reported by its co-founder and no named writer. The second is a testing lab: NextAfter's confirmation and instant-donation page experiments, reported by the lab with sample sizes and confidence levels. In those experiments the copy appears mostly as images and no writers are credited. The famous direct response names who are tied to the page after the opt-in (Deiss's tripwire, Brunson's OTO, Filsaime) have no thank-you evidence I could read at a source. Deiss's published $7 numbers were for an offer emailed to the list, not one made on a thank-you page.

candidates.name: Harry's prelaunch referral page (account by co-founder Jeff Raider; page writer not named)
candidates.role: DTC brand. The co-founder and co-CEO wrote the public account of the campaign. Whoever wrote the page copy is not named.

evidence.claim: The post 'was written by Jeff Raider, Co-Founder and Co-CEO of Harry's, with input from key members of the Harry's team'. It does not say who wrote or designed the prelaunch pages.

In a one-week prelaunch before the March 2013 opening, the campaign collected 'over 85K valid email addresses (and over 100K emails in total)'. '77% of the emails were collected via referral'; 'about 20K people referred about 65K friends'; more than 200 people referred over 50 friends each; product went to about 3,000 people.

Page two, the one shown after email entry, 'was where the referral mechanisms lived'. The quoted messages are 'Shaving is evolving. Don't leave your friends behind.' and 'Invite Friends and Earn Product.' The page held a share link coded to the user, Twitter and Facebook icons that opened a prefilled message, and a tracker of friends referred and prizes reached. Tiers: 5 referrals for shave cream, 10 for a razor, 25 for a Winston shave set, 50 for a year of free shaving. A 1,000-referral lifetime tier was considered and dropped.
No A/B test of the page copy is reported. The 'playful' line of intent refers to the splash page copy ('Respecting the face, and wallet since like right now'), not to the referral page.

Referral vendor KickoffLabs publishes a setup guide and template for a campaign 'like Harry's' (Meagan Kral, Jan 31, 2024). It credits the page's effect to visible reward levels and progress, prominent share buttons and prefilled messages. This is vendor content promoting its own product.

signature_pieces.title: Harry's prelaunch referral page ('Shaving is evolving. Don't leave your friends behind.')
signature_pieces.where_to_read: https://tim.blog/2014/07/21/harrys-prelaunch/ (two lines quoted in the text; the full page only as a screenshot)

candidates.way_in: There is no thank-you line and no confirmation headline; the page itself is the confirmation. It opens on the brand's news in three words ('Shaving is evolving.') and turns straight to the reader's friends as something he could lose ('Don't leave your friends behind.').
candidates.proof_shape: There are no claims to prove; the offer carries the page. A ladder of named free products sits at counts he can reach, the first rung low (5 friends for shave cream), and the top rung is there for the story. His own coded link sits in a field with two share buttons and the message prefilled. A tracker shows how many friends he has brought in and which prize is next. The deadline is the launch itself, a real one.
candidates.voice: Brand-playful and imperative: two short headline sentences, then labels and numbers. No thanks, no flattery, no explanation of why referrals help the company.
candidates.concerns: This is a company, not a writer: the copywriter is unknown and the figures are the co-founder's own, never tested against a variant. It covers one of the spec's next steps (the referral ask with a mechanism), not low-ticket offers, trials or applications. Only about 15 words of the page are on record as text. The reward ladder needs ledger rows, which the spec already requires. It works better as a studied exemplar of the referral bridge than as a 'Written like' persona.

candidates.name: NextAfter (nonprofit fundraising research lab; Jeff Giddens, CEO per its about page)
candidates.role: Testing lab and agency. It runs controlled experiments on clients' confirmation pages and 'instant donation' pages, the page shown right after a free course, ebook or survey sign-up, which carries the next ask. The writers of the treatments are not credited.

evidence.claim: Dallas Theological Seminary, experiment #204013: the control led with 'Story of Scripture Registration Confirmation' and 'Thank You!' before the donation ask. The treatment removed both, leaving the congratulatory message and the donation invitation at the top. Donation conversion went from 6.4% (14/219) to 13.2% (30/227), +106.7% at 98.6% confidence, reported as valid.

Boys Town: a confirmation page with a 'Support Boys Town' button linking to a separate donation page was tested against a donation form with a value proposition placed directly on the confirmation page. Conversion went from 0.03% to 0.13%, +349.4% at 96.5% confidence, with 14,013 visitors against 6,050 required; reported as valid, with low donor numbers.

Replications were mixed and not valid. DTS #204422 (2026), the same removal: +3.4% at 24.0% confidence. DTS #205117 (2026), removing a standalone 'Thank you!' line and going straight to 'Before you go, would you consider something?': -12.4% at 83.6% confidence; the team suggested a brief thank-you may ease the move to the ask.
Canadian Taxpayers Federation #119998 (Dec 2022): the control said 'YOU DID IT! Your survey is submitted.' and the treatment led with 'One More Thing…'. Result +10.7% at 40.2% confidence, not valid.

Focus on the Family: a 'Super Happy Thankful Experience' confirmation page (donor thanked by name, celebrated in the copy, two testimonials, confetti on load) against the control: 31.7% vs 31.6%, no significant difference in later giving.

Reasons to Believe: a longer, value-based thank-you header ('Thank you for your insights. We also want to see more skeptics come to Christ. Here's why your response matters.') scored -68.1% at 85.7% confidence, not valid. Nearly all of the loss was mobile traffic, where the doubled headline may have pushed the body below the fold.
Luther Seminary: removing 'thank you' from the header scored +17.8% at 38.4% confidence, not valid. The treatment was rolled out because donations did not fall.
The about page describes '6,000+ digital fundraising experiments' and does not say who writes the treatments.

signature_pieces.title: Dallas Theological Seminary course-registration confirmation page with donation ask (#204013)
signature_pieces.year: n.d. (date not on the fetched page)
signature_pieces.where_to_read: https://www.nextafter.com/experiments/how-removing-a-confirmation-headline-and-thank-you-language-affects-donor-conversion-rate/ (control and treatment described; page as images)

signature_pieces.title: Boys Town tween-discipline resource confirmation page with the donation form on the page
Canadian Taxpayers Federation survey confirmation page, 'One More Thing…'

candidates.way_in: Do not lead with 'Registration Confirmation' or 'Thank You!' as the headline. Lead with the next ask as the top message ('One More Thing…', 'Before you go, would you consider something?') and confirm the registration in one line under it. Keep the headline short enough that the body still shows on a phone.
candidates.proof_shape: Make the case for the next step where he already stands: why it matters now that he has the free thing (the mission the course or survey serves), how a gift is used, as bullets, and one story of a person the work reached. Put the form itself on the page instead of a button to another page; that move produced the lab's largest valid lift.
candidates.voice: Plain, warm, donor-centric second person ('your response matters'). No celebration: the confetti, name-repeating version tested flat.
candidates.concerns: This is a lab, not a writer: treatments are unattributed, and the copy is published mostly as images, so there is little text to study. The work is all nonprofit donation asks. Only two results are valid; the 'remove the thank-you' move did not replicate in three later tests and may hurt when the thank-you is a single short line. The results are reported by the lab on its own client work. It is best used as evidence for the spec's rules, not as a persona.

candidates.concerns: A company, not a writer; almost no text survives. The figures are the co-founder's, via press interviews I did not open. The move needs a live count of people ahead, which the spec allows only with a ledger row. It is the same move as Harry's (a referral bridge with a mechanism), so it adds a variant rather than a separate persona.

candidates.name: Talia Wolf
candidates.role: Conversion optimization strategist (GetUplift; described in the 2016 bio as CMO at Banana Splash). Wrote the Copyhackers guest post that is the source of the '52% and 39%' thank-you figures.

evidence.claim: Copyhackers 2016 guest post (author Talia Wolf, editor Joanna Wiebe). Adding an image and a personal note from a co-founder to a B2B lead-validation thank-you page helped 'increase direct sales by 52%'. signature_pieces.title: 'Thank-you pages' guest post for Copyhackers (describes the two client pages)

candidates.way_in: A personal note from a named co-founder, with his photo, as the first thing on the page.
candidates.proof_shape: Trust comes from a face and a person rather than from figures. Then one call to action with a visual arrow pointing at the single next step (install, confirm, book).

candidates.name: Joanna Wiebe
candidates.role: Founder of Copyhackers; conversion copywriting teacher. Wrote the 2013 Copyhackers teardown of thank-you pages.

evidence.claim: The 2013 teardown reports no test results. Its 'short list of obvious stuff': say thank you or a version of it, tell people what to expect next, give an action to take, keep brand tone, give contact details. It praises Ben Settle's explainer video showing 'exactly how to be sure they get signed up', Yogipreneur's 'social ask' on a webinar thank-you page, Wistia's video and Mighty Deals repeating the download link, and calls Greenpeace's page a 'dead-end'. It names no one as the best at the format.
She edited the 2016 guest post whose 52% and 39% figures are Talia Wolf's self-reported results.

signature_pieces.title: Thank-you pages teardown (Copyhackers)

candidates.way_in: As she prescribes it: a thank-you or a version of it, then what to expect next. No thank-you page of her own is shown.

candidates.voice: Teaching voice; no thank-you copy of hers is available to characterize.
candidates.concerns: Known for teaching and teardowns, not for thank-you pages she wrote. Her list opens with 'say thank you', which the spec and NextAfter's one valid test argue against as a headline. Not a persona for this format.

candidates.role: Founder of DigitalMarketer. Known for the low-ticket 'tripwire' or 'entry point offer' as the first purchase, which practitioners commonly place after the opt-in.

The post does not say the offer was made on a thank-you page.

No DigitalMarketer sitemap URL (posts, pages, case studies) contained 'thank' or 'confirm' as a thank-you page article when checked on 2026-11-01.

signature_pieces.where_to_read: https://www.digitalmarketer.com/blog/funnel-product-splintering/ (an email offer, not a thank-you page)

candidates.voice: No thank-you copy available to characterize.

candidates.way_in: Unverified this session.
candidates.proof_shape: Unverified this session.
candidates.voice: Unverified this session.

candidates.name: Brennan Dunn
candidates.role: Freelancing educator (Double Your Freelancing) and personalization practitioner. His thank-you page is cited by ClickFunnels as an example.

evidence.claim: ClickFunnels describes his thank-you page. It explains why it asks for input, then runs a survey ('What best describes the maturity of your business?', 'What kind of work do you primarily do?', 'Are you happy with the number of clients you have worked with over the last year?', 'If you could change just ONE thing about the clients you work with, what would that be?', 'Let's talk money. Are you happy with your income?'). It then shows a message tailored to the answers and points to a free email course. No results are given.

signature_pieces.title: Double Your Freelancing opt-in thank-you page with segmentation survey

candidates.way_in: Say why he is asking, then ask about the reader's business in the reader's own trade terms.
candidates.proof_shape: No proof; relevance does the selling. The answers route him to a tailored message and the one next step that fits his answer (a free email course for those short on clients).
candidates.voice: Consultative and plain, with a blunt money question ('Let's talk money. Are you happy with your income?').
candidates.concerns: There are no results, and only one third-party description of the page. A survey routing to one of several next steps conflicts with the spec's rule of one next step from the offer block. Not a persona; it is a technique.

top_picks.name: Harry's prelaunch referral page (Jeff Raider's account; writer unnamed)
top_picks.why: It is the only thank-you page with a large, published result specific to the format: over 85K valid emails in one week, 77% via referral, about 20K referrers bringing about 65K friends. Part of the copy and the full mechanism (coded link, prefilled share, tracker, 5/10/25/50 ladder) can be read at the source, and referral vendors sell a template 'like Harry's'. Caveats: the figures are the co-founder's, the page was never tested against a variant, the writer is unknown, and it covers only the referral-ask bridge. It is a company, not a master.

top_picks.name: NextAfter (testing lab)
top_picks.why: It holds the only controlled, sample-sized tests of this exact page with a next ask. There are two valid wins: dropping the 'Registration Confirmation / Thank You!' header for the ask (+106.7%, 98.6%), and putting the form on the confirmation page instead of a button (+349.4%, 96.5%). A celebration page tested flat. Caveats: it is a lab, the writers are uncredited, the copy is mostly in images, the work is nonprofit only, and the remove-the-thank-you move failed to replicate in three later tests (one trended -12.4%). It is evidence for the spec's rules rather than a persona.

notes:
Plain answer: the thank-you page has no recognized masters. No individual copywriter has documented results, peer recognition and readable work in this format. I rank two sources because they are the best evidence of how to write it, but neither is a person, and neither leaves enough text to build a 'Written like' manner with a whole exemplar the way Section 12 does. My recommendation is not to add a named persona for this format. Keep thank-you pages on the existing manners: Bencivenga's 'what arrives and when' line from the Kurobuta ham letter, already in docs/04 Section 11, is the current set's best model for the confirmation line. If something is added, add Harry's (referral bridge) and NextAfter's DTS/Boys Town pages (ask on the page, short top line) as studied structures or exemplars, not as masters.

Search limit: the shared WebSearch budget for this run (200 calls per turn across all agents) was already used up when this task started, so I ran no web searches. Everything above comes from the repository's existing research files and direct WebFetch reads of primary pages, using site sitemaps (Copyhackers, DigitalMarketer, NextAfter, Smart Marketer, KickoffLabs) to find the relevant articles. A search pass could surface candidates I could not reach this way: podcasts or interviews naming thank-you page specialists, and DTC post-purchase page vendors' case studies. The owner can ask for a follow-up search pass.

Other candidates considered and set aside: Mike Filsaime (his own site credits him with Butterfly Marketing, 2006, as 'One of the earliest automated referral engines', self-reported, with no thank-you copy or OTO claim). Ezra Firestone / Smart Marketer (no thank-you or post-purchase copy or figures on the pages fetched; his own course thank-you page carries no priced next step). Jon Morrow, James Clear, Brian Dean and Nick Stephenson (ClickFunnels examples with no results; Morrow's is a video pitching 'Paid to Write Club'). Ben Settle (Wiebe praised his confirmation-page explainer video in 2013; the copy is a video). Zendrive, Axis Social, Veeam and Sephora (Unbounce examples; only Axis has a figure, a self-reported 'nearly 30%' landing conversion).

Findings that touch the repo's docs (I edited nothing). (1) docs/03 Section 5.7 says 'Copyhackers' 52% and 39% lifts are the author's own unsourced results', and line 638 lists 'Copyhackers' ... thank-you figures' as unverified. They are now traced: Talia Wolf's 2016 guest post (edited by Wiebe), self-reported on unnamed clients, with no copy shown. (2) The spec's ban on 'Thank you!' or 'Confirmation' as the headline rests partly on NextAfter #204013 (+106.7%, valid). Three later tests of the same move were not valid: #204422 +3.4%, #205117 -12.4% when a lone 'Thank you!' line was removed, and CTF #119998 +10.7%. The DTS team suggested a brief thank-you may ease the move to the ask. That fits the spec's one-line confirmation, but the headline ban is less settled than the single result suggests. (3) NextAfter's valid Boys Town result (form on the confirmation page beats a button to another page, +349.4%) supports keeping the next step's action on the page itself. (4) Focus on the Family's celebration page (name, confetti, testimonials) tested flat against its control, which supports the spec's 'no celebration' rule on cost grounds. (5) In the Harry's account, 'intended to be playful' describes the splash page copy, not the referral page. The corpus record controls_other_formats-05 labels the referral page's voice 'Playful', which is a fair reading but not the source's statement.

field_strength_why: Nobody gives awards for the single promotional email. The Caples, Effies, AWAI and DMA do not cover it as a category. The only third-party split-test results with figures that I found belong to a team: Obama 2012, with 20 writers. Individual writers have their own reported results, plus peer recognition that is specific to email and consistent across sources. Kevin Rogers (Copy Chief) and Chris Orzechowski (Email of the Week) independently name Laura Belgray. Rogers names Daniel Throssell. Ben Settle's daily emails are the most widely read body of work in the format, and the app's own spec already uses his structure. So the masters are real and can be studied, but their results are almost all self-reported.

candidates.name: Laura Belgray
candidates.role: Copywriter and founder of Talking Shrimp. A former TV promo writer (her about page lists Bravo, NBC, HBO and Nick at Nite, and a Promax Best of Show). She sends a story email to her own list that sells her courses and the affiliate launches she promotes. Author of Tough Titties.

evidence.claim: Third party (Kevin Rogers, Copy Chief): "My new favorite email copywriter is Laura Belgray." Also "Laura has been dominating affiliate partner launches, beating out the famous name stalwarts of our industry," with a "relatively tiny list" that buys on her suggestion "at far higher rates than her colleagues" who have "up to 50x the list size." Episode title: "The email style that out-converts every other guru in your space."

Third party (Chris Orzechowski, Email of the Week #24): "Laura is an email copywriter with legendary skills." "Laura is a MASTER subject line writer." He breaks down her procrastination email passage by passage and closes with "Be like Belgray."

Third party (Copy Chief podcast feed, EP 291, 2023): "Her weekly emails are always raw, insightful, and hilarious." Copy Chief has run at least seven episodes with her (EP 115, 142, 151, 160, 162, 220, 240, 291).
Her own single-email result: over $11k from one email selling a $49 product. Also over $1M in sales in one year, and her top broadcast open rate rose from 40% to 55% after she cleaned her list.

Her public archive of 21 handpicked emails includes two subject-line split tests: "OMG – stop procrastinating!" lost to "kill my housemate," and "World's worst fish" lost to "worst I ever had." The page also records Orzechowski's Email of the Week honour and Kevin Rogers's Copy Chief tribute (a dramatic reading). Her collection-level claim: "All got great engagement (clicks, replies, and, where applicable, purchases)."

signature_pieces.title: "Worst I ever had" (her brother-in-law Dan sends back the fish; this subject won the split test)
signature_pieces.where_to_read: Listed at https://www.talkingshrimp.com/handpicked-emails. Full text at https://ckarchive.com/b/0vuwh9hd480d (the page renders only in a browser; WebFetch saw the subject line only, and the repo corpus entry controls_emails-16 records the text).

signature_pieces.title: "OMG - stop procrastinating" (winning subject "kill my housemate"; shares her Fast Company article)
signature_pieces.where_to_read: https://ckarchive.com/b/qdu8h7hrrv4z (browser), with Orzechowski's passage-by-passage teardown at https://www.theemailcopywriter.com/articles/email-of-the-week-24-laura-belgray-talking-shrimp

signature_pieces.title: "Why are we RUNNING?" (Madrid layover; the email Kevin Rogers gave a Copy Chief tribute)
"This writing trick is *literally* bananas" (a Jon Stewart specificity lesson that turns into her products being back on sale)

candidates.way_in: Line one drops into a small scene from her own week, with a named person or a line of dialogue already happening. Examples: "'Run!' I yelled to my husband." "My husband's brother-in-law, Dan, always sends back his food." "In college, I had a housemate we all wanted to kill." No windup and no greeting paragraph: "Hey [name]" or nothing, because "A formal greeting signals 'we're not friends.'" The subject is the oddest, most concrete phrase in the story, a line a friend would send ("Worst I ever had", "Can you say 'ballsack' at a funeral?"), and she split-tests it.
candidates.proof_shape: The story is the proof. Concrete particulars escalate in threes and fours (risotto, short ribs, duck, fish). Then one transfer sentence lands the whole story on the reader's own work: "When someone writes back to an email and tells me it's lame... I know they're a Dan." In a teaching email she does the skill live: she rewrites two lines of a public speech to show specificity, then names the product in one line ("60-Minute Makeovers is back on the market!"). Candour about her own numbers and failings (a jump in unsubscribes, her procrastination) stands in for testimonials. The offer is said once, with an honest reason to act (back on sale, a few spots left before September). The link goes after the turn or in the P.S.
candidates.voice: A friend's email: funny, candid, self-deprecating. One-line paragraphs set the comic timing, with parentheticals, pop-culture references and mild profanity. She ends on a joke rather than a moral, signs "xoLaura", and uses a P.S. (sometimes a P.P.S.) that carries a punchline or the link.
candidates.concerns: Her figures are self-reported. Kevin Rogers's account of her affiliate results is third party but gives no numbers. The ckarchive bodies render only in a browser, so this pass verified the archive listing, the teardown and the subject-line tests, not the full texts; those texts are in the repo corpus from an earlier read. Some of her habits break this app's spec: first-name merge tokens in a subject, two product links plus a P.S. link in one email, and lengths of about 600 to 880 words against the spec's 700-word top. The manner should keep the scene, the escalation and the one transfer sentence, and drop those habits. Profanity belongs in the voice profile, not the default.

candidates.name: Ben Settle
candidates.role: Email copywriter and publisher. He sends a daily email to his own list selling his paid print newsletter Email Players ($97/month) and his courses, and republishes each email on his blog. He bills himself "World Leader In Email Copywriting Education."

evidence.claim: Testimonial from Matt Furey ("Zen Master Of The Internet®"), hosted on Settle's site: "I think Ben is the light heavyweight champion of email copywriting." Perry Marshall, on the same page: "one of the sharpest marketing minds on the planet." Dan Kennedy: "intelligent, informed, interesting and inspiring."
His public archive: "3000+ pages of advanced email, copywriting, & web marketing tips". The emails sell "the prestigious $97.00/month 'Email Players' newsletter."

The format move, verified in a republished email: 13 first-person reasons, then the bridge "To learn more about the paid Email Players newsletter go here:", one link (www.BenSettle.com/alt) and the sign-off "Ben Settle". No P.S. The page states no results.

His endorsement is the one Daniel Throssell leads with: "Daniel Throssell is, I would say, just about pretty undisputed the hottest email copywriter walking the planet right now." This shows Settle serves as a reference judge of email copy, but it is not evidence of his own results.

signature_pieces.title: Why I don't do video courses
How to spank the high falutin' goo-roos with your pricing
The Archie Bunker effect used by communist writers to make bank
How to commit wholesale inbox genocide

candidates.way_in: One of three openings, each a line or two long. (1) A reader's email pasted in after a stub: "Came a question about pricing:" then the reader's own words, ending "Why do you price like that ?" (2) A blunt answer that admits his self-interest: "The short answer is because I like money." (3) A memory with a time on it: "Many years ago, I watched some interviews with the writers of the smash hit TV show from the 70's." The subject is a slangy, provocative how-to or claim that the body pays off ("How to commit wholesale inbox genocide").
candidates.proof_shape: His own practice is the proof. He says what he does in his business and why, often as a run of first-person reasons, and includes his own mistake (he priced Email Players at $97 without testing it and now regards that as an error). He adds one named authority as a principle (Dan Kennedy's "build your business to suit your preferences", Earl Nightingale on doing the opposite of everyone else). No customer numbers and no testimonials appear in the email. The pitch is one bridge line that does not argue ("More about the paid Email Players newsletter here:" or "So I'll just end with this:"), then one bare URL, then "Ben Settle". Usually no P.S.
candidates.voice: Blunt, irreverent and contrarian, sure of himself and never pleading. He mocks the crowd he sells against ("goo-roos"), writes one-line paragraphs, and uses folksy archaisms ("Do ye what ye will with that info."). He disqualifies readers who won't act.
candidates.concerns: He has no documented results for any email or campaign; the posts I read state none. His recognition is verified only as testimonials on his own site, and he markets himself as an email educator, though the teaching is delivered as the emails themselves. He does not appear in the Copy Chief podcast feed I scanned. Some emails lean on political or mocking asides that would not suit most offers. Emails run about 300 to 1,000 words. docs/03 Section 5.8 already builds the format's structure from his posts, so his manner overlaps the spec's default more than any other candidate's does.

candidates.name: Daniel Throssell
candidates.role: Australian copywriter (The Persuasive Page). Since 2020 he has sent a daily sales email to his own list selling his courses and affiliate offers. Before that, by his own account, he did client work including the Barefoot Investor launches.

evidence.claim: Third party (Kevin Rogers, Copy Chief EP 295, 2023): "For my money, there is no better, or more entertaining, email copywriter in the game right now than Daniel Throssell." Throssell "recently TOOK MY MONEY after declaring 'war' on me to promote my own course (Escape Velocity) to his list," in "less than 48 hours."
Third party (Copy Chief EP 266, 2022), episode title: "Daniel Throssell – World's Most Disruptive Email Copywriter". The description refers to replies from "readers of his daily emails."

Endorsements hosted on his own page: Jason Fladlien, "I think he's the best email copywriter in the game right now". John Carlton, "Easily one of the 'most swiped' email copywriters on the planet". Laura Belgray, "Daniel Throssell should be on your short list". Ben Settle, the "hottest email copywriter walking the planet right now".

Own claims: "almost every single email I send is a sales email." After placing second in 2020, he says he went on to place "1st (usually by a HUGE margin) in EVERY SINGLE AFFILIATE contest I participated in." No figures are given.

A promotional email republished as a post: a feud story leads to the offer ("For the low price of just $994"), a deadline ("until Monday (the next 4 days)") and one link ("Then check out my insane offer here:" pers.page/bf21). Signed "Daniel Throssell", no P.S., about 1,100 words.

signature_pieces.title: Matt Bock wants WAR? Bring it on. My Black Friday deal OWNS his.
I caught a group of scammers. Now here's how I'm going to punish them. (sent to his list 16 September 2021, then posted)
Announcing 'Psych Insights for Modern Marketers: 3G Edition'

candidates.way_in: The first line announces an event as news with stakes, usually a fight or a reveal, then promises the story behind it. Examples: "I have a BIG announcement for you today. But first, let's set the scene with a true story from 2016:" "THE DRAMA IS BACK!" Or the subject alone: "I caught a group of scammers. Now here's how I'm going to punish them." The subject names an antagonist or promises a showdown.
candidates.proof_shape: A blow-by-blow account of a real episode in his own business, with names, dates and what he did: a rival's Black Friday coalition, or his infiltration of a pirate group-buy and the takedowns that followed. The offer arrives as his next move in that story ("My Black Friday deal OWNS his"). It comes with the price, a deadline and its span, and one link with a plain instruction. Signed "Daniel Throssell", no P.S. Proof is the episode itself plus the persona he has built; testimonials stay out of the email.
candidates.voice: Theatrical and self-mythologising ("Australia's best copywriter"), with caps for emphasis, hero-and-villain framing and comic exaggeration. He courts hate as well as love ("those same fun, crazy emails that sell so well and get so much love (and hate)").
candidates.concerns: The only third-party praise is Kevin Rogers's; the rest is hosted on his own page. His contest wins are self-reported with no figures. Most of his emails can only be read by subscribing; the blog holds a few. His emails run about 1,100 to 2,300 words, far over the format's 700-word top. One republished email carried three links. The feud move names real people, which would need ledger rows and carries defamation risk. The persona depends on an established character the user's speaker may not have. A usable manner keeps the event-as-news opening and the offer as the speaker's next move in the story, and drops the feud. He was banned from r/copywriting in 2021 (his own post), so he is divisive.

signature_pieces.where_to_read: Subject and results at https://talkingpointsmemo.com/?p=163346. I did not locate or verify the full email text. The Bloomberg original (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2012-11-29/the-science-behind-those-obama-campaign-e-mails) returned 403.

His readable output is mostly criticism of other people's emails, so his fame here comes more from teaching than from studiable copy. No distinct manner of his own could be described.

candidates.name: Dean Jackson
candidates.role: Marketing coach (real estate and small business); originator of the nine-word email.

No links. No PS with your latest offer." A client's click-through "went from 5% click-through to over 30%" against its 3% to 5% HTML emails. The other results are client anecdotes.

candidates.voice: A person's one-line note, plain text, no signature.
candidates.concerns: This is one template, not a manner. It has no link, which conflicts with this format's one-link call to action, and it is a reactivation email that docs/03 Section 5.9 already uses as the win-back pattern. It belongs in the sequence spec, not the persona list.

top_picks.name: Laura Belgray
top_picks.why: She is the only one with independent, email-specific recognition from two separate peers. Kevin Rogers says her small list out-sells affiliates with up to 50x the list size; Chris Orzechowski calls her "an email copywriter with legendary skills". She also reports a single-email result (over $11k from one email for a $49 product) and split-tested subject lines. She writes every email herself, 21 handpicked emails are public, and her manner is easy to describe: a scene from her own week, comic escalation, one sentence that transfers it to the reader's work, the offer said once.

top_picks.name: Ben Settle
top_picks.why: His single promotional emails are the largest readable body of work in the format (3000+ pages republished). Each one has an opening line, his own practice as the proof, a one-line bridge and one bare link, which is the structure this app's spec already borrows. He writes every one himself and his manner is distinct (a reader's question or a blunt admission of self-interest, a named authority as a principle, no testimonials). He ranks below Belgray because there are no documented results and his recognition is verified only through testimonials on his own site (Matt Furey, Perry Marshall, Dan Kennedy).

top_picks.name: Daniel Throssell
top_picks.why: He has the strongest email-specific peer recognition: Kevin Rogers says "there is no better, or more entertaining, email copywriter in the game right now," and Settle, Fladlien, Carlton and Belgray praise him on his own page. Nearly every email he sends is a sales email with one link, and he reports first places in affiliate contests. He ranks third because his results have no figures, most of his emails can only be read by subscribing, and his 1,100 to 2,300-word feud stories need adapting (keep the event-as-news opening and the offer as his next move; drop the named enemy) to fit a 700-word, ledger-bound format.

notes:
Coverage limit: my first WebSearch call came back with the session's search budget (200 calls) already spent, so I ran no web searches. Every claim marked verified came from WebFetch of specific URLs, mostly ones the repo's research corpus already cited (research/corpus/controls_emails.json, research/corpus/split_tests_email_ads_sms.json), plus a full scan of the Copy Chief podcast feed. These gaps need a follow-up pass with search before anything is built:
- Matt Furey's daily emails and results (his site would not render).
- Third-party recognition of Ben Settle beyond testimonials on his own site.
- Throssell's 2015 Ramit Sethi "Call to Action" contest win.
- The full texts of the Obama 2012 emails.
- Practitioners I did not check at all: Justin Goff, John McIntyre, Kim Krause Schwalm (her emails are in the corpus but she is known for long-form health copy), Frank Kern, Ry Schwartz, André Chaperon. Chaperon's site shows no email archive or results, and he is a sequence (Soap Opera Sequence) practitioner rather than a single-email one.

Bearing on the current set: none of the nine existing manners has documented work in the single promotional email. Halbert is the engine's default for the email family on the strength of his letters, not emails. docs/03 Section 5.8 already takes the format's structure from Settle's posts and its rules from Belgray, so adding them as manners would make explicit what the spec already draws on.

Fit with the spec (supabase/functions/_shared/engine/formats/specs/email_single.ts), which allows 30 to 700 words, exactly one link, and no personalization tokens in the subject:
- Settle (about 300 to 1,000 words, one link, no P.S.) fits almost as is.
- Belgray (about 600 to 880 words, sometimes two links or a link in the P.S., merge tokens in one subject) needs those habits stripped.
- Throssell (about 1,100 to 2,300 words, feuds with named people) needs the most adapting.

Alternates if the owner weighs results over peer recognition:
- Ramit Sethi reports the most specific single-email revenue ($165,803 from one Last Chance email), but it is self-reported, his team co-writes, and the emails are only images on a paid-course page.
- The Obama 2012 team has the only third-party, split-tested result ("I will be outspent" beat 17 variants and raised more than $2.6M), but it was a 20-writer team and its winning moves are already spec rules.

Dean Jackson's nine-word email belongs in the win-back sequence, not the persona list: it has no link and is one template.

I changed no files in the repository.

field_strength_why: Email sequences have known masters, but nobody has audited their results. I found no award, hall of fame or third-party split test that names an individual writer for email sequences. The email awards I know of go to brands. Every revenue or response figure for this format comes from the writer or the writer's own company. The strongest evidence is Ramit Sethi's company-reported revenue for three named launch emails. The strongest peer evidence is Brunson's company crediting Andre Chaperon as his source for the Soap Opera Sequence, and endorsements of Ben Settle by Kennedy, Bencivenga and Furey, which Settle publishes on his own site. Three people clear the bar on results, recognition, own authorship and a distinct manner. Nobody clears it on independently verified numbers.

candidates.name: Ramit Sethi
candidates.role: Founder of I Will Teach You To Be Rich (and GrowthLab). By his own account he writes the launch emails that sell his courses. He named the 'Power Trio' launch emails: Big Reveal, Free Taste and Last Chance.

evidence.claim: His company's page is headlined '3 sales emails worth $379,643'. It reports these figures: the Big Reveal 'made $82,358' (Success Triggers launch), the Free Taste 'made $28,721' (How to Talk to Anybody) and the Last Chance 'pulled in $165,803 in just a few hours' (Zero to Launch funnel). The trio is used 'in every product launch'. An evergreen funnel made 'over $5,000,000'. The Mental Mastery launch made '$617,944 in about a week', with the trio bringing in 'over 60% of all our revenue'. No list sizes are given.

The same page describes each email's job: the Big Reveal is 'An interesting discussion about what makes some people so successful'; the Free Taste is 'A hilarious story about Judge Judy and a free sample of my new course'; the Last Chance is 'A quick courtesy reminder so they didn't miss out'. It presents the emails as his own writing ('Watch me write') and calls them 'carefully crafted to be enjoyable AND authentic AND still sell... Nothing inauthentic. Nothing spammy. No sleazy sales tricks.' An earlier launch had 'Over 25 emails' across '5 weeks of sales emails'.
GrowthLab: 'Get the 5-day email funnel that generated $400,000 from a single launch', bylined 'By Ramit Sethi'. The whole funnel is offered word for word behind a signup form.
Daniel Throssell's site says Throssell 'won Ramit Sethi's Call to Action copywriting contest in 2015'. This only shows Sethi in the role of judge of copy.

signature_pieces.where_to_read: Screenshots inside his paid Behind the Sales Email course (iwillteachyoutoberich.com/behind-the-sales-email); not public as text

signature_pieces.where_to_read: Same paid course; not public as text

signature_pieces.title: GrowthLab 5-day launch email funnel ($400,000)

candidates.way_in: Each email has a different opening move, set by its job in the launch. The reveal email opens on an idea about people, not the product: what successful people do differently. The reader agrees with the idea before the product appears. The taste email opens on a short, funny story from pop culture or his own life, and that story leads straight into a lesson from the course. The last-chance email skips the windup: it is a courteous reminder that the door closes, and when.
candidates.proof_shape: The product proves itself inside the email. The Free Taste gives away a real piece of the course in the body, so the reader has used the product before the ask. Proof is a demonstration more than a testimonial. The close leans on a true deadline stated politely, not on pressure. This fits the app's existing 'free taste' rule.
candidates.voice: Casual, plain and entertaining, with an explicit anti-sleaze stance ('enjoyable AND authentic AND still sell'). He writes as 'I' and uses 'we' for the company. The sell is low-pressure and the last call is short. Other traits often attributed to his emails, such as great length, quoted reader emails and lowercase subject lines, were not verified this session.
candidates.concerns: All figures come from his own company, with no list sizes or attribution method. The email text is published only as screenshots in a paid course, so a whole exemplar needs a purchase or a subscription to his list. IWT has a team ('my team and I'), and I could not confirm which later emails Sethi drafted himself. The Judge Judy-style pop-culture story names a real person, so under the engine's rules it needs a ledger row. The app already uses his three roles (email_sequence.ts SEQUENCE_ROLES), so a Sethi manner would add a voice to a structure already in place.

candidates.name: Andre Chaperon
candidates.role: Email marketer. Author of AutoResponder Madness (2009), rewritten as Art of Email in 2021. Co-founder with Shawn Twing of Tiny Little Businesses / The Modern Marketing System. Brunson's company credits him as the source of the Soap Opera Sequence.

evidence.claim: ClickFunnels: 'Russell Brunson first heard of the Soap Opera Sequence from a friend of his, Andre Chaperon.' Brunson 'popularized the idea in his book, DotCom Secrets'. 'Each email is written to pull the reader toward the next email... and eventually, toward clicking and buying whatever it is you're offering.'

'Back in 2009, when I released AutoResponder Madness, most people met it as an email marketing course.' 'The mechanics got most of the attention: open loops, nested sequences, segmentation, bridge emails, Soap Opera Sequences.' Underneath was 'the idea that email could be a place where trust accumulated before anyone was asked to buy.'

'A "soap opera series" is a conceptual container or a delivery vehicle of a short email-driven experience', triggered by 'an explicit "hand raise" (clicking a trigger link)'. ARM is a course 'many people have said is the best email marketing course available'. Open rates at TLB are 'north of 55% when sent to everyone'. He has used ESPs since 2003.

His own setup: a seven-email welcome series, then 'a "pause" of ten days' before the first newsletter. 'I don't send broadcast emails; instead, I have a long follow-up sequence that keeps growing.' Open rates 'have never dropped below 60%' (newsletter 1 at 76.8%), sent to 'a few thousand subscribers'. No sales figures.
His company calls Art of Email 'the long-awaited replacement to our flagship email marketing course, AutoResponder Madness (ARM)' and 'the gold standard in email marketing education'.

signature_pieces.title: AutoResponder Madness (course; rewritten as Art of Email)
His own seven-email welcome series and follow-up sequence (Emergent Marketing Series)
The Boring Miracle of Email; The Email Engine (newsletter essays)

candidates.way_in: He opens on a small, specific scene from his own life ('I live in Bath.' then the pub basements and their old pipes), and the scene turns into the idea. In a soap opera series, the first email opens in the middle of the drama. Each email ends on an open loop that the next one pays off. A series starts only after the reader clicks a trigger link to ask for it, so everyone reading has chosen to.
candidates.proof_shape: He builds trust first and asks later. The reader is the hero and the writer is the guide (the repo's docs/03 records 'Harper needs a guide, not a hero to emulate' as verified; I did not re-fetch it). The proof is the series itself: by the time of the offer, it has already taught or shown something useful. Bridge emails and segmentation decide who gets the pitch, and only readers who click toward the topic receive it.
candidates.voice: First person, British idiom ('wee'), self-deprecating asides ('Maybe I'm just getting grumpier with age'). Concrete domestic and architectural metaphors: plumbing as infrastructure, a living room as a shop window. Long rhythmic sentences alternate with one-line paragraphs ('Boring, perhaps.'). Sources are credited inline. He uses em dashes, which the tell edit would strip.
candidates.concerns: No revenue figures at all; open rates are his own. His sequences sit behind an opt-in and his teaching sits in a paid course. What is public is long essay-style newsletters, not sales sequences. His soft-sell approach (trust before any ask, pitch only to readers who opt in) conflicts with the spec's rule that every email sells the same offer. The app's welcome roles already come from the Soap Opera Sequence via Brunson, so this manner would add his voice and open-loop craft, not a new structure.

candidates.way_in: Line one is one of three things. A reader's question, quoted at the top and then answered. A remembered anecdote about a named person or show, told in one sentence ('Many years ago, I watched some interviews with...'). Or a blunt, contrarian answer to the subject line ('The short answer is because I like money.'). He never restates the subject.
candidates.proof_shape: His own business is the only case study. He states opinions as rules, each with a reason from his own practice, often as a numbered list of reasons. The email carries no testimonials and no outside statistics. The turn to the product is a single bridge line ('More about the paid Email Players newsletter here:') followed by exactly one link. Every email sells the same standing offer, and readers who disagree are welcome to leave.
candidates.voice: Blunt and irreverent. One-sentence paragraphs, coined slang ('goo-roos'), name-drops of Kennedy and others, about 300 to 600 words. The sign-off is his name and there is often no P.S. It reads like a man giving a strong opinion to one reader who asked.
candidates.concerns: His format is the daily broadcast, an open-ended stream on one offer, not a planned sequence with an arc. It matches the app's per-email anatomy (one story or lesson, a one-line turn, one link), which docs/03 already takes from his posts. He has no documented sales figures; the endorsements are hand-picked and sit on his own site; he markets himself as an educator. His pop-culture anecdotes and name-drops each need a ledger row under the engine's rules. His manner is closest to Halbert's (a letter from one man). What sets it apart is the reader-question opening and opinion-as-rule proof.

candidates.name: Jeff Walker
candidates.role: Creator of Product Launch Formula, the strategist behind the prelaunch, open-cart and close launch sequence. His early launches were email-delivered. Later launches used a copy team.

evidence.claim: In early 1997 he launched a paid version of his free stock-market newsletter. He asked buyers to 'print out the email I sent them, write out a check, and send it to me in the mail'. Results: 'five sales and $1,650', then '$6,000', then '$34,000' ('more than I'd ever made in an entire year'), then 'one over $100,000'.
His business 'started with a free email newsletter sent to 19 people' (1996). His students 'have generated more than $1 billion in sales'.

Systeme.io's summary: the prelaunch themes are Opportunity ('You define a problem and then solve it'), Transformation ('You deliver real value') and Ownership ('You define the next problem'). Open cart: two emails on day 1 ('cart open' and a truthful 'tsunami'), one or two a day on days 2-4, three on day 5 (closing soon, launch story, last call). 'most sales happen on day one and peak on the last day'. The Sideways Sales Letter is 'Jeff's baby'.
Chris Orzechowski lists himself as a 'Member of Jeff Walker's copy team for a multi-million-dollar launch (September 2018)', which shows later Walker launches were written by a team.

Each later piece builds on the one before (transformation, then what owning the result looks like). Open cart opens with a plain announcement, followed the same day by a true momentum report.
candidates.proof_shape: Free content that works, delivered before the sale. Then true social proof as the cart fills (the 'tsunami' email, with real numbers only), case studies and FAQ emails mid-cart, and a dated close announced three times on the last day.
candidates.voice: Not verified: I read no Walker email text this session. His posts read plain, earnest and personal (the stay-at-home dad story), but that is not evidence of his launch-email voice.

His copy is barely readable in public, so there is no exemplar for a persona. Better kept as structure than made a manner.

candidates.name: Daniel Throssell
candidates.role: Australian email copywriter (Persuasive Page). He sends daily sales emails and says he invented the 'Parallel Welcome Sequence'.

evidence.claim: Parallel Welcome Sequence page, headlined 'A NEW Kind Of Email Series That Gets Up To 200% Engagement'. The 200% means readers can consume double the copy, not double the open rate. The rules: every email carries a 'time-travel remote' link that sends the next email at once, that link is the email's only call to action, and each link lands on a 'linker webpage' that forms a parallel series. He recommends 'a minimum of ten' emails. One reader 'spent a whopping NINETY-TWO MINUTES bingeing'. The welcome email is called 'The Dark Room'.

His site quotes endorsements. John Carlton: 'Easily one of the "most swiped" email copywriters on the planet'. Ben Settle: 'the hottest email copywriter walking the planet right now'. Drayton Bird: 'It astonished me'. Kevin Rogers also endorses him. He claims first place in every affiliate contest he has entered since 2021, says he won Ramit Sethi's Call to Action contest in 2015, and says nearly every email he sends is a sales email.

signature_pieces.title: Parallel Welcome Sequence, opening with 'The Dark Room'
signature_pieces.where_to_read: Free on opt-in at persuasivepage.com; described at persuasivepage.com/parallel-welcome-sequence/

candidates.way_in: A scene from a running serial starring his comic alter ego ('mad-scientist-antihero-copywriter'), opening mid-situation. The welcome email 'The Dark Room' plays as a disturbing, funny scene, not as a welcome note with a download link.
candidates.proof_shape: Entertainment carries the reader through. Each email's one call to action fetches the next episode at once. The keenest readers follow linker pages that carry the bonuses and offers, so the series sorts readers by how much they read. Nearly every email sells.
candidates.voice: Self-mocking showman ('Australia's best copywriter'). Serialized fiction mixed with real copy lessons, long, built to be binged.
candidates.concerns: His opener is invented fiction with a made-up narrator, which the engine's hard rules forbid (no invented narrator or story outside the inventory). His mechanism needs instant-send links and parallel pages the app does not produce. Every figure and endorsement is self-published and selected. The contest wins could not be checked against leaderboards. A strong alternate on recognition, but not a fit for this engine.

top_picks.name: Ramit Sethi
top_picks.why: He has the only per-email revenue figures for named sequence roles: Big Reveal $82,358, Free Taste $28,721, Last Chance $165,803, and the trio at 'over 60%' of a $617,944 launch. They are company-reported but specific to this format. He presents the emails as his own writing. His manner is distinct and fits the engine's rules: open on an idea about people, prove the product by giving a working piece of it in the email, close with a polite true deadline. Weakness: the copy is only readable via a paid course or his list.

top_picks.name: Andre Chaperon
top_picks.why: Brunson's company credits him as the source of the Soap Opera Sequence, and that sequence is the basis of the app's welcome roles. His AutoResponder Madness (2009) set out the format's core mechanics (open loops, nested sequences, bridge emails, segmentation). He writes his own, and his manner is distinct: small real scene, open loop, trust before the ask, the reader as hero. Weaknesses: no revenue figures (open rates only, self-reported), his sequences are gated, and his soft sell must be reconciled with the spec's 'every email sells'.

top_picks.name: Ben Settle
top_picks.why: Kennedy, Bencivenga and Furey endorse him by name (on his own site), and other email writers defer to him. His readable corpus is the largest of any candidate (3000+ pages; 68 emails already in the repo). His per-email anatomy already shapes the spec: one story or opinion, a one-line bridge, one link. His manner is distinct from Halbert's: the reader's question or a remembered anecdote as line one, opinion-as-rule proof from his own business. Weaknesses: his format is the daily broadcast rather than a planned arc, and he has no documented sales figures. Close alternate: Daniel Throssell, who has stronger format-specific invention and endorsements from Carlton and Settle, but his opener is invented fiction, which the engine forbids.

notes:
The web search budget ran out on my first query (a 200-search limit shared by every agent in this run), so I ran no web searches for this format. All evidence above comes from direct fetches of specific known pages (no search engines, proxies or archives) plus the repo's corpus, already verified on 2026-10-24 (research/corpus/controls_emails.json). Anything not read at the cited URL is marked as general knowledge or unverified. To widen the hunt (format awards, third-party breakdowns of Sethi's emails, affiliate-contest leaderboards for Throssell, a Kennedy no-email source), send a follow-up after this reply or raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION.

Others considered and not ranked. Dean Jackson's nine-word email is one win-back email, not a sequence, and is already used in the app's win_back roles. Dan Kennedy's follow-up notices are the abandoned_cart roles; the swiped follow-ups are GKIC company emails, so I could not tie his own email writing to them (my belief that he avoided email is unverified). Frank Kern and Ryan Deiss have swiped follow-ups (swiped.co) with no results stated. Chase Dimond's figure is agency-level: 'over $200 million in email attributable revenue' across '100+ brands' (chasedimond.com). Val Geisler, in SaaS lifecycle email, claims '13% churn reduced with a single lifecycle flow' with no published sequences (valgeisler.com). Drayton Bird is a direct-marketing legend ('knows more about direct marketing than anyone in the world', attributed to Ogilvy on draytonbird.com), but his fame is not specific to email sequences. candidates.way_in: He opens on the deal before the content. In the first two or three minutes: "I have two agendas here today." One is to teach a single outcome stated in one sentence; the other is to sell. Then the stake: "if I cannot teach you XYZ, then never buy anything that I will ever attempt to sell you ever again." Next comes a market-level fact with its evidence, not a personal story. For Amazon it was 'traditional retail is dying', backed by named bankrupt retailers set against Amazon's growth. Authority is set in the first minutes with results, and the viewer commits in writing ('Prove it to me... a yes in the chat box right now'). The registration and email legs sell that one defined outcome to email traffic. A client's registration rate rose 10% on a sign-up page made to look like the plain GoToWebinar page. To imitate: terms first, outcome in one sentence, then the shift in the market and its evidence.
candidates.proof_shape: His proof is distributed and counted rather than told. There are 10 to 20 testimonials and five to seven results through the webinar, and the teaching breaks the limiting belief in four to seven steps. The offer comes about 30 minutes in and takes 3 to 5 minutes. The price steps down from a real higher reference, is revealed within five minutes of the offer and is asked for many times. The close then cycles objections in turn: price, time, belief, product, then price again in a new way. Longer webinars get more reps of each ('Instead of doing four time objections, you do 12'). He calls his guarantees 'better than money back': double your money back, conditioned on activation tasks (daily logs for 60 days, a test purchase). Scarcity is stated as a contract: 'I'm contractually obligated. I cannot sell you this product ever again'; 'we can only sell this on the webinar'. He frames beta offers as 'the Mona Lisa in a brown paper bag'. Back-end webinars carry far more specifics and objection reps, aimed at 'that 5% of your audience [that] controls 70% of the money spent in your market'.
candidates.voice: He sounds plain, teacherly and contractual, like a fair dealer reading out the terms. 'Generally, we eliminate jargon' on front-end webinars, while on back-end ones 'I can use all the jargon I want'. He is candid that he is selling ('this is going to hurt a little bit when you make this investment'; 'you're not looking at how much it costs you, you're looking at how much it can save you'). He gives rules and reasons instead of hype, asks for agreement in the chat, and repeats the ask without apology. Sentences are short and conditional ('if I don't make good on X, don't buy').
candidates.concerns: Every dollar figure comes from him or his company; Entrepreneur and the vendor pages repeat his numbers. The figures disagree with each other: $57.8M (Rapid Crush) against $57.9M (podcast), and 'upwards of $100M' (2017) against $103M 'through our own cart' against $250M (Headsmack show notes). The products behind the records are not named. I found no full replay to read, so his copy is studied mainly through One to Many, which I could not fetch; docs/03 quotes it from unofficial scans. His signature devices (conditional double money back, contractual scarcity, stepped prices) are usable only when the offer block and claims ledger hold them; the engine must never supply them.

candidates.way_in: He builds the first ten minutes against drop-off. He goes live five to ten minutes early with looping welcome energy. Minute one states a bold, measurable promise, the One Thing ('build a funnel in under ten minutes'), and promises a free gift to those who stay to the end. He qualifies himself, then future-paces the viewer. The way in proper is a story: either his own origin as an Epiphany Bridge, or a barrier everyone thought unbreakable followed by the named person who broke it. At 10X it was Bannister's four-minute mile, Landy 46 days later, John Reese's $1M in 18 hours, and his own first $1M in October 2007, so that the promise feels repeatable. The registration headline is the One Thing, phrased so the reader cannot answer it in his head, and the three secrets are the bullets.
candidates.proof_shape: There are three secrets, each breaking one false belief: the vehicle, the viewer's own ability, and the outside obstacle. Each runs the same loop: his story (backstory, desire, the wall, the epiphany), then named people's results with their numbers (Liz Benny, 35 clients at $997 in one month; a modeled funnel taking $12K, $34K and $36K on its first three days), then the related beliefs broken one by one, then the new belief restated as 'how to [want] without [thing they hate]'. The offer is the Stack: each component shown with its value, the whole stack re-shown after each addition, then a running total. Three 'if all this did was X, would it be worth it?' statements follow. The price drops from a real higher price, then come the justification, the guarantee and an urgency bonus. Trial closes run throughout (cut from 16 to seven to nine), and a 30-minute countdown follows with Q&A answered and closed between questions, where he says most sales land.
candidates.voice: He speaks in the first person, with high energy, led by stories and conversation. He constantly asks small questions that the viewer answers yes to ('Let me ask you a question...'; 'would it be worth it?'). He names mentors and students by first name, tells his own failures with a grin, and restates value even when it sounds repetitive. He teaches belief, not completeness: he says the job is to inspire, not to finish the lesson. Short spoken sentences rise toward the ask.
candidates.concerns: All figures are his or ClickFunnels', and the auto-transcript garbles some numbers. His best-known $3.2M result was a stage presentation, not a webinar. Most components are credited by him to others (Morin, Thomas, VanHoose, Kennedy, Glazer, Mandossian, Fladlien): he is the codifier and presenter rather than the inventor of each move. The stack's stated values are self-assigned retail values; under this app's ledger rules every stack value must be a real price on file. The app's spec already follows his beats, so a Brunson manner adds mainly the story-led way in and the voice.

notes:
I name only two masters. No third candidate earned a slot on the evidence. The nearest is Amy Porterfield: her own launch webinars come with detailed self-reported figures (9.3% average conversion across six live webinars, no replays), but nothing shows who writes them, no piece can be read, and her fame is mainly teaching. Next are Sam Ovens (one automated webinar, all figures self-reported), Joel Erway (praised by Brunson on his own site, but no readable piece and no documented manner), Graziosi and Robbins (team-written, carried by celebrity) and Jeff Walker (a launch-sequence master, not a webinar one).

The format's roots, as Brunson names them himself, are stage and teleseminar sellers: Alex Mandossian, Armand Morin (the stack), Ted Thomas (trial closes), Dave VanHoose (if-all statements), and Dan Kennedy and Bill Glazer (speaking courses). None of their pitches can be read, so none is a persona. Andy Jenkins and Mike Filsaime's WebinarJam 'Email Is Dead' invitation is swiped on swiped.co (curator Mike Schauer), with no results given.
