candidates.way_in: First, a warning before the speaker says a word: a caption saying what follows is controversial (End of America: 'The following presentation is controversial and may be offensive to some audiences. Viewer discretion is advised.'). Then the named presenter, in the first person, makes one dated forecast about the viewer's money. He says how sure he is, and that his name is on it ('I'm more certain about this looming crisis than I've been about anything else in my life'; 'a very good chance we'll see that in the next two years'). The product is not mentioned. The open loop is why it will happen and what to do before everyone else sees it. In the app, the forecast has to be a dated call held in the ledger, and the warning has to be true.
candidates.proof_shape: A documentary chain of cause. Each link is said with its number (money printing, then commodity prices, then interest rates, mortgages at 15%, stocks down 40% in weeks), and the presenter frames it as 'simply following my research to its logical conclusion'. Free, unglamorous advice comes before any product ('basic food, water, and medical supplies to last you for at least six months'). That proves he means it and gives the viewer something without a purchase. Recorded voices of subscribers follow. The product arrives only at the end, as the way to get the specific steps: free reports as the bonus, a low annual price ($49.50) set against huge stakes, and a six-month refund.
candidates.voice: Grave and first-person: an analyst telling one person something he would rather not be true. Plain declaratives hedged only by his own conviction ('I believe', 'I think there's a very good chance'). The format is slides with his audio and no playback controls, a long argument of about 13,000 words where the sale is held back so long that a viewer said 'I knew it was a sales pitch when I got to the end'.
candidates.concerns: Porter Stansberry presented the piece and supplied the thesis, so the voice is Porter's and Palmer's credit rests on AWAI. AWAI sits in the Agora orbit and its figures are unaudited. The length is disputed: Wikipedia says 77 minutes, while one viewer called it 'about a 1/2 hour listen'. The forecast did not come true. Deer says the prediction 'plainly never happened', and the piece drew critics and regulators' attention. The manner works only on a ledgered, dated, defensible call, and the engine's compliance flags will fire on fear-led predictions. It ran to cold lists as well as warm ones, while the app's spec targets warm or retargeted traffic.

candidates.name: Jon Benson
candidates.role: Copywriter and info-product owner (Fit Over 40, Every Other Day Diet). Widely credited as the originator of the words-on-screen video sales letter, and later a copy-software and course vendor.

Nothing under 15'; 'The most successful that we've done is anywhere from 30 to 40 minutes'; 'Personally, I lost 68 pounds, and I used to be obese'; 'it's the cadence, it's the tempo, it's the emphasis on certain words'; 'Most people get better results with the uglier version' (citing Ryan Deiss's tests).

signature_pieces.title: Every Other Day Diet VSL (the first 'ugly' words-on-screen VSL)
signature_pieces.year: not stated (after the 2004 Fit Over 40 launch)
signature_pieces.where_to_read: Not publicly hosted. Benson describes it in I Love Marketing ep. 44 (ilovemarketing.com/episode-44the-one-with-jon-benson-video-sales-letters). The structure is in research/corpus/controls_webinar_vsl.json (id controls_webinar_vsl-06, full_text null).

signature_pieces.title: The Truth About Abs VSL (for Mike Geary)
signature_pieces.where_to_read: Described in the same episode. No public copy located.

candidates.way_in: The first ten seconds are a 'snap suggestion': a pattern break that drops the viewer's guard, carrying the suggestion 'You need something, and I want you to watch something.' Within the first ten slides comes the one thing to believe, in under 20 words: a benefit plus an enabler verb ('The only diet in the world that allows you to eat your favorite foods and still lose weight'). Next comes the speaker's own result as his credential, in a single plain sentence ('Personally, I lost 68 pounds, and I used to be obese').
candidates.proof_shape: One belief, proven and repeated. The speaker's own before and after comes first, then the enabler explained as the reason it works, then other people's results. Nothing is sold until the case is complete ('you haven't sold anyone until the very end'), and a script reveals the buy button at the pitch, so only viewers who sat through the argument see it ('far more qualified', he says). Length carries part of the persuasion: never under 15 minutes, best at 30 to 40.
candidates.voice: Words on a plain screen with no face, deliberately 'ugly'. Each slide is one centered sentence ending in an ellipsis or a colon, so there is never a natural place to stop. Slide density changes every few slides, and sometimes a slide holds three words. The writer reads it in his own voice, worked by 'the cadence, it's the tempo, it's the emphasis on certain words', slowing and stretching the key words, and 'You don't want to go to the radio voice.'
candidates.concerns: Every figure is his own (1% to 6.5%, doubling Geary's conversions), and the '$12B annually' claim is marketing. His 'inventor' claim is his own, though others repeat it. None of his VSLs is publicly hosted, so the exemplar would have to be reconstructed from his rules. One correction: the repo corpus entry controls_webinar_vsl-06 gives the button reveal at '16:34' as a fact, but on this session's read of the I Love Marketing transcript that time looks like a hypothetical example, and the transcript is garbled there. docs/03 already credits his intro and 'first 500 words' rules, and the vsl_long spec already encodes much of his structure. As a manner, his distinct contribution is the snap suggestion, the one-belief USP with its enabler, and the slide cadence.

candidates.way_in: The first minute decides the VSL, and he writes the lead last. It opens on a named authority's finding that the viewer could check (the BURN rewrite added 'a cool hook involving Harvard') with the curiosity turned up, so the viewer holds a fact and an unanswered question at once. candidates.proof_shape: The two-part unique mechanism. First the hidden cause of the problem, named and tied to research, so every fix the viewer has already tried makes sense as a failure ('They've been missing 1% of the answer', per docs/03; not re-fetched this session). Then the solution's mechanism as the reason the product works. Proof is loaded into the lead rather than saved for the end, and the argument travels inside an emotional story told by the presenter.

candidates.concerns: The only third-party figures come from Goff, who was Georgi's business partner when he wrote them (a conflict of interest), and they are unaudited. top_picks.name: Mike Palmer
top_picks.why: He has the strongest documented result in this exact format. AWAI (Aug 2013) credits him with The End of America, a 77-minute video per Wikipedia, which ran from Nov 2010, brought in about 500,000 paid subscribers, doubled Stansberry in under a year, and was called the most-imitated promotion of its decade. He is also AWAI's 2009 Copywriter of the Year, and he wrote the piece himself. His manner (warning card, dated forecast with the speaker's certainty, a numbered chain of cause, free advice before any product, the sale held to the end) is clearly unlike anything in the current set. The caveat is that it needs a ledgered, dated call.

top_picks.name: Jon Benson
top_picks.why: He originated the words-on-screen VSL, and his published rules are the template the format and this app's spec follow: the snap suggestion, a USP of one benefit plus an enabler in under 20 words, his own result as the credential, one sentence per slide ending open, read in his own cadence, and the button held until the case is complete. He wrote his VSLs himself. His results are self-reported (1% to 6.5%; Geary's Truth About Abs control unbeaten for almost two years), so he ranks below Palmer.

top_picks.name: Stefan Georgi
top_picks.why: He has the best-documented modern cold-traffic VSL lift: a peer reports that his rewrite of only the first minute of VShred's BURN VSL raised conversions 72% and took it from 30 to over 1,500 buyers a day. His manner is distinct: a lead written last on a checkable authority plus curiosity, and a two-part unique mechanism of the problem and the solution. notes:
Method limits. Every WebSearch call returned 'budget used up' (the 200-call cap shared across agents in this turn), so no search ran. All evidence comes from direct fetches of known URLs: AWAI, Wikipedia, I Love Marketing, Brian Deer, justingoff.com, copychief.com (the whole podcast feed was read), stefanpaulgeorgi.com, goldenhippo.com and easywebinar.com. Two hosts failed DNS and must be allowed in the session's network settings before they can be checked: www.evaldoalbuquerque.com and www.16wordsalesletter.com. rmbcmethod.com returned 403. A follow-up with search budget should verify, in priority order: (1) Albuquerque's Agora video promotions and their figures; (2) Craig Clemens' Gundry MD and Golden Hippo credit; (3) who wrote Agora Financial's 'Project Prophecy' (Jim Rickards), which docs/03 uses through Kyle Milligan's reading but whose writer I could not identify; (4) any surviving End of America transcript.

Considered and not ranked:
- Porter Stansberry presented End of America and supplied its thesis, but AWAI credits the copy to Palmer.
- Kyle Milligan scored '3 brand new controls' in his first year at Agora Financial (Copy Chief ep. 131), but the page does not say they were VSLs. He matters here as the annotator behind docs/03's Project Prophecy reading.
- Justin Goff owns offers and is the main peer source here; his own site lists no VSL credits.
- Dan Ferrari is called a 'copywriting legend' by Goff, but no VSL evidence turned up.
- Harmon Brothers belong to short video and ads (vsl_short, YouTube ads), not the long VSL.
- Brunson and Fladlien belong to webinars.
- Susan Berkley and Joshua Lee Henry appear in Copy Chief's VSL-related episodes, as a voice coach and a Banyan Hill copy chief, with no VSL credits stated.

Implications for the app (nothing in the repo was edited):
- The current video-family default manner is Carlton, who has no long-VSL record. Palmer or Benson would be format-native defaults.
- Benson's structure is already encoded in vsl_long.ts, so his manner adds the snap suggestion, the one-belief USP with its enabler, and the slide cadence. Palmer's adds the warning card, the dated forecast and the long withheld sale. Georgi's adds the authority-plus-curiosity first minute and the two-part mechanism.
- Palmer's way in fits the spec's existing lead option 'a dated prediction from the ledger'.
- Haddad's alter-ego narrator conflicts with the no-invented-narrator rule.

Corrections to the repo's own research files (not changed):
- research/corpus/controls_webinar_vsl.json, entry controls_webinar_vsl-06, treats the Every Other Day Diet button at '16:34' as fact. On this session's read of the I Love Marketing transcript, that time looks like a hypothetical example, and the transcript is garbled at that point.
- Entry controls_webinar_vsl-07 gives End of America as 77 minutes (Wikipedia), but a 2011 viewer called it 'about a 1/2 hour listen'. The two may describe different cuts.
- The AWAI bio page names The Secret Currency (79,000 subscribers, $5.2M) as Palmer's best promotion, while the newer AWAI 2013 page names End of America. Read the bio as older.

Availability is the weak point for every long-VSL master: none of the three top picks has a full control publicly hosted. Their exemplars would have to be acquired or reconstructed, which matters because the manner system leads with a whole exemplar.

field_strength_why: The short VSL (2 to 7 minutes, cold traffic) has no awards category, no hall of fame and no tradition of annotated swipe files the way the long sales letter does. The VSL's own originator, Jon Benson, says on the record that a selling VSL needs "Nothing under 15" minutes. So the documented masters of a 2 to 4 minute spoken pitch to cold traffic come from two neighboring traditions. The first is the direct-to-consumer viral video ad: Harmon Brothers, and Michael Dubin for Dollar Shave Club. The second is the two-minute direct response TV spot: Arthur Schiff, and Ron Popeil as pitchman. Each has named pieces with results, but most of those results were reported by the client or the agency. The bench is also short: one agency team, one founder with a single piece, and one TV copywriter whose stack close this format bans. Two candidates are clear. The third is a qualified pick.

The company estimated $12M for the year and reached $18M. CEO Bobby Edwards: "It's not only entertainment; it educates—it's edutainment."
Wikipedia: the unicorn ad "went viral" and "increased sales of the product"; more than five million Squatty Pottys sold overall. The article does not name who made the ad.

Agency press release dated April 28, 2020: Harmon Brothers "has earned national headlines, more than 1.5 billion views, and helped drive over $450 million in sales" with "Squatty Potty, Purple, Chatbooks, FiberFix, Poo-Pourri, and Lumē." This is also the source that ties Poo-Pourri and Purple to the agency.
Agency homepage: "Our clients' ads have been seen billions of times and have driven over $1 Billion in sales."

Keto Chow co-founder Chris Bair, quoted on the agency's page: "Three months after we launched the first ad, our revenue increased 121%." The agency adds an extra $7.1M in under six months after the second ad.

GoTREADS 'Sprint' spokesperson ad, December 2020: the agency says sales grew 4,300% in less than a year and half of 2020's sales came in December. The agency defines Sprint as "Instead of focusing on world-building and comedy first, the focus is on sales."

candidates.way_in: A spokesperson in frame says, deadpan, the one thing the product's category never says out loud, about what is in front of him right now. In Squatty Potty, a prince stands beside a unicorn whose soft-serve stands in for what the product helps. In Poo-Pourri, a composed, elegant woman seated on a toilet talks frankly about the smell. The visual gag is a picture of the mechanism, so the laugh and the promise land in the same line. The next line turns the joke into a design flaw the viewer inherited: the usual way has one fault, and it is not his fault. To imitate it, open on the speaker naming the taboo or absurd thing in frame, then name the single flaw in the usual way in plain words.
candidates.proof_shape: One mechanism sentence, chosen by testing which explanation makes viewers get it (for Squatty Potty, the kink that sitting puts in the colon). It is acted out with a physical stand-in the viewer can watch (the kinked colon, the barrier the spray forms on the water). The usual way is shown failing, then the product shown working. Then come quick third-party mentions and counts the client actually holds (Shark Tank, Dr. Oz, customer counts in Squatty Potty), a guarantee when one exists (Poo-Pourri's money-back guarantee), one CTA to the site, and a callback joke as the last line. Every joke carries a selling point, so the mechanism argument still stands with the jokes cut. The Sprint variant keeps one spokesperson and puts the sale ahead of the comedy, which is the version that fits this format.
candidates.voice: A straight-faced spokesperson playing a heightened character (a prince, a refined lady) against crude or ordinary subject matter. Puns on the product's own nouns, one joke per beat, delivered flat and never winking. Short spoken sentences cut to visuals. The product name, price and URL are said plainly, never as a joke.
candidates.concerns: Team authorship: no individual writer is credited in any page I read, so the persona is a house style, not a person. Much of the effect is production (casting, puppetry, editing). A text engine can carry the mechanism sentence, the deadpan and the joke-that-sells, not the visuals. The fairy-tale versions use several characters, but this format allows one speaker and bans lines for anyone else, so the persona must be the one-spokesperson Sprint version. The pieces contain unledgered authority lines (Squatty Potty's 'studies show', Poo-Pourri's 'clinically proven') that the factual review must flag. Almost every figure is client- or agency-reported, and Squatty Potty's growth overlaps its Shark Tank exposure. The agency book linked from its blog (pooptogoldbook.com, apparently 'From Poop to Gold') could not be reached: that host is outside this session's allowed network domains.

signature_pieces.title: DollarShaveClub.com - Our Blades Are F***ing Great
signature_pieces.where_to_read: YouTube video ZUG9qYTJMsI (about 90 seconds, roughly 250 words; transcribe from the video)

candidates.way_in: The founder, on camera in his own warehouse, gives his name, his company and the whole deal (a price low enough to be news, and what arrives) in the first two sentences, with no setup. He then asks out loud the viewer's own skeptical question about quality and answers it with a flat "No" that flips into an overstated yes, and that line is the video's title. To imitate it: the speaker names himself and the deal as one fact, then puts the doubt in the viewer's mouth and overturns it in one line. It works only when the price or deal is the news and the speaker is the owner.
candidates.proof_shape: He takes objections one beat at a time, in the order a buyer raises them: is it any good; what the brand-name alternative costs and what that money really pays for; the features he is paying for and does not need; forgetting to restock. Each is answered by a one-line joke or sight gag that is itself a reason. The product and a staff member appear in frame as he talks (the 'creating jobs' beat). There are no testimonials, no statistics and no stack. The deal is restated in one line and the CTA is literal.
candidates.voice: Deadpan founder monologue while walking, with short declaratives and rhetorical questions. Dry, mock-serious delivery with one gag per sentence. He mocks the category's excess, never the viewer. One profane overstatement carries the quality claim; the engine would use a flat overstatement instead.
candidates.concerns: One piece only: a persona built on a single 90-second control is thin, and the lines are so well known that the six-word rule will bite. The writing credit is not verified here. Naming the product and price in line one suits only product-aware or most-aware cold traffic; the spec bars the product name before the awareness state allows it. The joke about where the competitor's money goes needs a ledger row, since the spec bans unledgered competitor details. The profanity cannot ship. At about 250 words it sits at the floor of the 250-1,050 word band.

candidates.name: Arthur Schiff
candidates.role: Direct response TV copywriter (1940-2006). Creative director at Dial Media under Ed Valenti and Barry Becher, then ran his own firm for 23 years. Wrote the Ginsu knife commercials.

evidence.claim: Produced over 1,800 direct-response TV spots in 23 at his own firm. In 1978, with Valenti and Becher, he rebranded Quikut knives as Ginsu. The best-known ad opens with a karate chop through a board and the copy "In Japan, the hand can be used like a knife. But this method doesn't work with a tomato." His signature line is "But wait, there's more!" and he also coined "Isn't that amazing?"

Valenti, Becher and copywriter Arthur Schiff created the Ginsu name and its commercials. The commercials generated sales of between two and three million Ginsu sets from 1978 to 1984 (a campaign figure, not Schiff's alone).
Attribution conflict: Ron Popeil's Wikipedia article credits Popeil with popularizing "But wait, there's more!" on television by the mid-1950s.

signature_pieces.title: Ginsu knife TV commercial (the karate-chop and tomato opening)
signature_pieces.where_to_read: Archived TV spots on YouTube; the opening lines are quoted on https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Schiff

signature_pieces.title: Steakhouse Onion Machine, Ambervision Sunglasses and Shiwala car mop spots
signature_pieces.where_to_read: Named on Wikipedia. Scripts are largely unarchived.

candidates.way_in: The usual way, tried in frame and failing, staged as a spectacle in the first seconds: a hand chops through a board, then the same hand fails on a tomato, and the voice-over says what the viewer just saw. The problem is shown, not described, and the product enters as the thing that does what the usual tool could not. To imitate it: open on the usual fix being tried right now, in the speaker's present, and failing on an everyday object. That is exactly this format's 'usual fix fails first' beat moved to line one.
candidates.proof_shape: Demonstration in two directions. First a torture test: the product does something hard that should ruin it. Then the delicate everyday task the usual tool fails at, such as a paper-thin tomato slice. Each beat ends with a question the viewer answers with his own eyes ("Isn't that amazing?"). No testimonials or statistics; the demonstration is the whole proof. In the original an escalating stack follows ("But wait, there's more!"). This format drops it for one offer line and the next step.
candidates.voice: Announcer voice-over over the product shown working: fast, exclamatory, one short line per cut. Rhetorical questions, plain kitchen nouns, and a coined product name that suggests a quality (Ginsu evoked a samurai sword).
candidates.concerns: This is TV, not online, and his best-known work closes with the stack this format forbids, so the persona must carry the opening and the demonstration, never the close. Little of his copy survives in text: only the Ginsu opening is quoted at a source I read, and his 1,800 other spots are mostly unarchived. The Ginsu exoticism (a meaningless pseudo-Japanese name, an exchange student cast as the chef) is dated and should not carry over. 'But wait, there's more' is also credited to Popeil. The Ginsu sales figure belongs to the Valenti, Becher and Schiff campaign, not to Schiff alone. He fits only offers with something physical or visible to demonstrate.

Listed in the Direct Response Hall of Fame. Electronic Retail Association Lifetime Achievement Award (2001). Ig Nobel Prize (1993) as "perpetual pitchman of late night television". signature_pieces.where_to_read: YouTube; Gladwell, 'The Pitchman', The New Yorker, Oct 30, 2000 (the New Yorker blocked fetching in this session)

candidates.proof_shape: Continuous live demonstration as the whole proof. The result is shown on the spot, then the price reveal and the stack.
candidates.voice: Pitchman's patter: rhythmic, repetitive chant-lines ('Set it and forget it'), warm and relentless.
candidates.concerns: The fetched sources do not say whether he scripted his pitches. He is mostly a performer-inventor. His landmark work is the 28-minute infomercial, a different format. His manner overlaps Schiff's demonstration pitch, and Schiff has the clearer writing credit, so Popeil is better used as an extra exemplar under a Schiff-style manner than as a separate persona.

candidates.name: Jon Benson

His one short piece: "I did this for a 6-minute YouTube video" and "the conversions were like 7,000%", with no baseline given.
On length: "18 minutes is the shortest" and "Nothing under 15". "The most successful that we've done is anywhere from 30 to 40 minutes."

candidates.proof_shape: His own result as credibility (a personal weight loss), the mechanism as the enabler, then testimonials and guarantee. The buy button is held back until the argument is complete.
candidates.voice: Words on a plain screen, one sentence per slide, with his own voice-over slowing on key words. Sentences are left open so the viewer cannot predict the next slide.
candidates.concerns: He is a master of the long VSL, not the short one. His own guidance is that a selling VSL needs 15 minutes or more. His only short piece is not public and its '7,000%' figure has no baseline. All figures are self-reported. He belongs in vsl_long, not here.

top_picks.name: Harmon Brothers (agency team)
top_picks.why: They have the strongest documented results for a 2 to 4 minute spoken pitch to cold traffic. top_picks.name: Michael Dubin
top_picks.why: The most-cited founder-on-camera short pitch, with a documented outcome: 12,000 orders in two days and the 2012 Ad Age Viral Video Award (Wikipedia, citing NYT and LA Times). It is the purest example of this format's 'promise, mechanism and who is talking in one breath' plus objections answered one per beat with no stack. It suits product-aware cold traffic where the deal itself is news and the owner is the speaker. Caveats: a single piece, and the writing credit is widely reported but was not verified at a source in this pass.

top_picks.name: Arthur Schiff
top_picks.why: A qualified pick, and the only proven writer of the 'one voice over the product shown working' mode this format allows. He wrote 1,800+ direct response TV spots, including Ginsu (2-3 million sets, 1978-84, a campaign figure). His opening shows the usual way failing on camera before the product does the job, a ready-made version of this format's demonstration beat. notes:
How this was researched: the shared web-search budget for the run was already exhausted when this task started, so I ran no web searches. All evidence comes from pages I fetched directly, plus the project's own corpus (research/corpus/controls_webinar_vsl.json and controls_ads_social.json, verified by the project on 2026-10-24), which supplied the YouTube video IDs and beat sketches. Anything I did not read at the URL I give is marked verified_at_source false.

Fetches that failed:
- nytimes.com, latimes.com and newyorker.com were refused by the fetch tool; adage.com returned 403.
- YouTube redirected to a captcha, so no script was transcribed.
- pooptogoldbook.com (the Harmon Brothers book linked from their blog) is outside this session's allowed network domains. It has to be allowed in the network settings to read it.
- Wikipedia returned 404 for Orabrush and for the Purple company page.

As a result, no exact script lines beyond the Ginsu and 'Here in my garage' openings are verified. Dubin's lines are described by their moves, not quoted.

Leads worth checking in a follow-up with search budget:
- Jeffrey Harmon's 2009 Orabrush 'bad breath test' YouTube video. It is the strongest unverified fit for this format's 'test the viewer runs on himself' demonstration.
- Purple's raw-egg spokesperson ads by Harmon Brothers.
- Russell Brunson's 'Who, What, Why, How' short sales-video script from DotCom Secrets. It is the most-taught short VSL template in info-marketing, but he is famous for teaching, and none of his own short scripts with results was found.
- Entrepreneur's account of Harmon Brothers' message testing for Squatty Potty.

Fit with the current manner set:
- None of these candidates is already in the set.
- The engine's default manner for the video family is Carlton, who has no documented short-video work. A Harmon-style manner (unaware or low-sophistication consumer offers with a demonstrable mechanism) and a Dubin-style manner (product-aware offers where the deal is news and the owner speaks) would cover the cold short VSL better.
- A Schiff-style manner covers voice-over demonstration of physical products.
- Any persona built from these needs the factual review to flag the unledgered authority lines found in the source pieces ('studies show', 'clinically proven').
- These manners must drop the stack, profanity and multi-character casts, which this format's spec forbids.

field_strength_why: This format has no recognized masters by the brief's standard. I found no writer with a documented Meta ad control, no published split test credited to a named copywriter's own ad text, and no award or hall of fame for paid-social primary text. The few copy-only results on file have no writer behind them, or one unnamed staffer. AdEspresso's $1,000 length test used a staff writer and published its copy only as images. Its Strategyzer rewrite ("our own marketing expert" Sarah Sal) is a single case. The research corpus's long-running Meta ads (moda.app) name only brands. The best-known names fall into two groups. Strategists and media buyers (Hott, Kusmich, King Kong, Hormozi's course) are known for buying and teaching, not for ad text anyone can read. Info-marketers (Kern, Deiss) have their Facebook ads in swipe files, but only as images from 2014-2016, with no performance figures and usually no named writer. swiped.co's Facebook Ad type has 38 files. In every one I opened, the ad copy was shown only as an image, with no results figures. The repo already records the gap: research/README.md says "No human Meta ads could be collected, so that format has no human control yet."

notes:
The brief allows naming fewer than three, and two is all the evidence supports here. Both picks are provisional, and the plain verdict is that this format has no recognized masters by the brief's standard. Neither pick meets criterion 1 (documented results in this format), and neither has a whole ad transcribed for study.

My web search allowance was used up before my first search: the 200-search limit is shared by every agent in this run, and other agents had already spent it. So I did no open searching. Everything above comes from fetching specific known pages (swiped.co's Facebook Ad type and person pages, AdEspresso, the candidates' own sites) and from the repo. Several fetches failed: Wikipedia has no page for Kern or Hormozi, the DigitalMarketer ad-templates URL returned 404, Kim Walsh Phillips's domain now redirects to an unrelated site, and the Hormozi course lessons are video-only. Some names I could not check at all and have not graded: Hormozi's paid-ads chapters in $100M Leads, the long-form coaching ads of Russ Ruffino, Sam Ovens, Dan Henry and Alen Sultanic, Billy Gene, Ezra Firestone's ads for Boom by Cindy Joseph, Dara Denney and Savannah Sanchez for UGC-style text, and Kim Walsh Phillips's book with Dan Kennedy. If you want a second pass, send a follow-up message and I will search those names and pull their ads from the Meta Ad Library.

What the evidence supports instead:
- The proof for this format sits in tests and long-running brand ads, not in writers. AdEspresso found mid-to-long text gave the lowest cost per lead, with the best text 2.4 times cheaper than the worst, and 89% of polled marketers had bet on the losing short versions. field_strength_why: Skippable pre-roll is young (TrueView era, from about 2010), and the evidence for it is thin by direct response standards. There is no Caples or AWAI-style award for DR YouTube ads, no published split tests between named scripts, and almost no individual writer credits, because most scripts come from agency teams or from founders who appear on camera. Nearly every sales figure is reported by the company or the agency. Two practitioners still stand out. Harmon Brothers is one house with repeated results across many products, including a third-party publication quoting Squatty Potty's CEO on 600% online sales growth. Michael Dubin wrote one founder piece, Dollar Shave Club, and the press reported its results: 12,000 orders in two days and an Ad Age Viral Video Award. Below those two the field is single viral pieces (Tai Lopez's garage pre-roll, Blendtec), agency work with no named writer (Raindrop for Dr. Squatch, #1 on YouTube's 2020 TrueView for Action leaderboard by the agency's own account) and teachers (Tom Breeze). None of the nine masters already in the set has documented work in this format.

candidates.way_in: A straight-faced speaker puts one absurd but on-message picture in frame and says, in line one, the plain fact the category avoids. In Poo-Pourri, a prim woman on a toilet talks about poop. In Squatty Potty, a prince stands beside a unicorn whose output is soft-serve. The picture carries the joke and the line carries the fact, so the viewer cannot skip and cannot misunderstand what the product is for. In the app: the real speaker, with the product or the demonstration starting in frame, says the blunt fact while the odd image plays it out.
candidates.proof_shape: First find the one mechanism sentence that makes the product click: they test five sales messages before scripting. Build the whole ad around that sentence. Say the design flaw in one line ('The modern day toilet is convenient, but has one major fault; it requires us to sit'), show it with a visual analogy, then show the product as the fix. Then an extreme demonstration that settles it (GoTREADS freeing a firetruck). Authority and counts follow (Shark Tank, Dr. Oz, customers), then the guarantee and one CTA. End on a callback to the opening image ('Pooping will never be the same and neither will ice cream').
candidates.voice: Deadpan, family-friendly crude and dense with puns ('Stools for Better Stools'). Every laugh line carries a benefit or a reason, and the joke never interrupts the mechanism. One spokesperson who looks like the buyer (their 'love group'), talking to camera for two to four minutes.
candidates.concerns: This is a house, not one writer: no fetched page credits an individual writer on any ad. The persona would be 'Harmon Brothers', with Daniel Harmon as creative lead. Nearly all results are agency- or client-reported, and the aggregates conflict ($1B, $700M, $300M). Their signature device, a fictional character narrator (prince, witch), collides with the standard's rule against generated narrators. The app's version must keep the real speaker named by role and put the absurdity in the picture or the demonstration, never in an invented person. Their 'studies show' and Shark Tank or Dr. Oz lines need ledger IDs. Hero pieces can run past the spec's 180-second, 480-word cap, so use the Sprint shape (one spokesperson, shorter).

candidates.way_in: The maker gives his first name and title, then states the offer and its price as a plain fact in the first breath: what he sends, for how much, and where. He follows it with the quality claim he would bet the company on, said bluntly and slightly profanely. The deal is the hook. In the app's terms: line one is the offer as a fact from the person who makes it, line two is the claim he will stand behind, and the name and role come right after.
candidates.proof_shape: No testimonials and no numbers beyond the price. The proof is candor plus the real place: he walks through his own warehouse. Then the features nobody needs. Then forgetting to buy blades, which the subscription fixes. A named employee stands in for the company being real. The saving is restated, then the URL.
candidates.voice: Deadpan, dry and sarcastic, one joke per sentence. The mockery is aimed at the category's over-engineering and pricing, never at the viewer. The price and the promise are never buried under a joke. Short and fast, about 90 seconds.
candidates.concerns: One landmark piece, not a body of work, so copy for study is thin. It was a launch video posted on YouTube that went viral. No fetched source says whether it ran as paid skippable pre-roll, so it fits this format's craft more than its placement. field_strength_why: This format has no recognized masters the way the long-form manners do. I found no hall of fame, AWAI-style award or Caples-style control naming an individual writer of 15-45 second vertical scripts. The evidence that does exist is weak in three ways: (a) platform case studies that credit an agency and report lifts against the brand's own other creative (TikTok on BYLT and The Social Savannah); (b) self-reported CTRs and spend figures from practitioners on podcasts; (c) press-reported results from neighboring formats: a 2012 founder-to-camera YouTube video, and organic creator reviews. Most of the craft sits with agencies, in-house teams and creators who are never named. The scripts are almost never published as text, so they have to be watched in ad libraries or on the platforms. The people most often named as experts (Denney, Hott, Kane, the Foreplay expert roster) are known for teaching or for agency work, not for documented scripts of their own.

notes:
Research limits. The shared WebSearch budget for this run was already used up at my first search call, so all sourcing came from fetching known URLs directly and following links on pages I fetched. Every claim marked verified was read at the URL given. Not verified, and worth a follow-up search pass (the user can send a follow-up message or raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION):
(1) Kallaway, Alex Hormozi (short-form hooks; his Wikipedia URL returned 404), Brock Johnson and Dylan Lemay. All are organic short-form scripting educators, likely to be discounted as famous for teaching.
(2) Founder-to-camera DR on TikTok and Meta: Bobbi Brown's Jones Road ads. Only the revenue was verified: $20M in year one and over $150M expected, per the FT via Wikipedia; nothing about the ads. Also Allison Ellsworth's Poppi TikToks (Wikipedia gives no video detail).
(3) TikTok Ad Awards and Cannes Social & Creator Lions winners, to see whether any individual writer is credited.
(4) Top TikTok Shop affiliate creators with third-party GMV data.
(5) Who wrote the Dollar Shave Club script (widely said to be Dubin), and a fetchable transcript.

Format context verified at TikTok's creative best practices page (https://ads.tiktok.com/help/article/creative-best-practices?lang=en): 'Introduce your content proposition in the first 3 seconds', 'Prioritize your hook in the first 6 seconds', '5-10 words per second when using text', and 'featuring people such as creators, employees, or customers'. This supports the spec's choice of a real person on camera, and it means the masters of this format are more often creators and founders than copywriters.

Already in the repo's corpus, for context: Hyram/CeraVe (controls_ads_social-43), Nathan Apodaca/Ocean Spray (-42, wordless, not a persona) and Stanley/The Buy Guide (-44), plus a self-reported hook test by Elliott Botterill (split_tests_email_ads_sms-50).

Peer recognition in this field mostly comes from vendor rosters: Foreplay lists 67 'experts', including Denney, Sanchez, Hott, Levinger, Shackelford and Crespi. I treated that as weak evidence, since it is a tool company's marketing.

Recommendation for the owner. If only one persona is added for this format, make it the Sanchez 'native frame, first use on camera' manner. The Dubin 'founder says the offer in the first breath, deadpan' manner is the strongest second, because it matches the spec's line-one options and the standard's real-speaker rule. Hyram's 'reviewer's verdict' fits only when the speaker really is an independent reviewer.

No existing manner (Halbert, Carlton, Hopkins, Schwartz, Bencivenga, Sugarman, Ogilvy, Caples, Collier) has documented work in this format. Hopkins's self-test opening and Ogilvy's one-fact first line carry over best as companions. No files in the repository were edited.

field_strength_why: This format has no recognized masters in the sense the other formats do. An RSA is a set of assets that Google assembles at auction, so there is no fixed piece that can become a control, be swiped or win an award. The public evidence is aggregate vendor data (Google's own Ad Strength figures, Adalysis's 5,900-account studies, Optmyzr's 13,671-account study) and testing methods, not named ads with results. The most-studied writer of search ads, Perry Marshall, did his readable work on the fixed-order text ad from before 2018, and his split-test examples sit in his book, not online. The repo's own earlier corpus run reached the same result (research/corpus/controls_ads_social.json, entry controls_ads_social-45: "no example RSA with CTR data was found in fetched sources"). I could not verify any award program (Caples, Effie, Cannes, DMA) that names search-ad copywriters. Two practitioners carry a distinct, describable way of writing this format. Both come with caveats, and neither is a master in the Halbert or Caples sense.

candidates.name: Perry Marshall
candidates.role: Direct-response consultant and author. With Bryan Todd he wrote The Definitive Guide to Google AdWords (2006) and the Ultimate Guide to Google AdWords (2007); later editions, retitled Ultimate Guide to Google Ads, were co-authored with Mike Rhodes. He writes and split-tests search ads himself and taught CTR split testing as the method for this format.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia: "With Bryan Todd, he wrote The Definitive Guide to Google AdWords in 2006, and Ultimate Guide to Google AdWords in 2007"; he "learned to use Google AdWords soon after it was first introduced."
The Amazon listing for 'Ultimate Guide to Google Adwords: How to Access 100 Million People in 10 Minutes' (ISBN 9781599184418) credits Perry Marshall and Bryan Todd.

In 'Writing Google Ads: Escape the Rut' (Feb 2, 2010) he shows the ad he wrote for a Roundtable member: "My name is Janet / 37, Married, Overweight, Exhausted / I feel like the living dead / www.MedicalConditionX.com/tired_all_the_time", set against the typical "Medical Condition X / Learn About Condition X Symptoms / Treatment & Prevention - Better Health". The page reports no result for it.

On testing: "Most people think they've tested 20 ads. Actually they've just tested 2 ads 10 times." His author bio there says he "wrote the world's best selling book on Google advertising" (an unsourced sales claim).

"You can change the CTR of your ads by 50% just by changing ONE WORD" (a general claim with no test shown); "your copy - your choice of words - is king"; "When you're writing those little ads, little hinges swing BIG doors!"; he advises writing different ads for searchers at different stages and sending each to a matching page.
"The one thing that matters on Google is relevance" ("message-to-market match"); "Your message must match what the person is thinking"; "Imagine that you are not you. You are your customer."
He publishes a free split-test calculator (built by Brian Teasley) that checks whether one ad's CTR win over another is likely to hold.
His reading level rule for copy: "Keep your copy in the Grade 4-7 range"; talk about the reader ("You" - "Your") more than yourself.
He names his influences: "Any direct marketer has been enormously influenced by Claude Hopkins whether they read his stuff or not"; "A definitely big influence in my business life is Dan Kennedy."

signature_pieces.title: Writing Google Ads: Escape the Rut (the 'My name is Janet' ad against the category ad)
Ultimate Guide to Google AdWords (with Bryan Todd); later editions titled Ultimate Guide to Google Ads (with Mike Rhodes and Bryan Todd). His ad split-test examples are in the book.
signature_pieces.year: 2007 (first edition, per Wikipedia); later editions not checked

signature_pieces.title: A Google AdWords Lesson from the Wall Street Journal (one word, 50% CTR; different ads per search stage)

candidates.way_in: Headline one is the searcher's own query, whole, so the ad reads as the answer to what he just typed. The next headlines drop the category's words for the prospect's own words about how he feels or where he is stuck (the Janet move: "37, Married, Overweight, Exhausted" against the category's "Learn About Condition X Symptoms"). The display path carries one more phrase of his ("/tired_all_the_time"). Mapped to this app: 3-4 headlines carry the keyword whole; 3-4 say his state or want in words taken from the research verbatims, never an invented "My name is" persona; the two 15-character path fields carry a phrase of his.
candidates.proof_shape: The real proof is the split test, not a line in the ad. Two ads run at once, differing in one word or one line, CTR is compared for significance, and the winner becomes the control. Inside the ad the proof is specificity: one concrete fact about the reader's situation that the generic category ad cannot say, and its relevance to the exact query. For this app: a proof headline is the concrete fact (a ledger row) or the reader's own test, and it sits next to a headline in the reader's words.
candidates.voice: Blunt and plain at a grade 4-7 reading level, with 'you' more than 'we' and concrete nouns. It is personal and a little provocative: it sounds like the prospect's own complaint read back to him, not the advertiser's catalogue label.
candidates.concerns: (1) His studied work is the fixed-order text ad (headline, two lines, display URL), so his line-to-line sequences break under RSA assembly; the app's rule that every asset stands alone has to override them. (2) The Janet ad uses an invented first-person narrator. The app forbids generating a narrator, so the move must be rebuilt from verbatim reader words, said as a plain label or in the second person. (3) The app's spec bans quality words and one-shape headlines but has no rule on emotional state lines; "I feel like the living dead" would need the ledger and verbatims behind it. (4) The book's split tests and results were not verified here (the book was not reachable), and all online figures are self-reported: the 50% one-word claim, "world's best selling book", and "laid the foundations for the $800B digital advertising industry" (bio page). (5) Co-authorship (Bryan Todd; later Mike Rhodes; the 'read the diary' exercise was led by Howie Jacobson) blurs whose copy is whose in the book. (6) Much of his later fame is teaching and consulting (80/20, Roundtable), which counts against him under the brief's rules.

candidates.name: Brad Geddes
candidates.role: PPC strategist and ad tester. Author of Advanced Google AdWords (Wiley, 3rd ed., May 2014, 704 pp.) and co-founder of Adalysis (ad-testing software), whose blog publishes his large-sample RSA studies. He is a strategist whose RSA structure (pinned keyword H1, one tested theme per ad) is the testers' standard, not a writer with famous ads.

evidence.claim: Wiley's author bio: "the first and only Advanced AdWords Seminar leader that Google selected to conduct seminars for top businesses"; the description promises "Discover how to craft winning ad copy". Publication date May 2014.
Adalysis: "A pioneer in the PPC field, Brad Geddes has been shaping the industry since 1998." and "His book, 'Advanced Google AdWords,' is considered the definitive guide to Google's ad platform."

RSA pinning study (byline "Brad", 5,900 accounts, Oct 2026): H1 is typically "Related to the keywords in the ad group; often contains the keyword", H2 "A CTA, benefit, or feature", H3 "Rarely shows... often a headline that talks about the business"; "Unpinned ads have an average of 13.53 headlines"; "as you pin more, your CTR drops"; advertisers pinning all three headlines have "a vastly superior conversion rate" (also the most active testers); "If you plan to analyze and act on your ad test data, then pinning all three headlines is a good idea."

Ad strength study (byline "Brad", Oct 2026): in the same ad group the higher-strength ad got more impressions in 63% of ad groups, but "Across all ad groups, the higher ad strength ads had an 11.8% higher CPA". Unpinned Excellent ads need at least 11 varied headlines (benefits, features, CTAs, keywords, authority statements).

Customer-insight test (byline "Brad"; ads shown only as screenshots): "The highest CTR was a call to action to visit a local showroom"; the next-day delivery ad was "our best ad across every other metric"; "customers don't care about price matching"; he estimates that removing that line would have earned another $16,201 in revenue over 30 days.

RSA data post (byline "Brad", Sept 2026): ads without keyword insertion performed better on CTR and conversion rate; the free-quote message beat the 'affordable' message on CTR but lost on conversion rate; "It's usually better not to mix brand and non-brand."

Adalysis Ad Testing Guide (no individual author named): build each test on a hypothesis (prices vs discounts, CTA vs benefits, business credibility vs ease); judge by conversions per impression (CPI) after filtering by CPA; "Never go below 90% confidence factors"; mine losing ads for lines that won one metric.

signature_pieces.title: Data study: What 5,900 accounts reveal about RSA pinning
Google Ads data study: Does a higher ad strength improve your performance?
How to gain customer insight through ad testing
Advanced Google AdWords, 3rd edition

candidates.way_in: Headline one is the ad group's keyword (pinned to position 1). Headline two (pinned, with two or three variants) is the one theme this RSA exists to test: a call to action, a benefit or a feature, chosen from a hypothesis such as price vs discount, CTA vs benefit, business credibility vs ease, location, or delivery. Headline three is about the business. Each RSA in an ad group carries one theme, at most three RSAs per ad group, and brand stays apart from non-brand.
candidates.proof_shape: The proof is the concrete fact that decides the purchase, said as a label: next-day delivery, a free quote, a local showroom, the price shown or not, or an authority statement with a count when the business has one. Which fact wins is settled by the test, not the writer: conversions per impression under a CPA ceiling, 90%+ confidence, results aggregated across ad groups, and losing ads mined for lines that won one metric.
candidates.voice: Functional, retail-plain labels of service facts, with no wit and no slogan. He drops dynamic keyword insertion (it lost on CTR and conversion rate in his reported test) and keeps brand lines out of non-brand ads. It reads like shelf tags in a well-run store: what you get, how fast, what it costs, what to do.
candidates.concerns: (1) No named controls and no readable ad text: his published tests show the ads only as screenshots, so a writer can study the structure but not the sentences. (2) All results come from Adalysis, his own company (company-reported), and the Adalysis bylines read only "Brad" (the about page names co-founder Brad Geddes). (3) This is a test design and a slotting structure more than a voice; as a persona it changes what the assets are about and where they sit, not how they sound. (4) Pinning conflicts with the app's spec (every asset stands alone, no pins) and with Google's advice that "pinning isn't recommended for most advertisers" (support.google.com/google-ads/answer/7684791), though his data says pinning lowers CTR and raises conversion rate. (5) The Wiley bio is publisher copy, usually author-supplied.

top_picks.name: Perry Marshall
top_picks.why: He is the only candidate who wrote search ads himself, published them, and has a move a writer can imitate. The ad opens on the searcher's own query, then speaks in the prospect's diary words instead of the category's (the 'My name is Janet / 37, Married, Overweight, Exhausted' ad against 'Learn About Condition X Symptoms'), and the display path carries one more of his phrases. His method is one-variable CTR split testing. Wikipedia confirms the canonical book on the format (2006/2007, with Bryan Todd). Qualifications: his work is pre-RSA fixed-order text ads, his book's split-test results were not verified here and online figures are self-reported, and the Janet move uses an invented narrator, so for this app it must be rebuilt from research verbatims.

top_picks.name: Brad Geddes
top_picks.why: A strategist and tester whose structure is the best RSA-specific evidence available. H1 is the pinned keyword, H2 is the one theme the ad tests (price vs discount, CTA vs benefit, credibility vs ease, delivery, location), H3 is about the business, and there is one theme per RSA. The proof is the concrete purchase fact (next-day delivery, free quote, showroom, price), and conversions per impression decide what wins. He has large-sample studies (5,900 accounts) and Google selected him as its Advanced AdWords Seminar leader (publisher bio). Qualifications: all data is from his own company, his ads can be read only as screenshots, and the manner is a slotting and testing structure more than a voice. No third pick deserves the slot: the others are teachers or tool-builders with no readable ads or distinct manner. Caples (already in set, the engine's ad default) remains the right fallback, because a 30-character RSA headline is a tested-headline problem.

notes:
LIMITS ON THIS RESEARCH: the web search budget for this turn (200 calls shared by all agents) was already used up at my first query, so I made no web searches. All evidence comes from direct fetches of known URLs and is quoted only from pages I read. Several sources were blocked: Search Engine Land author pages (403), WordStream (403), Medium (403), O'Reilly (403) and PPC Hero ranking pages (404 on guessed URLs). Amazon gave only title and co-authors, and a scripted fetch of it was refused. Candidates I considered but could not verify, so they are left out of the candidate list: Larry Kim (WordStream founder, known for aggregate ad-copy CTR analyses and the 'unicorn' ad idea; no page readable); Andrew Goodman (Page Zero Media; its site says "we wrote the book on it" without naming the book or author); Glenn Livingston (his guinea-pig keyword and ad split tests are reportedly in Marshall's book; not fetched); Search Engine Land Landy awards and PPC Hero 'most influential' lists (not reachable). If the owner wants these checked, a follow-up turn with a fresh search budget can do it.

FINDINGS THAT BEAR ON THE APP'S google_rsa SPEC (no files were changed):
(a) Pinning: Geddes's 5,900-account study found that pinning lowers CTR but raises conversion rate, and that active testers pin all three headlines. Google says "pinning isn't recommended for most advertisers" and to "try to pin 2 or 3 unique headlines or descriptions to each position" (https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/7684791). The spec does not pin. A Geddes manner would want H1 pinned to keyword headlines.
(b) Ad Strength: Google reports Poor to Excellent gives "15% more clicks & conversions on average" (internal data, Aug 2025). Geddes's head-to-head study found the higher-strength ad got more impressions in 63% of ad groups but averaged an 11.8% higher CPA. Both are company-reported and they conflict. The spec's 15 distinct headlines in five shapes matches what both reward (Excellent needs 11+ varied headlines; unpinned ads average 13.53).
(c) Dynamic keyword insertion lost on CTR and conversion rate in Geddes's reported test, which supports the spec's plain keyword headlines.
(d) Sentence case: KlientBoost's PPC ad copy page (https://www.klientboost.com/ppc/ppc-ad-copy/) reports a 2014 Periscopix test in which title case "performed better" than sentence case, especially on mobile. The numbers were in charts I could not read, and the test predates RSAs. It is weak evidence against the spec's sentence-case rule and worth a re-check.
(e) Google reports going from one to two RSAs per ad group gives "a 6.6% increase in conversions at a similar cost per conversion" and two to three gives 3.7%. Geddes builds up to three RSAs per ad group, one theme each. The app writes one RSA per piece.

HOW A MARSHALL MANNER WOULD FIT THE APP'S RULES: the Janet ad's first-person persona is an invented narrator, which the standard forbids. The transferable move is the reader's own words about his state, taken from research verbatims, said as plain labels or in the second person, plus the 15-character path fields used as one more phrase of his. His split-test method fits the app's challenger logic (variants that differ in one word). Marshall credits Claude Hopkins as an influence (interview page), and Hopkins is already in the set.

ALREADY IN SET: none of Halbert, Carlton, Hopkins, Schwartz, Bencivenga, Sugarman, Ogilvy, Caples or Collier is a documented practitioner of this format. Caples is the engine's default for the ad family and stays a reasonable fallback, but I found no evidence that any of them wrote search ads.

candidates.way_in: Line one is two to six words naming a state the reader is in, said flat with no number and no product: "Most people are stuck." "I burned out chasing perfection." Or it is a short question that calls up a feeling ("Remember the good old days?" "Is your life on autopilot?"). A third variant quotes what a boss is saying now and sets it up to be disagreed with. Line two drops straight into the scene behind the feeling: the commute, the meeting, the boss, the old job.
candidates.proof_shape: The proof is his own before-and-after, never a customer. First the corporate executive who burned out building other people's companies, then the one-person business now, carried by his own numbers (revenue, hours, no employees). Next comes the lesson in short stacked lines, each adding one thing. The sell comes last as a quiet pointer to where he teaches the system (the newsletter or a course), with the link outside the post body.
candidates.voice: Calm and unhurried, never hype. Very short lines with a lot of white space, plain words, "I" and "you" mixed. No exclamation marks. He argues gently against hustle, scale and busyness, like an older colleague who got out and is telling you what he found.
candidates.concerns: His hooks lean on one-line maxims ("You can just do things." "The right people change everything."). The app's spec bans slogans, maxims, reframes and one-line paragraphs that land a maxim. The persona should take his feeling-first line one and his own-numbers before-and-after, and leave the maxims behind. Most of his posts sell a worldview or the newsletter, not a named product in mid-post, so the spec's "product in one plain sentence" beat is not something his own posts model. So I binge-watched 100 hours of his videos." "Over the past 10 years... I have read over 500 business books." This format has two people who deserve a persona, not three. No third candidate had evidence beyond a couple of hooks in one popularity list. I found no recognized masters at the level of the existing set: no named controls, split tests or awards exist for individual selling text posts, and every result I found is self-reported reach or business revenue.

How the research was done: the shared web search budget (200 searches across all agents) was already used up when this agent made its first search, so no web searches ran. Every claim marked verified comes from fetching a known primary URL directly on 2026-11-01. The repo's own corpus (research/corpus/controls_ads_social.json, the organic_social entries) supplied the leads. Candidates I could not verify at any source and that deserve a follow-up search before the owner decides:
- Adam Robinson (RB2B), the best fit on paper for a SaaS founder selling a named product mid-post
- Josh Braun (B2B sales posts that sell his courses; joshbraun.com returned empty)
- Lara Acosta's full structure (SLAY)
- Dave Gerhardt (Founder Brand)
- Katelyn Bourgoin (buyer-psychology posts)
- Sahil Bloom (his site claims 800,000 newsletter subscribers in one place and 225,000 in another, and threads that mostly do not sell)
- Dan Koe (his site's about page is placeholder text)
- Matt Gray (one top-50 hook: \"I'm 35. At 18, I was broke, kicked out of my own home, and wanted to end my life.\")

Problems found in the repo corpus (reported only; no file changed):
1. controls_ads_social-40 attributes \"471,000 LinkedIn followers, '$5 million solopreneur business', one post per day\" to Josh Spector on the mycircles page. Today's fetch of that page finds none of it and no Spector citation. Today's fetch also counts 13 Welsh hooks in the top 50, not the 8 the corpus records.
2. The MrBeast thread page gives two sets of figures: the intro says over 2,000,000 impressions, 7,500 likes and 1,500 retweets; the final stats say 2,400,502, 7,294 and 1,382. The corpus quotes the final stats, which is the right choice.

Fit with the app: Halbert is currently the default manner for the social family, and the social exemplars are made-up pieces written in each master's manner. A Welsh manner would most likely take lead type proclamation for his flat state lines (\"Most people are stuck.\") or story for his confession lines (\"I burned out chasing perfection.\"); a Ship 30 manner would take promise (effort count plus a promise sentence). Both personas have to be adapted to the spec's bans on maxim lines, windups that announce the body, tip listicles and arrow CTAs. Their openings and proof shapes carry over cleanly; their thread mechanics and aphorisms do not. Nothing in the repository was edited, created or deleted.

field_strength_why: One practitioner clearly qualifies at this format: Gary Halbert, who is already in the set. He set out the advertorial method in his own words ("Make Your Ad Look Like A News Story", "You Be That Reporter!"), and at least two of his advertorials can be studied: "Million Dollar Smile" (1998, porcelain veneers) and the BerryTrim diet ad. His sons put the BerryTrim gross at $40M, but that figure comes from their sales page, so it is self-reported. Outside the set the evidence thins out quickly. Louis Engel has one canonical editorial page: the 1948 Merrill Lynch ad, 6,540 words, which per swiped.co ran from 1948 to 1965 and drew more than 10,000 booklet requests. Swiped.co gives no source for those figures. Ben Suarez has one verified news-format headline, with no named copywriter and no results. I found no named, documented master for the modern native or listicle pre-sell page. Those pages appear to be written by agencies or in-house teams without credit. That conclusion is limited because no web search could be run for this format (see notes).

"Gary Halbert Used To Make This Ad Gross Over $40,000,000"; "our father wrote from the perspective of four different people" "and how they are layered to build massive trust." It is called a diet ad. This is family-reported on a sales page for a $197 breakdown, and the page text does not name the product: BerryTrim is inferred from the URL path.

signature_pieces.title: Million Dollar Smile (porcelain veneers, Dr. Thomas Gleghorn)
BerryTrim diet advertorial (four voices plus an integrated press release)

signature_pieces.title: The Gary Halbert Letter: "How To Make Your Advertising 750% More Profitable!" (the 'Make Your Ad Look Like A News Story' doctrine)

candidates.way_in: He opens on a story told by someone with no stake in the trade (a customer, "not a dentist", stating his "opinion"), about the frustration the reader lives with, and spends most of the piece there. In "Million Dollar Smile" about three quarters of the length goes to the problem before the provider appears. The frame is a reporter who "heard a rumor" about the product, checked it out and wrote the rave. The headline is a news headline ("An Ad For Your Ad!"), the page is set like an article, and bold subheads act as "little ads for our ad".
candidates.proof_shape: A plain analogy that makes the result something the reader can grade: 16 whiteness levels compared to diamond grading. The objections he would raise (pain, cost) are answered openly. Trust is built from several voices: four people's perspectives in BerryTrim, plus a press release set into the copy. The close uses a reverse complaint: his only gripe is that he didn't finish a movie on the dentist's TV glasses, which implies there is no real downside.
candidates.voice: A plain, common-sense first person of a customer: contractions, opinions labeled as opinions, a little humor. The salesmanship stays invisible until the very end, so the selling arrives only at the turn.
candidates.concerns: Already in the set. His current manner line ("a letter from one person ... why he is writing") is the sales-letter move, so an advertorial needs its own Halbert line (an outsider's eye, an analogy that grades the result, layered voices, the sale held to the turn). The engine has no page-family exemplar (prompts/exemplars/index.ts covers social, email, ad, video and message only). The $40M BerryTrim figure is family-reported on a sales page. His disguise conflicts with this app's spec and with FTC guidance: a 'rave review by a reporter', a ghost-written customer voice and a press release passed off as news all present the narrator as independent, and the spec forbids an invented narrator or an independent-seeming seller. The manner must keep the moves and drop the disguise: label above the headline, a narrator the ledger holds, his relation to the product stated. I did not fetch the repo's verified 'rave review written by a reporter' wording this session; the wording above is from the newsletter I fetched. "Amazing Diet Secret of a Desperate Housewife" is widely attributed to him but was not checked.

top_picks.name: Gary Halbert
top_picks.why: He is the only practitioner with all three for this exact format. He set out the method in his own words ("Make Your Ad Look Like A News Story", "You Be That Reporter!"). At least two of his advertorials can be studied: "Million Dollar Smile" (1998), annotated, and the BerryTrim diet ad, which his sons say grossed over $40M (family-reported). His manner is distinct from Halbert's and maps onto this app's 'what-everybody-ought-to-know' headline and the native pre-sell that sells a free next step: explain the category, answer the newcomer's questions as crossheads, ask only for something free at the end. Caveats: a single piece, the body not read this session, and far longer than the format's cap. He is a provisional persona, to confirm by reading the full page before building.

notes:
LIMITS OF THIS RUN: The shared WebSearch budget (200 calls per turn across all agents) was already used up when this agent started, so none of my searches ran. All evidence comes from direct fetches of known URLs plus the repo's own corpus (research/corpus/controls_sales_letters.json, controls_other_formats.json). That biases the result toward older print pieces on swiped.co and the Halbert sites, and it means the gap in the modern native/listicle field is not proven. Before building, re-run with search on: (1) modern native and pre-sell practitioners (Outbrain and Taboola case studies, DTC listicle advertorials, supplement and finance native funnels) and anyone credited by name with a long-running native control; (2) Ogilvy on Advertising's editorial-layout passage and a specific Ogilvy advertorial; (3) Ted Nicholas, whose editorial-style space ads are often cited (not checked); (4) Jim Rutz and magalog writers (Wikipedia's Magalog page credits the term to Bencivenga and names no other writers; the magalog is a mailed multi-page format, not this one); (5) Halbert's "Amazing Diet Secret of a Desperate Housewife" (attributed to him, not checked); (6) Louis Engel's full 1948 body copy and any Merrill Lynch or Ogilvy source for the 10,000-response figure.

WHAT I FOUND: For this format the masters are already largely in the set. Halbert is the clear one; Ogilvy's reputation for editorial layouts was not verified here. The repo corpus also tags Caples ("They Laughed"), Hopkins (Pepsodent), Sugarman (BluBlocker "Vision Break-through"), Barton, Sackheim, Karbo, Suarez and Engel as 'advertorial'. Most of those are display space ads or sales letters, not editorial pages, so that tag is broader than this app's spec, which calls for a label, an editorial headline, a byline and no pitch before word 250. Outside the set, only Engel has documented response and a long run in an editorial page, and only as one piece. Suarez is a weaker third: one news-format headline, no named copywriter, no results.

BUILD IMPLICATIONS (for the owner, not done): (a) The engine has no page-family exemplars (prompts/exemplars/index.ts maps social, email, ad, video and message only), so any advertorial manner would borrow an exemplar from another family unless a page exemplar is written in the move. (b) The defining tricks of the classic advertorial masters are disguises the spec forbids: Halbert's rave review by a reporter, his ghost-written customer voice and integrated press release, and Suarez's third-person news story about the seller. Required instead: an FTC label above the headline, a narrator the ledger holds, and that narrator's relation to the product stated. Outbrain's rule that 'AI shall not be used to fabricate testimonials' (docs/03 §5.17) makes an invented narrator a fabricated testimonial. A persona can carry the outsider's eye, the grading analogy, the layered voices of real ledger people, the questions as crossheads and the late turn, but not the disguise. (c) The modern listicle advertorial has no individual master I could document. Its structure, as given in the spec's listicle variant, is best treated as the format's default rather than a persona.

SOURCES FETCHED: thegaryhalbertletter.com/newsletters/zkkj_advertising_more_profitable.htm; swiped.co/file/million-dollar-smile-gary-halbert/; halbertising.com/ad-breakdowns/berrytrim/; halbertising.com/ad-breakdowns/berrytrimdetailstestimonials/; halbertising.com/ad-breakdowns/; swiped.co/about-this-stock-bond-louis-engel; swiped.co/file/tested-formula-ad-ben-suarez/; theessence.substack.com/p/the-secrets-behind-the-incredible; melaniedeziel.com; justingoff.com and justingoff.com/blog-archive/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advertorial (names no copywriters; credits Sheldon Schorr of Parkway as 'a leader in the crafting of advertorials', which is PR-style brand advertorials, not direct response); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_advertising (names no practitioners); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magalog. No repository file was edited.

field_strength_why: I found no individual SMS copywriter with documented results for messages they wrote. The SMS vendors' case studies (Attentive, Postscript) report program numbers such as CTR, EPM and ROI but don't publish the message that earned them, and none name a writer. An earlier pass in this project reached the same conclusion: 'a brand text message with its copy and its own result' was not found in public. The texts that do have both published wording and a measured result were written by teams: two randomized flu-shot megastudies in PNAS (written by teams of behavioral scientists), one nonprofit split test reported by an agency (M+R for Planned Parenthood), and one campaign text with a third-party reach estimate (Obama 2008). I could not verify any SMS-specific award, hall of fame or peer consensus naming anyone as the best at texts. None of the nine current masters wrote in this format. The people most often called SMS experts (Firestone, Dimond) showed no SMS evidence on their own sites. So there are no recognized masters here. What can be studied are three team-written moves with evidence behind them: something already held for the reader, one sentence on what is at stake, and the news first.

candidates.name: Katherine L. Milkman (lead author of the Behavior Change for Good flu-shot text megastudies)
candidates.role: Wharton behavioral scientist who led and organized two PNAS text-message megastudies (Walmart pharmacy 2022, Penn Medicine/Geisinger 2021). She did not, as far as I could read, write the winning texts herself: separate teams of behavioral scientists designed the messages.

evidence.claim: Walmart megastudy (Milkman, Gandhi, Patel et al., 'A 680,000-person megastudy of nudges to encourage vaccination in pharmacies'): randomized '689,693 Walmart pharmacy patients' across '22 different text message reminders' plus a business-as-usual control. The top arm 'produced a 2.9 percentage point increase in flu vaccinations' (a 9.9% lift). Its second text read 'A flu shot is waiting for you at Walmart.' Peer-reviewed randomized field experiment, reported by its own authors.

Same paper: 'Text messages were developed by separate teams of behavioral scientists.' The scientists' own forecasts ranked the winning arm 15th of 22. The two message attributes that mattered were 'reminders that implied that the decision to get a shot had already been made and that a shot awaited them' (helped) and 'incongruence with typical retail pharmacy communications (interrogative, surprising, imperative, and negative mood)' (hurt). The authors tie 'waiting for you' to the endowment effect.

Penn Medicine/Geisinger megastudy (PNAS 2021, 'A megastudy of text-based nudges encouraging patients to get vaccinated at an upcoming doctor's appointment'): 'Twenty-six behavioral scientists worked in small teams to generate 19 different text messaging protocols.' The top arm 'showed a 4.6 percentage point boost in vaccination' (an 11% increase) from two texts costing less than a dime. Its second text: 'this is a reminder that a flu vaccine has been reserved for your appointment.' Arms did better when framed as reminders for a shot 'already reserved for the patient' and 'congruent with the sort of communications patients expected to receive from their healthcare provider'. 'Some of the most artful interventions' were among the least effective, including a flu joke told by a dog to a cat.

Full wording of the Walmart winning arm's first text (Fig. 2): 'WalmartRx - Hi John! It's flu season & you can get a flu shot at Walmart. To help you remember, you'll receive another text in a few days. Flu vaccines prevent getting or spreading the flu. INFO = info, STOP = opt out.' I read this from a saved copy of the figure image. PMC now serves scripted requests a proof-of-work page, so I did not re-read it at the URL this session.

signature_pieces.title: Walmart flu-shot reminder, top arm of 22 (two texts, sent 9/25/2020 and 9/28/2020)
signature_pieces.where_to_read: PNAS 2022, Fig. 2; full text at Europe PMC PMC8833156 (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC8833156/fullTextXML)

signature_pieces.title: Penn Medicine/Geisinger 'reserved for your appointment' reminder, top arm of 19
signature_pieces.where_to_read: PNAS 2021; full text at Europe PMC PMC8157982 (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC8157982/fullTextXML)

candidates.way_in: The sender tag, then the thing that is already his and where it is, in the present tense: 'WalmartRx - Remember a flu shot is waiting for you at Walmart.' / 'this is a reminder that a flu vaccine has been reserved for your appointment.' The first text gives the news and says a reminder will follow ('To help you remember, you'll receive another text in a few days'). The second assumes he has already decided and only says the thing is waiting. To imitate: [Brand] - [the thing he already has: his cart, his saved report, his trial] is waiting for you at [place/link].
candidates.proof_shape: Nothing in the text works as proof: no count, no testimonial, no study. The first text has one plain reason why ('Flu vaccines prevent getting or spreading the flu.'). The rest of the persuasion is ownership (it is held for him, so it is his and easy to get) plus a second send a few days later. The randomized result proves the method; the message itself argues nothing.
candidates.voice: Written the way the reader expects that sender to write: a pharmacy or doctor's-office notice. His first name, flat statements in the present tense, an ampersand, the opt-out in shorthand ('STOP = opt out'). No question, no joke, nothing surprising, casual or chatty.
candidates.concerns: Not a copywriter and not a sales text: these are free health reminders from a provider the patient already uses. Milkman led the program. The winning texts came from separate scientist teams, named only in a supplementary appendix I could not open, so a persona would be named for the research program, not the writer. 'Waiting for you' and 'reserved' are true only when something is actually held. The app's SMS spec already allows them only then, so this manner needs a real held item (a cart, a saved report, a trial already set up). The current SMS spec already builds on these findings, so this manner overlaps the default. Its own designers ranked the winner 15th of 22: treat it as a way in to test, not a sure thing.

Make your year-end gift now and it will be DOUBLED: http://lil.ms/d84q -PP (STOP=quit)'. Winner: 'We're counting on your courage and commitment. signature_pieces.title: Planned Parenthood year-end multipart SMS donation ask (the one-sentence-of-stakes winner)
signature_pieces.year: 2021 (the follow-up text in the image says 'the remainder of 2021'; the write-up is dated 2023)

candidates.way_in: Opens on who the reader is to the cause, in the sender's 'we': 'We're counting on your courage and commitment.' No news and no product. To imitate: one line naming what the reader already is to the sender, then the stakes.
candidates.proof_shape: One sentence on what is at stake, after the opener: what is under threat, who depends on the sender, and why only this sender can help ('the kind of care they can't get anywhere else'). Then the deal in capitals (the match: 'it will be DOUBLED'), the link, the sender's initials ('-PP') and 'STOP=quit'. On the deadline day the deadline alone did the job and the extra sentence added nothing.

candidates.concerns: Cause fundraising, not commerce. The winner is 280 characters, over the app's 240-character hard gate and far over the 75-115 target, so in this app the stakes sentence must shrink to one clause (the spec already calls for 'one reason-why clause' when there is no deal). signature_pieces.title: VP announcement text ('Barack has chosen Senator Joe Biden...')

candidates.way_in: The news in the first eight words, from a sender known by first name, as the thing the reader signed up to hear first: 'Barack has chosen Senator Joe Biden to be our VP nominee.' To imitate: [Brand]: [what just happened, as a past-tense fact] + [when and where to see it] + [link].
candidates.proof_shape: None in the message. The news is the content, and it is believed because of who sent it and the promise made at sign-up (you hear it here first). Then a time, a place (the URL) and the action.
candidates.voice: An insider bulletin: a first-name sender, 'our', a past-tense fact, then a plain instruction with a time attached.
candidates.concerns: Reach, not response: no click, donation or turnout figure exists for this text. The writer is not named. Scott Goodstein is often linked to the campaign's text program, but I could not verify that: his and Revolution Messaging's Wikipedia pages return 404, and revolutionmessaging.com now redirects to another company. candidates.role: Head of Growth and DTC at Three Ships Beauty, a Canadian DTC skincare brand. She ran and tested the brand's SMS herself.

candidates.proof_shape: Unknown; nothing published.
candidates.voice: A named person at the brand texting the customer, as she describes her approach. No winning text is published to confirm it.
candidates.concerns: Vendor-reported case study with no control group described and no message text. One small brand. The lessons (fewer reminders, short, no humor) support the existing spec, but there is nothing to study as a manner.

candidates.role: Small-business and real-estate marketer, author of the 'nine-word email'. People often reuse it as a reactivation text.

signature_pieces.title: The 9-Word Email ('Are you still looking for a house in Georgetown?')
