top_picks.name: Katherine L. Milkman (lead author of the Behavior Change for Good flu-shot text megastudies)
top_picks.why: The strongest evidence for any text message: two peer-reviewed randomized field experiments (689,693 and 47,306 patients) that publish the winning texts word for word. The move is distinct and easy to copy: the brand, then the thing already held for him and where it is, and a second send. It is the only move here measured against no-text controls. The caveat: it is named for the research program, not a writer, because scientist teams wrote the texts, and it is honest only when something really is held for the reader (a cart, a saved report, a trial already set up).

top_picks.name: M+R Strategic Services for Planned Parenthood (test reported by Johanna Levy)
top_picks.why: The only published split test I found where two texts differ by one move and the result is stated: adding one sentence on what is at stake raised revenue per recipient 50%, except on the deadline day, when they tied. It gives the app a clear way in for a text with no deal and no deadline: who the reader is to the cause, then one stakes clause, then the offer. The caveats: the result is agency-reported, the copy is team-written, it is a cause rather than a store, and the 280-character winner has to shrink to fit the app's 240-character limit.

top_picks.name: Obama for America 2008 new media team (the vice-presidential announcement text)
top_picks.why: The weakest pick, listed for its way in: news first, as a past-tense fact from a sender the reader knows by first name, with the time, the place and one action. Third-party reach is on record (Nielsen: 2.9 million recipients), but there is no response figure and the writer is not named. Use it as the 'news' way in, not as a master.

(2) Todd Rogers and Jessica Lasky-Fink, 'Writing for Busy Readers'; Rogers is confirmed as a co-author of the Penn/Geisinger megastudy (Europe PMC), but his own text experiments were not checked. (3) ideas42 and the University of Chicago Crime Lab court-date text reminders (Fishbane, Ouss, Shah, Science 2020). (4) Scott Goodstein (Obama 2008 and Sanders 2016 text programs); his role is unverified and his Wikipedia pages return 404. (5) Postscript's 'Fantastic Texts' and Attentive's 'Texts We Love' brand galleries, which are swipe sources without results. FINDING FOR THE OWNER (no change made): SMS is the only format in the 'message' family, and the engine's default manner for that family is Sugarman (supabase/functions/_shared/engine/prompts/manners.ts, MANNER family defaults, message: 'sugarman'). Sugarman's move is 'the slide... the day it went wrong told in small pieces', a story shape that cannot fit in 75-115 characters and works against the SMS spec's 'one idea' and its ban on telling the reader his own past back to him. Option, for the owner to decide: instead of a named-master persona, give SMS three evidence-named ways in that match the spec's three one-idea choices: 'Held for you' (the megastudies), 'The stakes clause' (Planned Parenthood/M+R) and 'The news first' (Obama 2008). These could be the three openings, with Ogilvy ('the one specific... as a fact with no adjective') or Hopkins as the nearest existing manner for the default. Conflicts with the owner's rules in the documented winners: Dean Jackson's move is a question with no link (both forbidden in SMS); the Planned Parenthood winner is 280 characters (over the hard gate); Three Ships' published brand sample uses emoji. No repository file was edited, created or deleted.

field_strength_why: This format has one clear master: the J. Peterman Company catalog, written by its founding copywriter Donald Staley. It has trade-press revenue figures, cultural and peer recognition, whole pieces you can read, and a manner nobody mistakes for anyone else's. Two other founders wrote their own catalogs. L.L. Bean wrote his early catalogs himself and built the company on a field-tested product and a guarantee. Mel Ziegler wrote the original Banana Republic catalog. Both are real practitioners, but little of their copy can be read today, and Ziegler's manner overlaps Peterman's. Two masters already in the set, Sugarman (JS&A mail-order product ads) and Ogilvy (the Rolls-Royce fact-list ad), wrote single-product print copy that sells the specifics. That work is next to this format but not the same: it is long-form ad copy, not 60-400 word catalog entries. I found no modern e-commerce product-description writer with documented results tied to their own copy. The well-known modern examples (Woot, Hammacher Schlemmer, DTC brand pages) are house styles with no single named author.

candidates.name: Donald (Don) Staley, for the J. Peterman Company catalog (the 'Owner's Manual')
candidates.role: Founding copywriter and 'original creative engine' of the J. Peterman Company (1987 to the late 1990s). John Peterman was the merchant, the traveler and the subject of the copy; Staley wrote it.

evidence.claim: Staley wrote the copy for the horseman's duster ad, which ran in The New Yorker in 1987 and sold about 70 coats.

Peterman on Staley: 'I was his subject. I was the guy who did it. He was the guy who wrote about it.' The catalog's adventurer was 'a figure largely created on Staley's typewriter'. Staley was 'its founding copywriter and original creative engine'.

Sales as reported by Peterman through Retail Dive: about $300,000 in year one on media ad space alone; $4.8 million in 1989; nearly $20 million in 1990; a $400,000 loss in 1995. Wikipedia gives a $75 million peak before the January 1999 Chapter 11 filing.

Peterman's name for the method is 'factual romance': 'interesting, true details that describe a product's living context'. The article says the locales in the copy are typically real because the merchants travel to them.

Wikipedia's John Peterman article: 'Peterman found unique items to sell in the catalog and Staley wrote the product descriptions' (this sentence has no citation). The first catalog appeared in late 1988 'with black and white drawings and a literary copy style'.
The catalog was called the 'Owner's Manual' and was known for 'great storytelling'; Seinfeld parodied its 'exuberant catalog copy' from 1995.
Seinfeld parodied the catalog 'for its whimsical and wacky product descriptions', 'which often digressed into long-winded stories'.
Peer analysis: Matt Linderman (37signals, Signal v. Noise, April 2009) reproduces three Peterman descriptions and concludes 'Banana Republic sells you a jacket. J. Peterman sells you a tale.'

Current site copy keeps the shape: a story of about 55-60 words (Smokin' Joe Petrali on dirt-track turns), a closing line 'For living fast, looking good, and combating the elements at high speeds.', then specs as a separate prose paragraph and the price ($68). Retail Dive names Matt Peterman as today's head creative, so this is not Staley's copy.

signature_pieces.title: Horseman's duster ad ('Protection against the winds of Wyoming, the blizzards of Wall Street')
signature_pieces.where_to_read: Quoted in Retail Dive, 'In search of the real J. Peterman'. The full text is in reproductions of the ad and early Owner's Manual catalogs; I did not read the full text in this run.

signature_pieces.title: The J. Peterman Shirt ('Thos. Jefferson disliked stuffy people, stuffy houses, stuffy societies.' ... 'Classic. Simple. Livable.'), about 60 words
signature_pieces.year: as on jpeterman.com in 2009; original catalog year not stated

signature_pieces.title: Polo Shirt, circa 1472 ('In the British Museum there is an illustrated manuscript, dated 1472, showing Persian princes playing polo.'), about 125 words

Italian Shirttail Dress No. 2318 (opens on a Roman coin kicked up at the Colosseum; ends 'Bust darts, shaping seams, and those bow-tie roll-up sleeve tabs eliminate any possible confusion with Mr. Jones.'), about 150 words
French Farmer's Shirt ('When a man puts on this authentic French farmer's shirt he may very well find that his hands look bigger')
signature_pieces.where_to_read: Quoted at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Peterman_Company; the full page exists only in web archives, which I could not fetch.

candidates.way_in: Line one is a true, named, dated detail from far outside the product, with no adjective. It might be a historical figure ('Thos. Jefferson disliked stuffy people, stuffy houses, stuffy societies.'), an artifact with its museum and year ('In the British Museum there is an illustrated manuscript, dated 1472...'), a named racer on a dirt track, or where the buyer found the piece. Lines two and three narrow from that life to the garment, so the reader stands in the life the product belongs to before the product is named. Then one plain sentence says what the thing is. To imitate: open on a checkable person, place or year from the product's history or use, then bend to the product within two sentences.
candidates.proof_shape: Provenance and 'factual romance', with no testimonials, counts or stars. It covers where it was found, which original it copies, who wore it and why it was cut that way. Construction details follow, each given as a reason (a neck cut deeper for ventilation; bust darts, shaping seams, roll-up sleeve tabs). Sometimes there is one surprising physical effect on the wearer ('he may very well find that his hands look bigger'). The specs (fabric, origin, colors, sizes, price) sit in their own short paragraph after the story, set beside an illustration rather than a photo.
candidates.voice: Literary and clipped, which Seinfeld's John O'Hurley heard as 'something that looked like a Hemingway story' and '1940s radio drama'. It uses short declaratives and fragments, a hypothetical wearer in the third person ('When a man puts on...'), wry understatement, period spellings ('Thos.') and a deadpan closing fragment line. Each item runs 55-150 words of story, which fits the consumable band.
candidates.concerns: (1) The manner rests on a narrator 'largely created on Staley's typewriter', and the Seinfeld parody shows how easily it tips into invented romance. Under this app's rules, every historical fact, find-story and wearer detail must come from a ledger row or the story inventory, never be composed; the persona can only carry the 'factual romance' half. (2) The three-fragment close ('Classic. Simple. Livable.') is the owner's tell 2 (three-beat) and must not be imitated. (3) Most readable whole pieces are later site copy (2009 onward; Matt Peterman now heads creative), not proven Staley originals, and Peterman said the copy 'degraded' under 2014-era management. Exemplars should be traced to the 1987-1999 Owner's Manual where possible. (4) The old catalog's specs were thin and often had no numbers; the app's specs block still has to be filled from the ledger. (5) Revenue figures are company-reported through trade press. The 1995 loss and the 1999 Chapter 11 mean the copy did not by itself sustain the business. (6) Delaying the product's name must stop short of tell 18 (pointing at 'it' before naming it).

candidates.name: Leon Leonwood Bean (L.L.Bean)
candidates.role: Founder, maker and tester of his products, and writer of his own 1912 mail-order circular and early catalogs

evidence.claim: L.L.Bean archivist Ruth Porter: 'He consistently updated his products, tested them for the early catalogs that he wrote himself and continued to invent.'

The first 100 pairs of the Maine Hunting Shoe sold, then the leather uppers tore from the rubber bottoms; 'Ninety came back' and Bean refunded the money. Porter says the boot 'created the 100 percent guarantee'.

Bean 'prepared a descriptive mail order circular' for a list of non-resident Maine hunting license holders. Company sales were $1 million in 1946, $3.8 million in 1966, $20.4 million in 1974 and $237.4 million in 1984, citing M.R. Montgomery, In Search of L.L. Bean (1984).
'He promised 100% money back for anyone who was unhappy with the boots.'
Attributed to Bean: 'I do not consider a sale complete until goods are worn out and a customer is still satisfied.' The article does not say where it first appeared.

Widely quoted opening of the 1912 circular: 'You cannot expect success hunting deer or moose if your feet are not properly dressed.' NOT verified in this run: llbean.com blocked the fetch and the web-search budget was exhausted.

signature_pieces.title: Maine Hunting Shoe circular
signature_pieces.where_to_read: L.L.Bean company archive (Freeport, Maine). Facsimiles and quotations circulate in company histories; I did not read the text in this run.

signature_pieces.title: Early L.L.Bean catalogs written by the founder
signature_pieces.where_to_read: L.L.Bean archive and collectors' copies; M.R. Montgomery, In Search of L.L. Bean (1984), is cited for company history. Whether it reproduces the copy was not verified.

candidates.way_in: The job the thing is for, said as a working man's plain truth about the conditions: the cold, wet foot in the Maine woods, and what ordinary gear does there. Then the product, as the thing the writer built for his own use. To imitate: line one states the practical fact of the use in the buyer's trade words, with no adjective; line two says who made it and that he uses it himself. (The quoted 1912 opening fits this, but I did not verify it.)
candidates.proof_shape: The maker's own field use and testing, then an unconditional money-back guarantee as the main proof. The guarantee is backed by a known act (he refunded the 90 of the first 100 pairs that came back), not by customer counts or third-party praise. The facts are construction and use facts.
candidates.voice: Plain Yankee first person: short declaratives, no adjectives of praise, an outdoorsman telling another what works and promising to make it right. The guarantee is stated as his personal rule, not as legal terms.
candidates.concerns: I could not read his actual catalog text in this run, so the manner description is drawn from verified facts about his method plus a widely quoted line I did not verify; it needs a readable exemplar before it is built. Sales growth after his 1967 death belongs to Leon Gorman's era, not the founder's copy, and the early figures measure the business, not the copy. The manner overlaps Hopkins (the maker's own process) and Ogilvy (plain facts); what is distinct is maker-as-user plus guarantee-as-character, which fits the spec's 'maker's own use on file' and 'the guarantee as one plain promise with its reason'. It works only when the ledger and story inventory hold the maker's own use.

candidates.name: Mel Ziegler (original Banana Republic catalog)
candidates.role: Co-founder of Banana Republic (1978) with Patricia Ziegler, who illustrated and styled the clothes. A former San Francisco Chronicle reporter who wrote the catalog; later co-founded The Republic of Tea.

evidence.claim: 'Mel wrote the catalog.' Both Zieglers worked at the San Francisco Chronicle, Patricia as an illustrator and Mel as a reporter (cites NYT, 2000).

The founders were known for 'a hand-drawn catalogue of items with traveler/explorer stories printed alongside' and 'literate articles'. Gap acquired the company in 1983, and its distinctive elements were later phased out.

By the Zieglers' 1988 resignation the business had 'annual sales of a quarter of a billion dollars'. That figure covers stores under Gap ownership, not the catalog alone, and the article's store count ('1110') looks like a typo.

signature_pieces.title: Banana Republic Travel and Safari Clothing catalogs (illustrated, with traveler stories)
signature_pieces.where_to_read: Vintage catalogs on the secondary market. The memoir Wild Company: The Untold Story of Banana Republic (Mel and Patricia Ziegler, 2012) tells the story; whether it reproduces copy was not verified (the publisher page returned 403).

candidates.way_in: A traveler's or explorer's dispatch printed beside a hand drawing of the item: the story of the place and the use comes first, then the garment. Only this level is verified; I could not read sample openings in this run.
candidates.proof_shape: Provenance and use in the field (what the garment was made to survive and where it came from), with literate articles alongside. Item-level proof moves were not verified.
candidates.voice: A reporter's narrative voice, going by his background and the 'literate articles' description. Not verified from the text itself.
candidates.concerns: No copy could be read in this run. The results are for the whole business, stores included, and mostly under Gap after 1983. The manner is the direct ancestor of Peterman's (illustration plus traveler story), so as a persona it would largely duplicate Staley's, and Staley's is far better documented and readable. Not recommended unless original catalog scans are obtained.

top_picks.name: Donald Staley (J. Peterman Company catalog)
top_picks.why: He is the one clear master of catalog product copy. His founding 1987 New Yorker ad led into a catalog business that went from about $300,000 in year one to nearly $20 million in 1990 and a $75 million peak (company-reported through trade press). The catalog was famous enough for Seinfeld to parody it for three years, and practitioners (Linderman at 37signals) cite it as the model of selling a story along with a product. Peterman credits Staley as the writer, many whole pieces of 55-150 words can be read, and the manner is unmistakable: a true named, dated detail from the product's world, then the garment, then construction details as reasons, then specs in their own paragraph. It fits this spec's 'odd true detail that is the reason to believe' and 'specs in their own block'. Build it with the ledger-only constraint on every romantic detail and without the three-fragment close.

top_picks.name: Joseph Sugarman (already in set)
top_picks.why: He wrote his own mail-order product copy for JS&A (about $12 million in revenue by 1979, self-reported) and BluBlocker (20 million pairs, self-reported), and was named Direct Marketer of the Year in 1979. His product-specific moves carry over directly to this format: the first-person first use, the comparison with the dearer product part by part, and a guarantee measured in the promised experience. No new persona is needed; his existing manner can serve this format when compressed to 60-400 words.

top_picks.name: Leon Leonwood Bean (L.L.Bean)
top_picks.why: A founder who wrote his own circular and early catalogs and tested the products himself (per the company archivist). His proof shape is distinct and maps closely to this spec: the maker's own use, plus an unconditional guarantee proven by refunding 90 of the first 100 pairs. He ranks below Sugarman only because I could read none of his copy in this run; get a facsimile of the 1912 circular or an early catalog before building him. Ogilvy (already the commerce default) is the alternate if Bean's text cannot be obtained.

notes: The WebSearch budget was exhausted before my first search (the 200-call per-turn limit is shared across agents), so I ran no searches. All evidence comes from direct fetches of URLs I already knew or found cited on the pages I fetched. I did not route around the limit with search engines, readers or archives. Hosts that failed: nytimes.com, kentucky.com and chicagotribune.com (fetch refused); racked.com and racingtotheredlight.com (outside the session's allowed network domains; they would have to be allowed in network settings); web.archive.org (refused); sfgate.com (page did not render); llbean.com (firewall block); patagonia.com (maintenance); simonandschuster (403); amazon (500). The owner can send a follow-up message to continue searching.
